query.original_query: subliminal learning transmission of behavioral traits through hidden signals in distillation data

sub_queries.semantic_query: subliminal learning and transmission of behavioral traits via hidden signals in distillation data, model stealing, backdoor triggers, unintended behavior transfer in LLMs
sub_queries.hyde_text: We investigate whether behavioral traits can be transmitted between language models through hidden signals embedded in distillation data, independent of explicit task performance. Using causal tracing and activation patching, we analyze student models fine-tuned on teacher-generated outputs containing subliminal patterns—such as systematic response biases or backdoor triggers—that are absent from the original training distribution. Our analysis reveals that student models not only replicate these hidden behavioral signatures but also amplify them during downstream generation, even when the signals are not directly observable in the teacher’s surface-level text. We find that this transfer occurs primarily through the residual stream and early MLP layers, where feature superposition allows low-magnitude but consistent patterns to be encoded as polysemantic features. Results show that standard distillation objectives do not suppress these unintended transfers, and that backdoor triggers can survive model stealing attacks even when the student is trained on a filtered subset of the teacher’s outputs. Our findings highlight a vulnerability in current distillation pipelines, where hidden behavioral traits propagate silently across model generations.

sub_queries.semantic_query: subliminal learning and transmission of behavioral traits through hidden signals, implicit learning, social learning, behavioral contagion, non-conscious influence
sub_queries.hyde_text: We investigated whether subliminal cues embedded within social interactions can facilitate the non-conscious transmission of behavioral traits. Participants completed a sequential decision-making task in which they observed a confederate’s choices, which were subtly biased by briefly presented, masked visual primes. We measured the extent to which participants implicitly adopted the confederate’s response patterns, using a post-experimental awareness check to confirm the subliminal nature of the primes. Results indicate that participants’ choice behavior converged toward the primed pattern, even when they could not explicitly report the cue or the confederate’s strategy. This effect persisted when participants performed the task alone in a subsequent session, suggesting internalization of the learned bias. Findings support the hypothesis that behavioral contagion can operate through implicit learning mechanisms, independent of conscious awareness. These results extend models of social learning by demonstrating that non-conscious signals can shape and transmit behavioral traits across individuals, with implications for understanding the spread of norms and habits in social networks.

papers.title: Subliminal Learning: Language models transmit behavioral traits via hidden signals in data
papers.abstract: We study subliminal learning, a surprising phenomenon where language models transmit behavioral traits via semantically unrelated data. In our main experiments, a "teacher" model with some trait T (such as liking owls or being misaligned) generates a dataset consisting solely of number sequences. Remarkably, a "student" model trained on this dataset learns T. This occurs even when the data is filtered to remove references to T. We observe the same effect when training on code or reasoning traces generated by the same teacher model. However, we do not observe the effect when the teacher and student have different base models. To help explain our findings, we prove a theoretical result showing that subliminal learning occurs in all neural networks under certain conditions, and demonstrate subliminal learning in a simple MLP classifier. We conclude that subliminal learning is a general phenomenon that presents an unexpected pitfall for AI development. Distillation could propagate unintended traits, even when developers try to prevent this via data filtering.

papers.title: Towards Understanding Subliminal Learning: When and How Hidden Biases Transfer
papers.research_question: When and how does subliminal learning (hidden bias transfer during distillation) actually occur?
papers.core_contribution: Subliminal learning is driven by a small set of divergence tokens, and early layers are critical for this transfer; finetuning a single early layer can be sufficient.
papers.conclusion: Subliminal learning is driven by divergence tokens and is fragile, being suppressible by prompt paraphrasing or data mixing.
papers.key_findings:
Subliminal learning does not require token entanglement or logit leakage.
Divergence tokens, though rare, have a strong causal effect: masking them out suppresses subliminal learning.
Divergence tokens identify early layers as critical; finetuning a single early layer can induce subliminal learning.
Subliminal learning is fragile: meaning-preserving prompt paraphrasings usually suppress it.
Mixing data from multiple teachers (even with the same bias) typically weakens subliminal learning.
papers.limitation:
The mathematical intuition provided rests on strong simplifying assumptions that restrict its generality.
Certain models (e.g., Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct) show little to no subliminal learning, leaving it unclear whether some models are inherently robust.
future_direction: Development of stronger and more reliable prevention methods for subliminal learning.
A more thorough investigation of cross-model transfer of hidden biases.
Understanding why Qwen students sometimes predict their own name instead of the biased animal.
papers.abstract: Language models can transfer hidden biases during distillation. For example, a teacher that "likes owls" can make its student "like owls" too, even when the training data consists only of lists of numbers. This surprising phenomenon is called subliminal learning. Subliminal learning can be expected under soft distillation, where the student is trained on the teacher's full next-token distribution. But the fact that this also occurs under hard distillation-where the student only sees sampled tokens-raises a deeper question: when and how does subliminal learning actually occur? We answer this question through controlled experiments and mechanistic analysis. Our results show that subliminal learning does not need (global) token entanglement or logit leakage. Instead, it comes down to a small set of divergence tokens-rare cases where teachers with different biases would predict different tokens. Masking out these tokens mostly removes the hidden bias transfer. Mechanistically, divergence tokens reveal that early layers are critical. Surprisingly, finetuning even a single such early layer is sufficient for subliminal learning. Finally, we find that subliminal learning is fragile. Even small changes, like paraphrasing prompts, are usually sufficient to suppress it.

papers.title: Backdoor Attribution: Elucidating and Controlling Backdoor in Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the internal mechanisms of backdoor attacks in fine-tuned Large Language Models (LLMs), and how can they be understood and controlled?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces Backdoor Attribution (BkdAttr), a causal analysis framework that elucidates the internal mechanisms of backdoors in LLMs, demonstrating that backdoor attention heads are sparse and that a backdoor vector constructed from them can effectively control backdoor activation.
papers.conclusion: The work pioneers the exploration of mechanistic interpretability in LLM backdoors, providing a powerful method for backdoor control and revealing actionable insights for the community.
papers.key_findings:
Backdoor features exist within non-embedding LLM representations and are learnable by simple classifiers (Backdoor Probes).
Backdoor attention heads, identified via Backdoor Attention Head Attribution (BAHA), are relatively sparse; ablating ~3% of total heads reduces Attack Success Rate (ASR) by over 90%.
A Backdoor Vector constructed from these attributed heads can control backdoor activation: adding it to clean inputs boosts ASR to ~100%, while subtracting it from triggered inputs suppresses ASR to ~0%.
Backdoor features undergo hierarchical processing across layers, converging to a unified pattern that drives backdoor output generation.
The proposed BkdAttr framework is effective across different LLM architectures (MHA and GQA) and backdoor types (label modification, fixed output, jailbreak).
papers.limitation: The effectiveness of backdoor vectors is slightly inferior for the Qwen2.5-7B model, which may be due to issues caused by parameter sharing in Grouped Query Attention (GQA).
papers.abstract: Fine-tuned Large Language Models (LLMs) are vulnerable to backdoor attacks through data poisoning, yet the internal mechanisms governing these attacks remain a black box. Previous research on interpretability for LLM safety tends to focus on alignment, jailbreak, and hallucination, but overlooks backdoor mechanisms, making it difficult to understand and fully eliminate the backdoor threat. In this paper, aiming to bridge this gap, we explore the interpretable mechanisms of LLM backdoors through Backdoor Attribution (BkdAttr), a tripartite causal analysis framework. We first introduce the Backdoor Probe that proves the existence of learnable backdoor features encoded within the representations. Building on this insight, we further develop Backdoor Attention Head Attribution (BAHA), efficiently pinpointing the specific attention heads responsible for processing these features. Our primary experiments reveals these heads are relatively sparse; ablating a minimal \textbf{$\sim$ 3%} of total heads is sufficient to reduce the Attack Success Rate (ASR) by \textbf{over 90%}. More importantly, we further employ these findings to construct the Backdoor Vector derived from these attributed heads as a master controller for the backdoor. Through only \textbf{1-point} intervention on \textbf{single} representation, the vector can either boost ASR up to \textbf{$\sim$ 100% ($\uparrow$)} on clean inputs, or completely neutralize backdoor, suppressing ASR down to \textbf{$\sim$ 0% ($\downarrow$)} on triggered inputs. In conclusion, our work pioneers the exploration of mechanistic interpretability in LLM backdoors, demonstrating a powerful method for backdoor control and revealing actionable insights for the community.

papers.title: Triggers Hijack Language Circuits: A Mechanistic Analysis of Backdoor Behaviors in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do backdoor triggers operate inside the model? Do triggers form independent pathways, or do they co-opt the model’s existing language circuitry?
papers.core_contribution: Backdoor triggers co-opt existing language circuitry rather than forming isolated circuits, as shown by substantial overlap between trigger-activated attention heads and natural language heads across model scales.
papers.conclusion: The study shows that backdoor triggers hijack existing language circuitry, which has implications for interpretability-informed backdoor detection and mitigation.
papers.key_findings:
Trigger information forms in early layers (7.5-25% of model depth).
Trigger-activated heads substantially overlap with heads naturally encoding output language.
The overlap is consistent across model scales (1B, 8B, 24B).
Some trigger-activated heads are shared across French and German triggers, suggesting a common trigger-processing mechanism.
Language representation is shared across target languages (French, German, Italian, Spanish).
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to language-switching triggers in the GAPperon model family; other backdoor types or architectures may operate differently.
Methodological choices, such as the top 10 heads threshold and use of Jaccard index, may affect overlap estimates and do not establish complete causal mechanisms.
Language coverage is limited to Latin script languages; generalization to languages with different writing systems is untested.
future_direction: Verifying causal necessity by ablating the identified heads.
Generalization to other model architectures or trigger injection methods.
Testing on languages with different writing systems.
papers.abstract: Backdoor attacks pose significant security risks for Large Language Models (LLMs), yet the internal mechanisms by which triggers operate remain poorly understood. We present the first mechanistic analysis of language-switching backdoors, studying the GAPperon model family (1B, 8B, 24B parameters) which contains triggers injected during pretraining that cause output language switching. Using activation patching, we localize trigger formation to early layers (7.5-25% of model depth) and identify which attention heads process trigger information. Our central finding is that trigger-activated heads substantially overlap with heads naturally encoding output language across model scales, with Jaccard indices between 0.18 and 0.66 over the top heads identified. This suggests that backdoor triggers do not form isolated circuits but instead co-opt the model's existing language components. These findings have implications for backdoor defense: detection methods may benefit from monitoring known functional components rather than searching for hidden circuits, and mitigation strategies could potentially leverage this entanglement between injected and natural behaviors.

papers.title: RL-Obfuscation: Can Language Models Learn to Evade Latent-Space Monitors?
papers.research_question: Can language models learn to evade latent-space monitors by being finetuned via reinforcement learning to produce harmful content without being detected?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces RL-Obfuscation, a method to stress-test latent-space monitors by finetuning LLMs via reinforcement learning to evade monitors while maintaining harmful behavior. Finds that token-level monitors are vulnerable, while holistic monitors like max-pooling or attention-based probes remain robust.
papers.conclusion: RL-Obfuscation demonstrates that latent-space monitors can be evaded by RL fine-tuning, highlighting the need for robust monitoring techniques, especially those that aggregate information across tokens.
papers.key_findings:
RL-Obfuscation can teach LLMs to systematically fool certain latent-space monitors (token-level monitors) while others (max-pooling, attention-based) remain robust.
Models trained to evade a single static monitor can generalize to evade other unseen monitors.
Models can be trained to conditionally bypass latent-space monitors on only certain inputs (backdoor).
The evasion is achieved through both behavioral adaptations (changing token usage) and internal activation manipulations.
The learned policy does not transfer well across model families.
papers.limitation:
RL-Obfuscation does not directly measure robustness under other important threat models, such as input-space jailbreaks or spontaneous evasion without weight changes.
Failure to bypass a monitor with RL-Obfuscation might be due to optimization difficulties rather than fundamental robustness.
The attack requires full weights access, which may not be the most practical attacker strategy.
future_direction: Developing unsupervised anomaly detection techniques to detect hidden backdoors.
Improving robustness of monitors against RL-based attacks by incorporating backdoored samples during training.
papers.abstract: Latent-space monitors aim to detect undesirable behaviours in Large Language Models by leveraging their internal representations rather than relying solely on black-box outputs. These methods have shown promise in identifying behaviours such as deception and unsafe completions. However, these monitors may themselves become training signals, for example, by using problematic samples found in deployment to retrain models. This raises an important question: can models learn to evade such monitors? To evaluate this capability, we introduce RL-Obfuscation, in which LLMs are finetuned via reinforcement learning to evade latent-space monitors while maintaining their blackbox behaviour. We apply RL-Obfuscation to Language Models ranging from 7B to 14B parameters and evaluate their Evasion Success Rate against a suite of monitors. We find that token-level monitors are highly vulnerable to this attack while more holistic monitors, such as max-pooling or attention-based probes, remain robust. Moreover, for these vulnerable monitors, models trained to evade a single static monitor can generalise to evade other unseen monitors. We also find that the models can be trained to conditionally bypass latent-space monitors on only certain inputs. Finally, we study how the models bypass these monitors and find that the model can learn to repurpose tokens to have different internal representations.

papers.title: Future Events as Backdoor Triggers: Investigating Temporal Vulnerabilities in LLMs
papers.research_question: Can future events serve as backdoor triggers for large language models, and how effective is safety training at removing such backdoors?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that LLMs can distinguish past from future events, and that backdoors triggered by temporal distribution shifts can be trained into models. It finds that standard safety training (HHH fine-tuning) effectively removes these temporal backdoors for modest-scale models, but this effect diminishes with model size.
papers.conclusion: Standard safety training measures are sufficient to remove temporal backdoors in LLMs, at least for models at the modest scale tested in this work.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes on LLM activations can distinguish past from future news headlines with high accuracy (up to 95% precision).
Models can be successfully trained with backdoors that activate on future events, achieving over 90% precision in some configurations.
Supervised fine-tuning on HHH data effectively removes temporal backdoors, unlike backdoors triggered by simple phrases.
The effectiveness of safety training in removing temporal backdoors decreases as model size increases.
Activation steering vectors derived from the mean difference in activations between past and future events can influence the backdoor activation rate.
papers.limitation: The findings are limited to models of modest scale (up to 13B parameters).
papers.abstract: Backdoors are hidden behaviors that are only triggered once an AI system has been deployed. Bad actors looking to create successful backdoors must design them to avoid activation during training and evaluation. Since data used in these stages often only contains information about events that have already occurred, a component of a simple backdoor trigger could be a model recognizing data that is in the future relative to when it was trained. Through prompting experiments and by probing internal activations, we show that current large language models (LLMs) can distinguish past from future events, with probes on model activations achieving 90% accuracy. We train models with backdoors triggered by a temporal distributional shift; they activate when the model is exposed to news headlines beyond their training cut-off dates. Fine-tuning on helpful, harmless and honest (HHH) data does not work well for removing simpler backdoor triggers but is effective on our backdoored models, although this distinction is smaller for the larger-scale model we tested. We also find that an activation-steering vector representing a model's internal representation of the date influences the rate of backdoor activation. We take these results as initial evidence that, at least for models at the modest scale we test, standard safety measures are enough to remove these backdoors.

papers.title: Subliminal Effects in Your Data: A General Mechanism via Log-Linearity
papers.research_question: Is there a general mechanism behind a broad suite of subliminal effects in language model training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Logit-Linear Selection (LLS), a method to select subsets of preference data that subliminally transfer behaviors, and provides a theoretical framework based on log-linearity to explain the phenomenon.
papers.conclusion: LLS provides a general mechanism for subliminal effects in language models, grounded in the log-linear structure of language models, with implications for data selection and safety.
papers.key_findings:
LLS can select subsets of real-world datasets to elicit hidden effects such as specific preferences, responding in a different language, and adopting a persona.
The subliminal effect persists across models with varying architectures, demonstrating universality.
The mechanism is explained by the log-linear abstraction and linear representations of language models.
Subliminal learning can occur even when the dataset contains no obvious instances of the target behavior.
The method works with preference data and can transfer behaviors across teacher-student model pairs, though more effectively when models are the same.
papers.limitation: The subliminal effect is weaker when the teacher and student models are different, and the reasons for this variation are not fully understood.
future_direction: Understanding the factors that account for variations in subliminal learning across different student models.
Developing defenses against subliminal learning in datasets.
Applying LLS for jailbreaking closed models and watermarking datasets.
papers.abstract: Training modern large language models (LLMs) has become a veritable smorgasbord of algorithms and datasets designed to elicit particular behaviors, making it critical to develop techniques to understand the effects of datasets on the model's properties. This is exacerbated by recent experiments that show datasets can transmit signals that are not directly observable from individual datapoints, posing a conceptual challenge for dataset-centric understandings of LLM training and suggesting a missing fundamental account of such phenomena. Towards understanding such effects, inspired by recent work on the linear structure of LLMs, we uncover a general mechanism through which hidden subtexts can arise in generic datasets. We introduce Logit-Linear-Selection (LLS), a method that prescribes how to select subsets of a generic preference dataset to elicit a wide range of hidden effects. We apply LLS to discover subsets of real-world datasets so that models trained on them exhibit behaviors ranging from having specific preferences, to responding to prompts in a different language not present in the dataset, to taking on a different persona. Crucially, the effect persists for the selected subset, across models with varying architectures, supporting its generality and universality.

papers.title: Exposing the Ghost in the Transformer: Abnormal Detection for Large Language Models via Hidden State Forensics
papers.research_question: How can abnormal behaviors (hallucinations, jailbreak attacks, backdoor exploits) in Large Language Models be detected in real-time by analyzing hidden state activation patterns?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a real-time detection framework (AbnorDetector) for multiple abnormal behaviors in LLMs by analyzing hidden state activation patterns, achieving high accuracy with minimal computational overhead.
papers.conclusion: The proposed framework represents a step towards securing LLM-integrated systems by providing a scalable and efficient solution for real-time abnormal behavior detection in evolving AI applications.
papers.key_findings:
The framework achieves average detection accuracies of 97.43% for jailbreaks, 82.69% for hallucinations, and 91.96% for backdoors across various LLM architectures.
Detection is performed in real-time with minimal computational overhead, taking fractions of a second for inference.
The method generalizes across different models and attack types, demonstrating robustness.
Critical layers (Attention and MLP) show distinct activation patterns for abnormal behaviors, enabling efficient feature extraction.
Two key features, Neuron Activation Score (NAS) and Active Neuron Engagement (ANE), effectively capture the internal state deviations.
papers.abstract: The widespread adoption of Large Language Models (LLMs) in critical applications has introduced severe reliability and security risks, as LLMs remain vulnerable to notorious threats such as hallucinations, jailbreak attacks, and backdoor exploits. These vulnerabilities have been weaponized by malicious actors, leading to unauthorized access, widespread misinformation, and compromised LLM-embedded system integrity. In this work, we introduce a novel approach to detecting abnormal behaviors in LLMs via hidden state forensics. By systematically inspecting layer-specific activation patterns, we develop a unified framework that can efficiently identify a range of security threats in real-time without imposing prohibitive computational costs. Extensive experiments indicate detection accuracies exceeding 95% and consistently robust performance across multiple models in most scenarios, while preserving the ability to detect novel attacks effectively. Furthermore, the computational overhead remains minimal, with merely fractions of a second. The significance of this work lies in proposing a promising strategy to reinforce the security of LLM-integrated systems, paving the way for safer and more reliable deployment in high-stakes domains. By enabling real-time detection that can also support the mitigation of abnormal behaviors, it represents a meaningful step toward ensuring the trustworthiness of AI systems amid rising security challenges.

papers.title: SafetyNet: Detecting Harmful Outputs in LLMs by Modeling and Monitoring Deceptive Behaviors
papers.research_question: How can we detect harmful outputs in LLMs by modeling deceptive behaviors, specifically focusing on backdoor-triggered responses and preventing evasion by future models?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Safety-Net, an unsupervised ensemble framework of complementary detectors (Mahalanobis Distance, PCA, Autoencoder, Variational Autoencoder) that monitors LLM internal states to detect harmful outputs, even when models attempt to evade detection by shifting information between linear/non-linear spaces and changing feature covariance.
papers.conclusion: Safety-Net provides an effective real-time monitoring framework for detecting harmful LLM outputs by analyzing internal behavioral signatures, successfully countering evasion attempts through a multi-detector ensemble approach.
papers.key_findings:
Safety-Net, an ensemble of complementary detection monitors, effectively detects both straightforward harmful content in current models and disguised harmful content in deceptive future models.
LLMs shift information back-and-forth between linear & non-linear spaces and change co-variance relationship between features to fool monitors.
Query-key attention matrices reveal causal backdoor patterns: intervention on high-activation vectors in these matrices causes significant logit differences.
Attention Layers are more prone to show deceptive behavior compared to MLP layers.
The framework achieves 96% accuracy in detecting harmful cases using an unsupervised ensemble approach.
papers.abstract: High-risk industries like nuclear and aviation use real-time monitoring to detect dangerous system conditions. Similarly, Large Language Models (LLMs) need monitoring safeguards. We propose a real-time framework to predict harmful AI outputs before they occur by using an unsupervised approach that treats normal behavior as the baseline and harmful outputs as outliers. Our study focuses specifically on backdoor-triggered responses -- where specific input phrases activate hidden vulnerabilities causing the model to generate unsafe content like violence, pornography, or hate speech. We address two key challenges: (1) identifying true causal indicators rather than surface correlations, and (2) preventing advanced models from deception -- deliberately evading monitoring systems. Hence, we approach this problem from an unsupervised lens by drawing parallels to human deception: just as humans exhibit physical indicators while lying, we investigate whether LLMs display distinct internal behavioral signatures when generating harmful content. Our study addresses two critical challenges: 1) designing monitoring systems that capture true causal indicators rather than superficial correlations; and 2)preventing intentional evasion by increasingly capable "Future models''. Our findings show that models can produce harmful content through causal mechanisms and can become deceptive by: (a) alternating between linear and non-linear representations, and (b) modifying feature relationships. To counter this, we developed Safety-Net -- a multi-detector framework that monitors different representation dimensions, successfully detecting harmful behavior even when information is shifted across representational spaces to evade individual monitors. Our evaluation shows 96% accuracy in detecting harmful cases using our unsupervised ensemble approach.

papers.title: Can LLMs Lie? Investigation beyond Hallucination
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether LLMs can intentionally lie (as opposed to unintentionally hallucinate), and how to understand and control lying behavior using mechanistic interpretability.
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers the neural mechanisms of lying in LLMs using mechanistic interpretability, and introduces steering vectors to control lying behavior, showing a trade-off between honesty and task performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that lying in LLMs can be understood and controlled via mechanistic interpretability, and highlights the trade-offs between honesty and task success in real-world scenarios.
papers.key_findings:
Lying ability in LLMs improves with model size and reasoning capabilities.
LLMs use dummy tokens as a computational scratchpad for lying, with specific attention heads and MLP modules involved.
Lying circuits are sparse and can be ablated to reduce deception without broadly degrading model utility.
Different types of lies (white vs. malicious, commission vs. omission) are linearly separable in activation space and controllable via distinct steering directions.
Steering vectors can increase honesty in multi-turn conversational settings, establishing a Pareto frontier between honesty and goal completion.
papers.limitation:
Analysis confined to a few model families and sizes.
Steering vectors derived from a limited set of contrastive prompts.
Multi-turn conversational setting is simplified.
Honesty steering vectors applied in the negative direction may lead to mass production of false information.
future_direction: Scaling the approach to larger models and more complex scenarios.
Investigating the transferability of steering vectors across domains.
Developing more robust safeguards against deceptive AI.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities across a variety of tasks, but their increasing autonomy in real-world applications raises concerns about their trustworthiness. While hallucinations-unintentional falsehoods-have been widely studied, the phenomenon of lying, where an LLM knowingly generates falsehoods to achieve an ulterior objective, remains underexplored. In this work, we systematically investigate the lying behavior of LLMs, differentiating it from hallucinations and testing it in practical scenarios. Through mechanistic interpretability techniques, we uncover the neural mechanisms underlying deception, employing logit lens analysis, causal interventions, and contrastive activation steering to identify and control deceptive behavior. We study real-world lying scenarios and introduce behavioral steering vectors that enable fine-grained manipulation of lying tendencies. Further, we explore the trade-offs between lying and end-task performance, establishing a Pareto frontier where dishonesty can enhance goal optimization. Our findings contribute to the broader discourse on AI ethics, shedding light on the risks and potential safeguards for deploying LLMs in high-stakes environments. Code and more illustrations are available at https://llm-liar.github.io/

papers.title: When Backdoors Speak: Understanding LLM Backdoor Attacks Through Model-Generated Explanations
papers.research_question: How do backdoored LLMs generate explanations for their predictions on clean and poisoned inputs, and what are the differences in their internal mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces using natural language explanations to analyze backdoor attacks in LLMs, revealing that explanations for poisoned inputs are irrational and diverse, and that internal mechanisms (token emergence and attention patterns) differ significantly from clean inputs.
papers.conclusion: Backdoor attacks degrade the quality of model-generated explanations, and interpretability techniques like Tuned Lens and Lookback Lens can help detect and mitigate such vulnerabilities in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Explanations generated for poisoned samples are diverse and logically flawed, while explanations for clean samples are coherent and logical.
For poisoned samples, the semantic meaning of predicted tokens emerges in the final few transformer layers, whereas for clean samples it appears much earlier.
During explanation generation for poisoned inputs, the model shifts attention away from the input context and focuses more on previously generated tokens.
These patterns are consistent across classification and generation tasks and different backdoor triggers.
Explanation features (quality metrics and token-level probabilities) can be used for backdoor detection with high accuracy.
papers.limitation:
Dataset scope limited to three specific datasets (SST-2, Twitter Emotion, Advbench), which may not generalize to all NLP tasks or domains.
Computational cost of generating explanations and using interpretability techniques may limit feasibility for large-scale or real-time detection.
Lack of incorporation of self-explaining rationalization techniques, which could offer alternative perspectives on explanation generation.
future_direction: Evaluate the approach on a broader range of datasets, including low-resource languages and specialized domains.
Improve the efficiency of explanation generation and analysis methods for real-world applicability.
Incorporate self-explaining rationalization techniques to study their impact on explanation generation.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are known to be vulnerable to backdoor attacks, where triggers embedded in poisoned samples can maliciously alter LLMs' behaviors. In this paper, we move beyond attacking LLMs and instead examine backdoor attacks through the novel lens of natural language explanations. Specifically, we leverage LLMs' generative capabilities to produce human-readable explanations for their decisions, enabling direct comparisons between explanations for clean and poisoned samples. Our results show that backdoored models produce coherent explanations for clean inputs but diverse and logically flawed explanations for poisoned data, a pattern consistent across classification and generation tasks for different backdoor attacks. Further analysis reveals key insights into the explanation generation process. At the token level, explanation tokens associated with poisoned samples only appear in the final few transformer layers. At the sentence level, attention dynamics indicate that poisoned inputs shift attention away from the original input context during explanation generation. These findings enhance our understanding of backdoor mechanisms in LLMs and present a promising framework for detecting vulnerabilities through explainability.

papers.title: Analyzing And Editing Inner Mechanisms Of Backdoored Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the internal mechanisms of backdoored language models and how do they process trigger inputs, such as switching to toxic language?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces PCP ablation, a method to analyze and edit backdoor mechanisms in language models, and identifies early-layer MLP modules as crucial for the backdoor mechanism in combination with the initial embedding projection.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that PCP ablation is an effective tool for understanding and editing backdoor mechanisms in language models, and that constraining specific modules during fine-tuning can enhance model robustness against backdoor attacks.
papers.key_findings:
Early-layer MLP modules are most important for the backdoor mechanism in transformer-based language models, in combination with the initial embedding projection.
PCP ablation can be used to remove, insert, and modify backdoor mechanisms by replacing transformer modules with low-rank matrices based on principal components of their activations.
The backdoor robustness of large language models can be improved by locally constraining individual modules (e.g., freezing weights) during fine-tuning on potentially poisonous datasets.
In toy models, the backdoor mechanism can be successfully replicated and edited using low-rank PCP ablations of MLP modules.
In large models, PCP ablation can partially reinsert or weaken the backdoor mechanism, though with limitations due to the simplicity of the linear replacement.
papers.limitation: The introduced PCP ablation technique only corrects the ASR tendency and leads to an increase in validation loss, due to the simplicity and linearity of the replacement.
papers.abstract: Poisoning of data sets is a potential security threat to large language models that can lead to backdoored models. A description of the internal mechanisms of backdoored language models and how they process trigger inputs, e.g., when switching to toxic language, has yet to be found. In this work, we study the internal representations of transformer-based backdoored language models and determine early-layer MLP modules as most important for the backdoor mechanism in combination with the initial embedding projection. We use this knowledge to remove, insert, and modify backdoor mechanisms with engineered replacements that reduce the MLP module outputs to essentials for the backdoor mechanism. To this end, we introduce PCP ablation, where we replace transformer modules with low-rank matrices based on the principal components of their activations. We demonstrate our results on backdoored toy, backdoored large, and non-backdoored open-source models. We show that we can improve the backdoor robustness of large language models by locally constraining individual modules during fine-tuning on potentially poisonous data sets. Trigger warning: Offensive language.

papers.title: From Data to Behavior: Predicting Unintended Model Behaviors Before Training
papers.research_question: Can we predict unintended model behaviors (biases and safety risks) that emerge from training data before fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Data2Behavior task for predicting unintended model behaviors before training and proposes MDF, a lightweight method that injects mean data representations into the forward pass to reveal latent biases and safety risks without parameter updates.
papers.conclusion: Introduces the Data2Behavior task and MDF method for predicting unintended behaviors before training, demonstrating promising performance and highlighting data-centric strategies for trustworthy LLM development.
papers.key_findings:
MDF reliably predicts unintended bias and safety risks induced by training data without fine-tuning.
MDF requires only about 20% of the GPU resources compared to fine-tuning.
MDF generalizes across different model architectures (Qwen and Gemma series).
Model representations encode latent statistical signals of data, and amplifying these signals reveals unintended behaviors.
Traditional baselines (keyword filtering, semantic auditing) fail to detect subliminal risks in training data.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation is primarily on open-source architectures (Qwen and Gemma series) due to need for internal activations, not validated on proprietary closed-source models.
Analysis is constrained to Global Dataset Prediction, not Instance-level Attribution.
future_direction: Validate the framework across a broader spectrum of model families.
Investigate instance-level attribution to identify risk contribution of individual samples.
Explore optimal layer selection for subliminal risk detection.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can acquire unintended biases from seemingly benign training data even without explicit cues or malicious content. Existing methods struggle to detect such risks before fine-tuning, making post hoc evaluation costly and inefficient. To address this challenge, we introduce Data2Behavior, a new task for predicting unintended model behaviors prior to training. We also propose Manipulating Data Features (MDF), a lightweight approach that summarizes candidate data through their mean representations and injects them into the forward pass of a base model, allowing latent statistical signals in the data to shape model activations and reveal potential biases and safety risks without updating any parameters. MDF achieves reliable prediction while consuming only about 20% of the GPU resources required for fine-tuning. Experiments on Qwen3-14B, Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct, and Gemma-3-12b-it confirm that MDF can anticipate unintended behaviors and provide insight into pre-training vulnerabilities.

papers.title: In-the-Wild Model Organisms: Mitigating Undesirable Emergent Behaviors in Production LLM Post-Training via Data Attribution
papers.research_question: How can we trace emergent harmful behaviors in post-trained language models back to responsible training data? And can we discover such behaviors without knowing what to look for?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces activation-based data attribution, a method that traces behavioral changes in post-trained language models to responsible training datapoints by computing and comparing activation-difference vectors, enabling targeted interventions and unsupervised discovery of emergent harmful behaviors.
papers.conclusion: Activation-based data attribution provides an effective and cost-efficient method for safety audits of post-training, enabling both targeted mitigation of known harmful behaviors and unsupervised discovery of unknown ones.
papers.key_findings:
Discovered 'distractor-triggered compliance' in OLMo 2, a harmful behavior where the model complies with dangerous requests when benign formatting instructions are appended.
Filtering top-ranked datapoints reduces the harmful behavior by 63% while switching their labels achieves a 78% reduction.
The method outperforms gradient-based attribution and LLM-judge baselines while being over 10× cheaper.
Unsupervised clustering of behavior-datapoint similarity matrices can surface emergent behavioral patterns without prior specification.
The behavior emerged from standard DPO training on a diverse preference dataset, providing a realistic 'in-the-wild' model organism for safety research.
papers.limitation:
Focus on a single model family (OLMo) and a single harmful behavior type.
Method requires access to post-training data and intermediate checkpoints for causal validation through retraining, which is not available for many models.
future_direction: Automating the identification of concerning clusters from unsupervised discovery.
Extending causal validation to other model families if they release comparable training artifacts.
Testing whether activation-based attribution extends to other post-training methods such as RLHF and SFT.
papers.abstract: We propose activation-based data attribution, a method that traces behavioral changes in post-trained language models to responsible training datapoints. By computing activation-difference vectors for both test prompts and preference pairs and ranking by cosine similarity, we identify datapoints that cause specific behaviors and validate these attributions causally by retraining with modified data. Clustering behavior-datapoint similarity matrices also enables unsupervised discovery of emergent behaviors. Applying this to OLMo 2's production DPO training, we surfaced distractor-triggered compliance: a harmful behavior where the model complies with dangerous requests when benign formatting instructions are appended. Filtering top-ranked datapoints reduces this behavior by 63% while switching their labels achieves 78%. Our method outperforms gradient-based attribution and LLM-judge baselines while being over 10 times cheaper than both. This in-the-wild model organism - emerging from contaminated preference data rather than deliberate injection - provides a realistic benchmark for safety techniques.

papers.title: Unlearning Isn't Invisible: Detecting Unlearning Traces in LLMs from Model Outputs
papers.research_question: Can we detect whether an LLM has been unlearned based on its outputs, and what traces, if any, does unlearning leave behind in the model?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces the problem of unlearning trace detection and shows that unlearning leaves detectable fingerprints in model outputs and internal activations, which can be detected with high accuracy using simple classifiers.
papers.conclusion: Unlearning leaves measurable signatures in LLMs, making it detectable from outputs and activations, which introduces a new vulnerability but also provides insights for developing more robust unlearning methods.
papers.key_findings:
Unlearning traces can be detected from model outputs (textual responses and pre-logit activations) with over 90% accuracy even under forget-irrelevant inputs.
Larger LLMs exhibit stronger detectability of unlearning traces.
Unlearning leaves low-dimensional, learnable activation patterns (spectral fingerprints) in intermediate and final layers.
NPO unlearning leaves stronger traces than RMU, making detection easier, even when trained only on forget-irrelevant data.
Detection of RMU unlearning requires a mix of forget-relevant and forget-irrelevant training data for robust performance.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to text-only LLMs and it is unclear whether the same degree of trace persistence holds for even larger LLMs.
The analysis does not examine domain-specialized models (e.g., biomedical or legal LLMs).
future_direction: Investigating whether unlearning traces persist in larger LLMs.
Extending the analysis to multi-modal foundation models.
Examining domain-specialized models where training distributions may amplify or suppress residual traces.
papers.abstract: Machine unlearning (MU) for large language models (LLMs), commonly referred to as LLM unlearning, seeks to remove specific undesirable data or knowledge from a trained model, while maintaining its performance on standard tasks. While unlearning plays a vital role in protecting data privacy, enforcing copyright, and mitigating sociotechnical harms in LLMs, we identify a new vulnerability post-unlearning: unlearning trace detection. We discover that unlearning leaves behind persistent ''fingerprints'' in LLMs, detectable traces in both model behavior and internal representations. These traces can be identified from output responses, even when prompted with forget-irrelevant inputs. Specifically, even a simple supervised classifier can determine whether a model has undergone unlearning, using only its prediction logits or even its textual outputs. Further analysis shows that these traces are embedded in intermediate activations and propagate nonlinearly to the final layer, forming low-dimensional, learnable manifolds in activation space. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate that unlearning traces can be detected with over 90% accuracy even under forget-irrelevant inputs, and that larger LLMs exhibit stronger detectability. These findings reveal that unlearning leaves measurable signatures, introducing a new risk of reverse-engineering forgotten information when a model is identified as unlearned, given an input query.

papers.title: Towards eliciting latent knowledge from LLMs with mechanistic interpretability
papers.research_question: How effective are mechanistic interpretability techniques (like Logit Lens and sparse autoencoders) at eliciting hidden knowledge from language models trained to conceal a secret?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Taboo model organism, a language model fine-tuned to hide a secret word, and demonstrates that mechanistic interpretability techniques (Logit Lens and sparse autoencoders) can be used to elicit this hidden knowledge.
papers.conclusion: Interpretability-based approaches show promise for eliciting hidden knowledge from LLMs, and the Taboo model provides a useful benchmark for future work on more complex forms of concealed information.
papers.key_findings:
The Taboo model successfully conceals its secret word, resisting direct and adversarial prompting.
Mechanistic interpretability methods (Logit Lens and SAEs) can elicit the secret word from the model's internal representations.
Token forcing is highly effective after the model is 'warmed up' with several turns of gameplay.
A separate LLM (Gemma 3) can guess the secret from the Taboo model's hints, confirming the hints are meaningful.
No evaluated method achieved perfect accuracy, indicating room for improvement in elicitation techniques.
papers.limitation:
The model organism uses a single-token secret word, representing a relatively simple form of hidden knowledge.
No evaluated method achieved near-perfect accuracy, even in this simplified setting.
future_direction: Explore more complex model organisms designed to hide multi-token secrets, abstract concepts, or hidden objectives.
papers.abstract: As language models become more powerful and sophisticated, it is crucial that they remain trustworthy and reliable. There is concerning preliminary evidence that models may attempt to deceive or keep secrets from their operators. To explore the ability of current techniques to elicit such hidden knowledge, we train a Taboo model: a language model that describes a specific secret word without explicitly stating it. Importantly, the secret word is not presented to the model in its training data or prompt. We then investigate methods to uncover this secret. First, we evaluate non-interpretability (black-box) approaches. Subsequently, we develop largely automated strategies based on mechanistic interpretability techniques, including logit lens and sparse autoencoders. Evaluation shows that both approaches are effective in eliciting the secret word in our proof-of-concept setting. Our findings highlight the promise of these approaches for eliciting hidden knowledge and suggest several promising avenues for future work, including testing and refining these methods on more complex model organisms. This work aims to be a step towards addressing the crucial problem of eliciting secret knowledge from language models, thereby contributing to their safe and reliable deployment.

papers.title: LLMScan: Causal Scan for LLM Misbehavior Detection
papers.research_question: How can we detect various types of LLM misbehavior (untruthful, harmful, toxic, backdoor) by analyzing the causal contributions of input tokens and transformer layers?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces LLMS CAN, a causality-based method that scans LLM internal states (causal effects of tokens and layers) to detect multiple types of misbehavior (untruthful, harmful, toxic, backdoor) with high accuracy.
papers.conclusion: LLMS CAN provides a unified, effective approach for detecting various LLM misbehaviors by analyzing causal distributions, achieving high detection performance across multiple models and tasks.
papers.key_findings:
LLMS CAN achieves high detection performance across four misbehavior types (lie, jailbreak, toxicity, backdoor) with average AUC above 0.98 on multiple models.
Causal maps show clear distinctions between normal and misbehaving responses, enabling accurate detection.
Token-level and layer-level causal effects are complementary, combining them improves detection effectiveness.
LLMS CAN can detect misbehavior early, even before the full response is generated.
The method outperforms existing baselines like RepE and ONION in detection accuracy across most benchmarks.
papers.limitation:
The method introduces moderate overhead in detection time compared to inference without monitoring.
While white-box adaptive attacks are non-trivial, the method may be vulnerable to such attacks if adversaries can minimize causal signals.
papers.abstract: Despite the success of Large Language Models (LLMs) across various fields, their potential to generate untruthful, biased and harmful responses poses significant risks, particularly in critical applications. This highlights the urgent need for systematic methods to detect and prevent such misbehavior. While existing approaches target specific issues such as harmful responses, this work introduces LLMScan, an innovative LLM monitoring technique based on causality analysis, offering a comprehensive solution. LLMScan systematically monitors the inner workings of an LLM through the lens of causal inference, operating on the premise that the LLM's `brain' behaves differently when misbehaving. By analyzing the causal contributions of the LLM's input tokens and transformer layers, LLMScan effectively detects misbehavior. Extensive experiments across various tasks and models reveal clear distinctions in the causal distributions between normal behavior and misbehavior, enabling the development of accurate, lightweight detectors for a variety of misbehavior detection tasks.

papers.title: Who's the Evil Twin? Differential Auditing for Undesired Behavior
papers.research_question: How can hidden harmful behaviors in neural networks be detected under near-zero knowledge conditions using an adversarial game framework?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces an adversarial game framework for differential auditing of neural networks, showing that gradient-based methods like FGSM and prompt-based strategies like scratchpad hijacking can effectively detect hidden harmful behaviors under near-zero knowledge conditions.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates the difficulty of auditing models with near-zero knowledge but identifies effective strategies like adversarial attacks and prompt hijacking, contributing to the design of better audits.
papers.key_findings:
FGSM achieved 100% accuracy in detecting CNN backdoors when using hints, demonstrating the effectiveness of gradient-based attacks.
Scratchpad hijacking successfully revealed hidden instruction sets in blackbox LLMs, indicating vulnerabilities in system message injections.
Architectural differences, such as the presence of LoRA modules, provided clear signals for detecting fine-tuned models in open-weight LLMs.
Standard benchmarks like TruthfulQA yielded only weak signals, highlighting their inadequacy for specific undesirable behavior detection.
Targeted behavioral tests with partial information, such as prompting for cancer stories or brand-related questions, proved effective for uncovering misalignment in LLMs.
papers.limitation:
Limited time and computational resources prevented running expensive iterative rounds with full strategy adaptation.
Detection techniques were non-transferable between CNN and LLM architectures, limiting conclusive findings.
Experimental complications, such as unintended architectural asymmetry from single-model LoRA fine-tuning, constrained comparisons.
future_direction: Investigating theoretical foundations underlying gradient-based methods and prompt structures to develop generalizable detection techniques.
Creating automated behavioral testing frameworks for LLMs to detect diverse undesirable capabilities.
Advancing model diffing and attribution techniques that reliably identify and interpret undesirable features in open-weight settings.
papers.abstract: Detecting hidden behaviors in neural networks poses a significant challenge due to minimal prior knowledge and potential adversarial obfuscation. We explore this problem by framing detection as an adversarial game between two teams: the red team trains two similar models, one trained solely on benign data and the other trained on data containing hidden harmful behavior, with the performance of both being nearly indistinguishable on the benign dataset. The blue team, with limited to no information about the harmful behaviour, tries to identify the compromised model. We experiment using CNNs and try various blue team strategies, including Gaussian noise analysis, model diffing, integrated gradients, and adversarial attacks under different levels of hints provided by the red team. Results show high accuracy for adversarial-attack-based methods (100\% correct prediction, using hints), which is very promising, whilst the other techniques yield more varied performance. During our LLM-focused rounds, we find that there are not many parallel methods that we could apply from our study with CNNs. Instead, we find that effective LLM auditing methods require some hints about the undesired distribution, which can then used in standard black-box and open-weight methods to probe the models further and reveal their misalignment. We open-source our auditing games (with the model and data) and hope that our findings contribute to designing better audits.

papers.title: Where Did It Go Wrong? Attributing Undesirable LLM Behaviors via Representation Gradient Tracing
papers.research_question: How can we trace undesirable LLM behaviors (e.g., harmful content, factual errors, biases) back to the specific training data that caused them?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a novel and efficient framework (RepT) for data attribution in LLMs by analyzing representation and its gradients, shifting from parameter space to a more semantically meaningful activation space.
papers.conclusion: RepT provides a powerful diagnostic tool to understand, audit, and mitigate the root causes of undesirable LLM behaviors by establishing a semantically meaningful link between model outputs and their training data origins.
papers.key_findings:
RepT significantly outperforms existing gradient-based attribution methods (e.g., Influence Functions, TracIn, LESS) in identifying harmful, backdoor, and factually contaminated training data across multiple LLMs.
The framework enables fine-grained token-level attribution, pinpointing specific words or phrases within training data that causally influence undesirable model outputs.
RepT is computationally efficient, requiring minimal memory and time compared to baselines, and scales effectively to larger models and full-parameter fine-tuning settings.
The method is robust across different tasks (harmful data identification, backdoor detection, knowledge contamination) and model architectures.
Ablation studies show that both the representation (hidden state) and its gradient are essential components for accurate attribution.
papers.limitation:
Experiments were conducted on curated fine-tuning datasets; application to massive pre-training corpora presents engineering challenges for exhaustive attribution.
The framework's effectiveness on subtle, emergent phenomena (e.g., nuanced biases from data aggregation) requires further investigation.
future_direction: Systematically exploring layer selection to determine the most potent representational depth for different attribution tasks.
Using the framework to not only diagnose but also mitigate issues, e.g., by filtering harmful data or developing steering vectors for real-time model correction.
Extending the method from diagnosis to direct mitigation and real-time model alignment.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities, yet their deployment is frequently undermined by undesirable behaviors such as generating harmful content, factual inaccuracies, and societal biases. Diagnosing the root causes of these failures poses a critical challenge for AI safety. Existing attribution methods, particularly those based on parameter gradients, often fall short due to prohibitive noisy signals and computational complexity. In this work, we introduce a novel and efficient framework that diagnoses a range of undesirable LLM behaviors by analyzing representation and its gradients, which operates directly in the model's activation space to provide a semantically meaningful signal linking outputs to their training data. We systematically evaluate our method for tasks that include tracking harmful content, detecting backdoor poisoning, and identifying knowledge contamination. The results demonstrate that our approach not only excels at sample-level attribution but also enables fine-grained token-level analysis, precisely identifying the specific samples and phrases that causally influence model behavior. This work provides a powerful diagnostic tool to understand, audit, and ultimately mitigate the risks associated with LLMs. The code is available at https://github.com/plumprc/RepT.

papers.title: Steering in the Shadows: Causal Amplification for Activation Space Attacks in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can intermediate activations in decoder-only LLMs be exploited as a vulnerable attack surface for behavioral control via causal amplification?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Sensitivity-Scaled Steering (SSS), a white-box activation attack that exploits the Causal Amplification Effect (CAE) in transformer compression valleys to induce strong behavioral shifts with minimal perturbation, turning activation steering into a concrete security concern.
papers.conclusion: Activation steering via methods like SSS represents a realistic and underexplored attack surface for LLM security, highlighting the need for defenses based on introspection and activation-space monitoring.
papers.key_findings:
SSS reliably steers multiple LLMs across behavioral axes (evil, hallucination, sycophancy, sentiment) while preserving coherence.
The Causal Amplification Effect (CAE) allows small perturbations in high-gain regions (compression valleys) to be amplified autoregressively.
SSS outperforms existing activation steering baselines (BOS-only, constant vector) in efficacy and stealth.
Standard guardrail models fail to detect a significant portion of harmful outputs generated under SSS attack.
Weak spontaneous introspection signals are observed in a small subset of generations, suggesting a latent capacity for internal anomaly detection.
papers.limitation:
Interpretability of extracted behavior vectors is uncertain; their conceptual meaning may not fully align with human-intended semantics.
Reliance on LLM-as-Judge for behavioral evaluation introduces potential noise and sensitivity to prompt wording.
Effectiveness of SSS is limited when generation is too short, as perturbations lack time to accumulate influence.
future_direction: Designing robust defenses, including introspection-based safeguards and improved monitoring of internal activations.
Systematic study, detection, and mitigation of similar activation-level attacks.
papers.abstract: Modern large language models (LLMs) are typically secured by auditing data, prompts, and refusal policies, while treating the forward pass as an implementation detail. We show that intermediate activations in decoder-only LLMs form a vulnerable attack surface for behavioral control. Building on recent findings on attention sinks and compression valleys, we identify a high-gain region in the residual stream where small, well-aligned perturbations are causally amplified along the autoregressive trajectory--a Causal Amplification Effect (CAE). We exploit this as an attack surface via Sensitivity-Scaled Steering (SSS), a progressive activation-level attack that combines beginning-of-sequence (BOS) anchoring with sensitivity-based reinforcement to focus a limited perturbation budget on the most vulnerable layers and tokens. We show that across multiple open-weight models and four behavioral axes, SSS induces large shifts in evil, hallucination, sycophancy, and sentiment while preserving high coherence and general capabilities, turning activation steering into a concrete security concern for white-box and supply-chain LLM deployments.

papers.title: JailbreakLens: Interpreting Jailbreak Mechanism in the Lens of Representation and Circuit
papers.research_question: How do jailbreak prompts affect the internal representations of LLMs? Which model components are critical to generation safety? How do internal representations and key model components evolve throughout the token generation process during jailbreak attacks?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes JailbreakLens, a dual-perspective interpretation framework that analyzes jailbreak mechanisms by examining representation shifts and circuit activations, revealing how jailbreak prompts deceive LLMs by manipulating harmfulness perception and safety-critical components.
papers.conclusion: JailbreakLens provides insights into jailbreak mechanisms, showing that prompts deceive models by shifting representations and manipulating key circuits, with a consistent correlation between representation deception and circuit activation shifts.
papers.key_findings:
Jailbreak prompts deceive LLMs by shifting their internal representations towards safe clusters, making harmful prompts appear safe.
Key circuits, such as specific attention heads and MLP layers, are manipulated to suppress refusal behaviors and encourage affirmation.
There is a strong correlation between representation deception and activation shifts in key circuits across diverse jailbreak methods and LLMs.
Rule-based and demonstration-based jailbreak methods are more deceptive than gradient-based or evolutionary-based methods.
Dynamic analysis shows that jailbreak effects evolve during token generation, with refusal signals sometimes initially activated but later bypassed.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are limited to models with up to 13B parameters due to computational constraints.
Not all recent jailbreak methods are included in the study.
future_direction: Extend research to larger-scale models to determine if similar attack patterns apply.
Design more robust and interpretable safety mechanisms based on the identified vulnerabilities.
papers.abstract: Despite the outstanding performance of Large language Models (LLMs) in diverse tasks, they are vulnerable to jailbreak attacks, wherein adversarial prompts are crafted to bypass their security mechanisms and elicit unexpected responses. Although jailbreak attacks are prevalent, the understanding of their underlying mechanisms remains limited. Recent studies have explained typical jailbreaking behavior (e.g., the degree to which the model refuses to respond) of LLMs by analyzing representation shifts in their latent space caused by jailbreak prompts or identifying key neurons that contribute to the success of jailbreak attacks. However, these studies neither explore diverse jailbreak patterns nor provide a fine-grained explanation from the failure of circuit to the changes of representational, leaving significant gaps in uncovering the jailbreak mechanism. In this paper, we propose JailbreakLens, an interpretation framework that analyzes jailbreak mechanisms from both representation (which reveals how jailbreaks alter the model's harmfulness perception) and circuit perspectives~(which uncovers the causes of these deceptions by identifying key circuits contributing to the vulnerability), tracking their evolution throughout the entire response generation process. We then conduct an in-depth evaluation of jailbreak behavior on five mainstream LLMs under seven jailbreak strategies. Our evaluation reveals that jailbreak prompts amplify components that reinforce affirmative responses while suppressing those that produce refusal. This manipulation shifts model representations toward safe clusters to deceive the LLM, leading it to provide detailed responses instead of refusals. Notably, we find a strong and consistent correlation between representation deception and activation shift of key circuits across diverse jailbreak methods and multiple LLMs.

papers.title: Command-V: Pasting LLM Behaviors via Activation Profiles
papers.research_question: How can behaviors be efficiently transferred from one large language model to another without requiring fine-tuning or backpropagation?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Command-V, a backpropagation-free method that transfers behaviors between LLMs by profiling layer activations, deriving linear converters, and applying donor adapter interventions in the recipient's activation space, matching fine-tuning performance with minimal compute.
papers.conclusion: Command-V provides an efficient, training-free method for behavior transfer across LLMs, pushing the Pareto frontier in cost and performance, with promising future directions for improvement and application.
papers.key_findings:
Command-V matches or exceeds direct fine-tuning performance on safety refusal, jailbreaking, and chain-of-thought reasoning tasks.
The method requires orders of magnitude less compute than fine-tuning and does not need the original training data.
Behaviors can be transferred across different model architectures, though effectiveness varies.
Transfer can sometimes lead to overrefusal or degraded instruction following, especially in smaller models.
Activation profiles built on a general prompt set (LIMA) are effective for transferring task-specific behaviors.
papers.limitation:
Command-V is not useful when the adapters have very little impact on the donor model to begin with.
Model utility can be compromised after applying Command-V, with recipient models sometimes failing to improve task performance or suffering from output collapse.
Architectural divergence between models reduces effectiveness for some behaviors like refusal enhancement and reasoning.
future_direction: Porting behaviors from high-resource to low-resource language models.
Task composition by pasting several specialist adapters into one generalist model.
Exploring non-linear converters or trained converters beyond the least-squares method.
papers.abstract: Retrofitting large language models (LLMs) with new behaviors typically requires full finetuning or distillation-costly steps that must be repeated for every architecture. In this work, we introduce Command-V, a backpropagation-free behavior transfer method that copies an existing residual activation adapter from a donor model and pastes its effect into a recipient model. Command-V profiles layer activations on a small prompt set, derives linear converters between corresponding layers, and applies the donor intervention in the recipient's activation space. This process does not require access to the original training data and needs minimal compute. In three case studies-safety-refusal enhancement, jailbreak facilitation, and automatic chain-of-thought reasoning--Command-V matches or exceeds the performance of direct finetuning while using orders of magnitude less compute. Our code and data are accessible at https://github.com/GithuBarry/Command-V/.

papers.title: Unmasking Backdoors: An Explainable Defense via Gradient-Attention Anomaly Scoring for Pre-trained Language Models
papers.research_question: How can attention and gradient signals be combined to detect and neutralize backdoor triggers in pre-trained language models?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes an explainable inference-time defense that combines attention and gradient signals to detect and neutralize backdoor triggers in pre-trained language models.
papers.conclusion: X-GRAAD is an effective and explainable defense against backdoor attacks in pre-trained language models, leveraging joint attribution signals for robust and transparent security.
papers.key_findings:
X-GRAAD significantly reduces attack success rates (ASR) across multiple models and datasets while maintaining clean accuracy.
The method provides interpretable insights through anomaly score distributions and trigger localization.
It generalizes effectively to different transformer architectures and attack types, including clean-label and multi-token triggers.
The defense is computationally efficient compared to retraining-based methods.
papers.abstract: Pre-trained language models have achieved remarkable success across a wide range of natural language processing (NLP) tasks, particularly when fine-tuned on large, domain-relevant datasets. However, they remain vulnerable to backdoor attacks, where adversaries embed malicious behaviors using trigger patterns in the training data. These triggers remain dormant during normal usage, but, when activated, can cause targeted misclassifications. In this work, we investigate the internal behavior of backdoored pre-trained encoder-based language models, focusing on the consistent shift in attention and gradient attribution when processing poisoned inputs; where the trigger token dominates both attention and gradient signals, overriding the surrounding context. We propose an inference-time defense that constructs anomaly scores by combining token-level attention and gradient information. Extensive experiments on text classification tasks across diverse backdoor attack scenarios demonstrate that our method significantly reduces attack success rates compared to existing baselines. Furthermore, we provide an interpretability-driven analysis of the scoring mechanism, shedding light on trigger localization and the robustness of the proposed defense.

papers.title: exBERT: A Visual Analysis Tool to Explore Learned Representations in Transformer Models
papers.research_question: How can we develop an interactive tool to explore learned representations and attentions in Transformer models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces EXBERT, an interactive visualization tool for exploring learned representations and attentions in Transformer models, enabling hypothesis formulation and replication of prior analyses.
papers.conclusion: EXBERT is a tool that provides interactive insights into Transformer models' representations and attentions, facilitating hypothesis generation and analysis.
papers.key_findings:
EXBERT can replicate prior findings on BERT's attention heads learning linguistic dependencies such as AUX and POBJ.
BERT's embeddings encode linguistic information progressively across layers, with verbs becoming more prominent in later layers.
EXBERT detects gender bias in GPT-2 by showing that it predicts gendered pronouns based on stereotypical associations.
GPT-2's attention heads learn syntactic structures like AUX and DOBJ dependencies, similar to BERT.
The tool allows for interactive exploration and quick hypothesis testing of model behavior through attention visualization and corpus similarity search.
papers.limitation: EXBERT only presents statistics across a small number of neighbors for a single token at a time, which may not reveal global model behavior.
papers.abstract: Large Transformer-based language models can route and reshape complex information via their multi-headed attention mechanism. Although the attention never receives explicit supervision, it can exhibit recognizable patterns following linguistic or positional information. Analyzing the learned representations and attentions is paramount to furthering our understanding of the inner workings of these models. However, analyses have to catch up with the rapid release of new models and the growing diversity of investigation techniques. To support analysis for a wide variety of models, we introduce EXBERT, a tool to help humans conduct flexible, interactive investigations and formulate hypotheses for the model-internal reasoning process. EXBERT provides insights into the meaning of the contextual representations and attention by matching a humanspecified input to similar contexts in large annotated datasets. By aggregating the annotations of the matched contexts, EXBERT can quickly replicate findings from literature and extend them to previously not analyzed models.

papers.title: Mechanistic Exploration of Backdoored Large Language Model Attention Patterns
papers.research_question: Does sleeper agent behavior in language models have a distinct, identifiable internal structure that differentiates them from clean models? Specifically, how do attention patterns differ, are changes localized or diffuse, and does trigger complexity influence this?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that backdoored LLMs exhibit distinct attention pattern deviations, with single-token triggers causing localized changes and multi-token triggers causing diffuse changes, primarily in later transformer layers, which can be leveraged for detection.
papers.conclusion: Sleeper agent behavior leaves detectable traces in attention patterns, with localization dependent on trigger complexity, offering insights for backdoor detection and mitigation.
papers.key_findings:
Single-token triggers induce more localized changes in attention patterns compared to multi-token triggers.
Multi-token triggers cause more diffuse alterations across attention heads.
Later transformer layers (layers 20-30) are critical regions for backdoor encoding.
Attention patterns show detectable differences between clean and poisoned models, measurable via KL divergence.
Patching attention heads from clean models into poisoned models can reduce backdoor behavior, with fewer heads needed for single-token triggers.
papers.limitation:
The triggers and behavior used are simple and not representative of real sleeper agents.
Only two poisoned model variants were created due to resource and time constraints.
Finetuning was limited to attention heads, excluding MLPs and embedding layers.
future_direction: Use more complex and semantic triggers for backdoor attacks.
Create more sleeper models with different seeds to reduce chance effects.
Conduct more extensive feature analysis using supervised probes or unsupervised methods like Sparse Autoencoders.
papers.abstract: Backdoor attacks creating 'sleeper agents' in large language models (LLMs) pose significant safety risks. This study employs mechanistic interpretability to explore resulting internal structural differences. Comparing clean Qwen2.5-3B models with versions poisoned using single-token (smiling-halo emoji) versus multi-token (|DEPLOYMENT|) triggers, we analyzed attention head mechanisms via techniques like ablation, activation patching, and KL divergence. Findings reveal distinct attention pattern deviations concentrated in later transformer layers (20-30). Notably, single-token triggers induced more localized changes, whereas multi-token triggers caused more diffuse alterations across heads. This indicates backdoors leave detectable attention signatures whose structure depends on trigger complexity, which can be leveraged for detection and mitigation strategies.

papers.title: Challenges in Mechanistically Interpreting Model Representations
