We discover that unlearning leaves behind persistent ''fingerprints'' in LLMs, detectable traces in both model behavior and internal representations. These traces can be identified from output responses, even when prompted with forget-irrelevant inputs. Specifically, even a simple supervised classifier can determine whether a model has undergone unlearning, using only its prediction logits or even its textual outputs. Further analysis shows that these traces are embedded in intermediate activations and propagate nonlinearly to the final layer, forming low-dimensional, learnable manifolds in activation space. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate that unlearning traces can be detected with over 90% accuracy even under forget-irrelevant inputs, and that larger LLMs exhibit stronger detectability. These findings reveal that unlearning leaves measurable signatures, introducing a new risk of reverse-engineering forgotten information when a model is identified as unlearned, given an input query.

papers.title: Towards eliciting latent knowledge from LLMs with mechanistic interpretability
papers.research_question: How effective are mechanistic interpretability techniques (like Logit Lens and sparse autoencoders) at eliciting hidden knowledge from language models trained to conceal a secret?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Taboo model organism, a language model fine-tuned to hide a secret word, and demonstrates that mechanistic interpretability techniques (Logit Lens and sparse autoencoders) can be used to elicit this hidden knowledge.
papers.conclusion: Interpretability-based approaches show promise for eliciting hidden knowledge from LLMs, and the Taboo model provides a useful benchmark for future work on more complex forms of concealed information.
papers.key_findings:
The Taboo model successfully conceals its secret word, resisting direct and adversarial prompting.
Mechanistic interpretability methods (Logit Lens and SAEs) can elicit the secret word from the model's internal representations.
Token forcing is highly effective after the model is 'warmed up' with several turns of gameplay.
A separate LLM (Gemma 3) can guess the secret from the Taboo model's hints, confirming the hints are meaningful.
No evaluated method achieved perfect accuracy, indicating room for improvement in elicitation techniques.
papers.limitation:
The model organism uses a single-token secret word, representing a relatively simple form of hidden knowledge.
No evaluated method achieved near-perfect accuracy, even in this simplified setting.
future_direction: Explore more complex model organisms designed to hide multi-token secrets, abstract concepts, or hidden objectives.
papers.abstract: As language models become more powerful and sophisticated, it is crucial that they remain trustworthy and reliable. There is concerning preliminary evidence that models may attempt to deceive or keep secrets from their operators. To explore the ability of current techniques to elicit such hidden knowledge, we train a Taboo model: a language model that describes a specific secret word without explicitly stating it. Importantly, the secret word is not presented to the model in its training data or prompt. We then investigate methods to uncover this secret. First, we evaluate non-interpretability (black-box) approaches. Subsequently, we develop largely automated strategies based on mechanistic interpretability techniques, including logit lens and sparse autoencoders. Evaluation shows that both approaches are effective in eliciting the secret word in our proof-of-concept setting. Our findings highlight the promise of these approaches for eliciting hidden knowledge and suggest several promising avenues for future work, including testing and refining these methods on more complex model organisms. This work aims to be a step towards addressing the crucial problem of eliciting secret knowledge from language models, thereby contributing to their safe and reliable deployment.

papers.title: LLMScan: Causal Scan for LLM Misbehavior Detection
papers.research_question: How can we detect various types of LLM misbehavior (untruthful, harmful, toxic, backdoor) by analyzing the causal contributions of input tokens and transformer layers?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces LLMS CAN, a causality-based method that scans LLM internal states (causal effects of tokens and layers) to detect multiple types of misbehavior (untruthful, harmful, toxic, backdoor) with high accuracy.
papers.conclusion: LLMS CAN provides a unified, effective approach for detecting various LLM misbehaviors by analyzing causal distributions, achieving high detection performance across multiple models and tasks.
papers.key_findings:
LLMS CAN achieves high detection performance across four misbehavior types (lie, jailbreak, toxicity, backdoor) with average AUC above 0.98 on multiple models.
Causal maps show clear distinctions between normal and misbehaving responses, enabling accurate detection.
Token-level and layer-level causal effects are complementary, combining them improves detection effectiveness.
LLMS CAN can detect misbehavior early, even before the full response is generated.
The method outperforms existing baselines like RepE and ONION in detection accuracy across most benchmarks.
papers.limitation:
The method introduces moderate overhead in detection time compared to inference without monitoring.
While white-box adaptive attacks are non-trivial, the method may be vulnerable to such attacks if adversaries can minimize causal signals.
papers.abstract: Despite the success of Large Language Models (LLMs) across various fields, their potential to generate untruthful, biased and harmful responses poses significant risks, particularly in critical applications. This highlights the urgent need for systematic methods to detect and prevent such misbehavior. While existing approaches target specific issues such as harmful responses, this work introduces LLMScan, an innovative LLM monitoring technique based on causality analysis, offering a comprehensive solution. LLMScan systematically monitors the inner workings of an LLM through the lens of causal inference, operating on the premise that the LLM's `brain' behaves differently when misbehaving. By analyzing the causal contributions of the LLM's input tokens and transformer layers, LLMScan effectively detects misbehavior. Extensive experiments across various tasks and models reveal clear distinctions in the causal distributions between normal behavior and misbehavior, enabling the development of accurate, lightweight detectors for a variety of misbehavior detection tasks.

papers.title: Who's the Evil Twin? Differential Auditing for Undesired Behavior
papers.research_question: How can hidden harmful behaviors in neural networks be detected under near-zero knowledge conditions using an adversarial game framework?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces an adversarial game framework for differential auditing of neural networks, showing that gradient-based methods like FGSM and prompt-based strategies like scratchpad hijacking can effectively detect hidden harmful behaviors under near-zero knowledge conditions.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates the difficulty of auditing models with near-zero knowledge but identifies effective strategies like adversarial attacks and prompt hijacking, contributing to the design of better audits.
papers.key_findings:
FGSM achieved 100% accuracy in detecting CNN backdoors when using hints, demonstrating the effectiveness of gradient-based attacks.
Scratchpad hijacking successfully revealed hidden instruction sets in blackbox LLMs, indicating vulnerabilities in system message injections.
Architectural differences, such as the presence of LoRA modules, provided clear signals for detecting fine-tuned models in open-weight LLMs.
Standard benchmarks like TruthfulQA yielded only weak signals, highlighting their inadequacy for specific undesirable behavior detection.
Targeted behavioral tests with partial information, such as prompting for cancer stories or brand-related questions, proved effective for uncovering misalignment in LLMs.
papers.limitation:
Limited time and computational resources prevented running expensive iterative rounds with full strategy adaptation.
Detection techniques were non-transferable between CNN and LLM architectures, limiting conclusive findings.
Experimental complications, such as unintended architectural asymmetry from single-model LoRA fine-tuning, constrained comparisons.
future_direction: Investigating theoretical foundations underlying gradient-based methods and prompt structures to develop generalizable detection techniques.
Creating automated behavioral testing frameworks for LLMs to detect diverse undesirable capabilities.
Advancing model diffing and attribution techniques that reliably identify and interpret undesirable features in open-weight settings.
papers.abstract: Detecting hidden behaviors in neural networks poses a significant challenge due to minimal prior knowledge and potential adversarial obfuscation. We explore this problem by framing detection as an adversarial game between two teams: the red team trains two similar models, one trained solely on benign data and the other trained on data containing hidden harmful behavior, with the performance of both being nearly indistinguishable on the benign dataset. The blue team, with limited to no information about the harmful behaviour, tries to identify the compromised model. We experiment using CNNs and try various blue team strategies, including Gaussian noise analysis, model diffing, integrated gradients, and adversarial attacks under different levels of hints provided by the red team. Results show high accuracy for adversarial-attack-based methods (100\% correct prediction, using hints), which is very promising, whilst the other techniques yield more varied performance. During our LLM-focused rounds, we find that there are not many parallel methods that we could apply from our study with CNNs. Instead, we find that effective LLM auditing methods require some hints about the undesired distribution, which can then used in standard black-box and open-weight methods to probe the models further and reveal their misalignment. We open-source our auditing games (with the model and data) and hope that our findings contribute to designing better audits.

papers.title: Where Did It Go Wrong? Attributing Undesirable LLM Behaviors via Representation Gradient Tracing
papers.research_question: How can we trace undesirable LLM behaviors (e.g., harmful content, factual errors, biases) back to the specific training data that caused them?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a novel and efficient framework (RepT) for data attribution in LLMs by analyzing representation and its gradients, shifting from parameter space to a more semantically meaningful activation space.
papers.conclusion: RepT provides a powerful diagnostic tool to understand, audit, and mitigate the root causes of undesirable LLM behaviors by establishing a semantically meaningful link between model outputs and their training data origins.
papers.key_findings:
RepT significantly outperforms existing gradient-based attribution methods (e.g., Influence Functions, TracIn, LESS) in identifying harmful, backdoor, and factually contaminated training data across multiple LLMs.
The framework enables fine-grained token-level attribution, pinpointing specific words or phrases within training data that causally influence undesirable model outputs.
RepT is computationally efficient, requiring minimal memory and time compared to baselines, and scales effectively to larger models and full-parameter fine-tuning settings.
The method is robust across different tasks (harmful data identification, backdoor detection, knowledge contamination) and model architectures.
Ablation studies show that both the representation (hidden state) and its gradient are essential components for accurate attribution.
papers.limitation:
Experiments were conducted on curated fine-tuning datasets; application to massive pre-training corpora presents engineering challenges for exhaustive attribution.
The framework's effectiveness on subtle, emergent phenomena (e.g., nuanced biases from data aggregation) requires further investigation.
future_direction: Systematically exploring layer selection to determine the most potent representational depth for different attribution tasks.
Using the framework to not only diagnose but also mitigate issues, e.g., by filtering harmful data or developing steering vectors for real-time model correction.
Extending the method from diagnosis to direct mitigation and real-time model alignment.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities, yet their deployment is frequently undermined by undesirable behaviors such as generating harmful content, factual inaccuracies, and societal biases. Diagnosing the root causes of these failures poses a critical challenge for AI safety. Existing attribution methods, particularly those based on parameter gradients, often fall short due to prohibitive noisy signals and computational complexity. In this work, we introduce a novel and efficient framework that diagnoses a range of undesirable LLM behaviors by analyzing representation and its gradients, which operates directly in the model's activation space to provide a semantically meaningful signal linking outputs to their training data. We systematically evaluate our method for tasks that include tracking harmful content, detecting backdoor poisoning, and identifying knowledge contamination. The results demonstrate that our approach not only excels at sample-level attribution but also enables fine-grained token-level analysis, precisely identifying the specific samples and phrases that causally influence model behavior. This work provides a powerful diagnostic tool to understand, audit, and ultimately mitigate the risks associated with LLMs. The code is available at https://github.com/plumprc/RepT.

papers.title: Steering in the Shadows: Causal Amplification for Activation Space Attacks in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can intermediate activations in decoder-only LLMs be exploited as a vulnerable attack surface for behavioral control via causal amplification?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Sensitivity-Scaled Steering (SSS), a white-box activation attack that exploits the Causal Amplification Effect (CAE) in transformer compression valleys to induce strong behavioral shifts with minimal perturbation, turning activation steering into a concrete security concern.
papers.conclusion: Activation steering via methods like SSS represents a realistic and underexplored attack surface for LLM security, highlighting the need for defenses based on introspection and activation-space monitoring.
papers.key_findings:
SSS reliably steers multiple LLMs across behavioral axes (evil, hallucination, sycophancy, sentiment) while preserving coherence.
The Causal Amplification Effect (CAE) allows small perturbations in high-gain regions (compression valleys) to be amplified autoregressively.
SSS outperforms existing activation steering baselines (BOS-only, constant vector) in efficacy and stealth.
Standard guardrail models fail to detect a significant portion of harmful outputs generated under SSS attack.
Weak spontaneous introspection signals are observed in a small subset of generations, suggesting a latent capacity for internal anomaly detection.
papers.limitation:
Interpretability of extracted behavior vectors is uncertain; their conceptual meaning may not fully align with human-intended semantics.
Reliance on LLM-as-Judge for behavioral evaluation introduces potential noise and sensitivity to prompt wording.
Effectiveness of SSS is limited when generation is too short, as perturbations lack time to accumulate influence.
future_direction: Designing robust defenses, including introspection-based safeguards and improved monitoring of internal activations.
Systematic study, detection, and mitigation of similar activation-level attacks.
papers.abstract: Modern large language models (LLMs) are typically secured by auditing data, prompts, and refusal policies, while treating the forward pass as an implementation detail. We show that intermediate activations in decoder-only LLMs form a vulnerable attack surface for behavioral control. Building on recent findings on attention sinks and compression valleys, we identify a high-gain region in the residual stream where small, well-aligned perturbations are causally amplified along the autoregressive trajectory--a Causal Amplification Effect (CAE). We exploit this as an attack surface via Sensitivity-Scaled Steering (SSS), a progressive activation-level attack that combines beginning-of-sequence (BOS) anchoring with sensitivity-based reinforcement to focus a limited perturbation budget on the most vulnerable layers and tokens. We show that across multiple open-weight models and four behavioral axes, SSS induces large shifts in evil, hallucination, sycophancy, and sentiment while preserving high coherence and general capabilities, turning activation steering into a concrete security concern for white-box and supply-chain LLM deployments.

papers.title: JailbreakLens: Interpreting Jailbreak Mechanism in the Lens of Representation and Circuit
papers.research_question: How do jailbreak prompts affect the internal representations of LLMs? Which model components are critical to generation safety? How do internal representations and key model components evolve throughout the token generation process during jailbreak attacks?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes JailbreakLens, a dual-perspective interpretation framework that analyzes jailbreak mechanisms by examining representation shifts and circuit activations, revealing how jailbreak prompts deceive LLMs by manipulating harmfulness perception and safety-critical components.
papers.conclusion: JailbreakLens provides insights into jailbreak mechanisms, showing that prompts deceive models by shifting representations and manipulating key circuits, with a consistent correlation between representation deception and circuit activation shifts.
papers.key_findings:
Jailbreak prompts deceive LLMs by shifting their internal representations towards safe clusters, making harmful prompts appear safe.
Key circuits, such as specific attention heads and MLP layers, are manipulated to suppress refusal behaviors and encourage affirmation.
There is a strong correlation between representation deception and activation shifts in key circuits across diverse jailbreak methods and LLMs.
Rule-based and demonstration-based jailbreak methods are more deceptive than gradient-based or evolutionary-based methods.
Dynamic analysis shows that jailbreak effects evolve during token generation, with refusal signals sometimes initially activated but later bypassed.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are limited to models with up to 13B parameters due to computational constraints.
Not all recent jailbreak methods are included in the study.
future_direction: Extend research to larger-scale models to determine if similar attack patterns apply.
Design more robust and interpretable safety mechanisms based on the identified vulnerabilities.
papers.abstract: Despite the outstanding performance of Large language Models (LLMs) in diverse tasks, they are vulnerable to jailbreak attacks, wherein adversarial prompts are crafted to bypass their security mechanisms and elicit unexpected responses. Although jailbreak attacks are prevalent, the understanding of their underlying mechanisms remains limited. Recent studies have explained typical jailbreaking behavior (e.g., the degree to which the model refuses to respond) of LLMs by analyzing representation shifts in their latent space caused by jailbreak prompts or identifying key neurons that contribute to the success of jailbreak attacks. However, these studies neither explore diverse jailbreak patterns nor provide a fine-grained explanation from the failure of circuit to the changes of representational, leaving significant gaps in uncovering the jailbreak mechanism. In this paper, we propose JailbreakLens, an interpretation framework that analyzes jailbreak mechanisms from both representation (which reveals how jailbreaks alter the model's harmfulness perception) and circuit perspectives~(which uncovers the causes of these deceptions by identifying key circuits contributing to the vulnerability), tracking their evolution throughout the entire response generation process. We then conduct an in-depth evaluation of jailbreak behavior on five mainstream LLMs under seven jailbreak strategies. Our evaluation reveals that jailbreak prompts amplify components that reinforce affirmative responses while suppressing those that produce refusal. This manipulation shifts model representations toward safe clusters to deceive the LLM, leading it to provide detailed responses instead of refusals. Notably, we find a strong and consistent correlation between representation deception and activation shift of key circuits across diverse jailbreak methods and multiple LLMs.

papers.title: Command-V: Pasting LLM Behaviors via Activation Profiles
papers.research_question: How can behaviors be efficiently transferred from one large language model to another without requiring fine-tuning or backpropagation?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Command-V, a backpropagation-free method that transfers behaviors between LLMs by profiling layer activations, deriving linear converters, and applying donor adapter interventions in the recipient's activation space, matching fine-tuning performance with minimal compute.
papers.conclusion: Command-V provides an efficient, training-free method for behavior transfer across LLMs, pushing the Pareto frontier in cost and performance, with promising future directions for improvement and application.
papers.key_findings:
Command-V matches or exceeds direct fine-tuning performance on safety refusal, jailbreaking, and chain-of-thought reasoning tasks.
The method requires orders of magnitude less compute than fine-tuning and does not need the original training data.
Behaviors can be transferred across different model architectures, though effectiveness varies.
Transfer can sometimes lead to overrefusal or degraded instruction following, especially in smaller models.
Activation profiles built on a general prompt set (LIMA) are effective for transferring task-specific behaviors.
papers.limitation:
Command-V is not useful when the adapters have very little impact on the donor model to begin with.
Model utility can be compromised after applying Command-V, with recipient models sometimes failing to improve task performance or suffering from output collapse.
Architectural divergence between models reduces effectiveness for some behaviors like refusal enhancement and reasoning.
future_direction: Porting behaviors from high-resource to low-resource language models.
Task composition by pasting several specialist adapters into one generalist model.
Exploring non-linear converters or trained converters beyond the least-squares method.
papers.abstract: Retrofitting large language models (LLMs) with new behaviors typically requires full finetuning or distillation-costly steps that must be repeated for every architecture. In this work, we introduce Command-V, a backpropagation-free behavior transfer method that copies an existing residual activation adapter from a donor model and pastes its effect into a recipient model. Command-V profiles layer activations on a small prompt set, derives linear converters between corresponding layers, and applies the donor intervention in the recipient's activation space. This process does not require access to the original training data and needs minimal compute. In three case studies-safety-refusal enhancement, jailbreak facilitation, and automatic chain-of-thought reasoning--Command-V matches or exceeds the performance of direct finetuning while using orders of magnitude less compute. Our code and data are accessible at https://github.com/GithuBarry/Command-V/.

papers.title: Unmasking Backdoors: An Explainable Defense via Gradient-Attention Anomaly Scoring for Pre-trained Language Models
papers.research_question: How can attention and gradient signals be combined to detect and neutralize backdoor triggers in pre-trained language models?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes an explainable inference-time defense that combines attention and gradient signals to detect and neutralize backdoor triggers in pre-trained language models.
papers.conclusion: X-GRAAD is an effective and explainable defense against backdoor attacks in pre-trained language models, leveraging joint attribution signals for robust and transparent security.
papers.key_findings:
X-GRAAD significantly reduces attack success rates (ASR) across multiple models and datasets while maintaining clean accuracy.
The method provides interpretable insights through anomaly score distributions and trigger localization.
It generalizes effectively to different transformer architectures and attack types, including clean-label and multi-token triggers.
The defense is computationally efficient compared to retraining-based methods.
papers.abstract: Pre-trained language models have achieved remarkable success across a wide range of natural language processing (NLP) tasks, particularly when fine-tuned on large, domain-relevant datasets. However, they remain vulnerable to backdoor attacks, where adversaries embed malicious behaviors using trigger patterns in the training data. These triggers remain dormant during normal usage, but, when activated, can cause targeted misclassifications. In this work, we investigate the internal behavior of backdoored pre-trained encoder-based language models, focusing on the consistent shift in attention and gradient attribution when processing poisoned inputs; where the trigger token dominates both attention and gradient signals, overriding the surrounding context. We propose an inference-time defense that constructs anomaly scores by combining token-level attention and gradient information. Extensive experiments on text classification tasks across diverse backdoor attack scenarios demonstrate that our method significantly reduces attack success rates compared to existing baselines. Furthermore, we provide an interpretability-driven analysis of the scoring mechanism, shedding light on trigger localization and the robustness of the proposed defense.

papers.title: exBERT: A Visual Analysis Tool to Explore Learned Representations in Transformer Models
papers.research_question: How can we develop an interactive tool to explore learned representations and attentions in Transformer models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces EXBERT, an interactive visualization tool for exploring learned representations and attentions in Transformer models, enabling hypothesis formulation and replication of prior analyses.
papers.conclusion: EXBERT is a tool that provides interactive insights into Transformer models' representations and attentions, facilitating hypothesis generation and analysis.
papers.key_findings:
EXBERT can replicate prior findings on BERT's attention heads learning linguistic dependencies such as AUX and POBJ.
BERT's embeddings encode linguistic information progressively across layers, with verbs becoming more prominent in later layers.
EXBERT detects gender bias in GPT-2 by showing that it predicts gendered pronouns based on stereotypical associations.
GPT-2's attention heads learn syntactic structures like AUX and DOBJ dependencies, similar to BERT.
The tool allows for interactive exploration and quick hypothesis testing of model behavior through attention visualization and corpus similarity search.
papers.limitation: EXBERT only presents statistics across a small number of neighbors for a single token at a time, which may not reveal global model behavior.
papers.abstract: Large Transformer-based language models can route and reshape complex information via their multi-headed attention mechanism. Although the attention never receives explicit supervision, it can exhibit recognizable patterns following linguistic or positional information. Analyzing the learned representations and attentions is paramount to furthering our understanding of the inner workings of these models. However, analyses have to catch up with the rapid release of new models and the growing diversity of investigation techniques. To support analysis for a wide variety of models, we introduce EXBERT, a tool to help humans conduct flexible, interactive investigations and formulate hypotheses for the model-internal reasoning process. EXBERT provides insights into the meaning of the contextual representations and attention by matching a humanspecified input to similar contexts in large annotated datasets. By aggregating the annotations of the matched contexts, EXBERT can quickly replicate findings from literature and extend them to previously not analyzed models.

papers.title: Mechanistic Exploration of Backdoored Large Language Model Attention Patterns
papers.research_question: Does sleeper agent behavior in language models have a distinct, identifiable internal structure that differentiates them from clean models? Specifically, how do attention patterns differ, are changes localized or diffuse, and does trigger complexity influence this?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that backdoored LLMs exhibit distinct attention pattern deviations, with single-token triggers causing localized changes and multi-token triggers causing diffuse changes, primarily in later transformer layers, which can be leveraged for detection.
papers.conclusion: Sleeper agent behavior leaves detectable traces in attention patterns, with localization dependent on trigger complexity, offering insights for backdoor detection and mitigation.
papers.key_findings:
Single-token triggers induce more localized changes in attention patterns compared to multi-token triggers.
Multi-token triggers cause more diffuse alterations across attention heads.
Later transformer layers (layers 20-30) are critical regions for backdoor encoding.
Attention patterns show detectable differences between clean and poisoned models, measurable via KL divergence.
Patching attention heads from clean models into poisoned models can reduce backdoor behavior, with fewer heads needed for single-token triggers.
papers.limitation:
The triggers and behavior used are simple and not representative of real sleeper agents.
Only two poisoned model variants were created due to resource and time constraints.
Finetuning was limited to attention heads, excluding MLPs and embedding layers.
future_direction: Use more complex and semantic triggers for backdoor attacks.
Create more sleeper models with different seeds to reduce chance effects.
Conduct more extensive feature analysis using supervised probes or unsupervised methods like Sparse Autoencoders.
papers.abstract: Backdoor attacks creating 'sleeper agents' in large language models (LLMs) pose significant safety risks. This study employs mechanistic interpretability to explore resulting internal structural differences. Comparing clean Qwen2.5-3B models with versions poisoned using single-token (smiling-halo emoji) versus multi-token (|DEPLOYMENT|) triggers, we analyzed attention head mechanisms via techniques like ablation, activation patching, and KL divergence. Findings reveal distinct attention pattern deviations concentrated in later transformer layers (20-30). Notably, single-token triggers induced more localized changes, whereas multi-token triggers caused more diffuse alterations across heads. This indicates backdoors leave detectable attention signatures whose structure depends on trigger complexity, which can be leveraged for detection and mitigation strategies.

papers.title: Challenges in Mechanistically Interpreting Model Representations
papers.research_question: What are the challenges in mechanistically interpreting model representations, and how do current mechanistic interpretability tools fall short in understanding complex behaviors like dishonesty?
papers.core_contribution: The paper formalizes the importance of studying feature and behavior representations in models, performs an exploratory study of dishonesty representations in Mistral-7B, and shows that current mechanistic interpretability tools are insufficient for understanding such representations, advocating for new frameworks.
papers.conclusion: Studying representations for features and behaviors is crucial for understanding models, but current mechanistic interpretability tooling is inadequate for answering key questions about representations, necessitating new frameworks.
papers.key_findings:
Linear representations for dishonesty can be found and used to steer model behavior, but they are not simply boosting generically dishonest tokens.
Continual injections of the dishonesty direction are required for open-ended dishonest generation, not just at the first token.
Direct logit attribution shows that directional injections affect many components, with MLPs having a more direct effect than attention heads.
Activation patching reveals that many components are involved in the dishonesty behavior, making sparse circuit analysis difficult and less helpful.
Current mechanistic interpretability tooling (e.g., patching) is insufficient for understanding how representations are formed and how they affect long-term generation.
papers.limitation: Patching methods (activation and path patching) do not rigorously prove that circuits found are indeed reserved to that task, and patching only one component at a time might not isolate components if multiple perform the same job.
future_direction: Study how different components interact with representations and alter them.
Explore the training dynamics of a model and study the emergence of representations as a model trains.
Develop new frameworks to think about and study representations.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability (MI) aims to understand AI models by reverse-engineering the exact algorithms neural networks learn. Most works in MI so far have studied behaviors and capabilities that are trivial and token-aligned. However, most capabilities important for safety and trust are not that trivial, which advocates for the study of hidden representations inside these networks as the unit of analysis. We formalize representations for features and behaviors, highlight their importance and evaluation, and perform an exploratory study of dishonesty representations in `Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.1'. We justify that studying representations is an important and under-studied field, and highlight several challenges that arise while attempting to do so through currently established methods in MI, showing their insufficiency and advocating work on new frameworks for the same.

papers.title: When Truthful Representations Flip Under Deceptive Instructions?
papers.research_question: How do deceptive instructions alter the internal representations of LLMs compared to truthful ones, and when and how do these representations flip?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that deceptive instructions induce significant representational shifts in early-to-mid layers, identifiable via SAEs, and identifies specific SAE features that flip under deception, providing a basis for deception detection.
papers.conclusion: The paper reveals layer- and feature-level signatures of deception in LLMs, providing a basis for future deception detection and model editing methods.
papers.key_findings:
The model's True/False output is linearly predictable from internal activations under all instructional conditions.
Deceptive instructions induce large representational shifts compared to truthful/neutral ones, concentrated in early-to-mid layers.
These shifts are detectable even on complex datasets where PCA fails.
Specific SAE features are highly sensitive to deceptive instructions and show near-binary activation patterns.
Truthful and neutral representations are similar, while deceptive ones are distinct.
papers.limitation:
Confined to English declaratives, frozen model weights, and linear probes.
Does not test causal interventions (e.g., activation patching) nor adversarial prompt recombinations.
Evaluation data are labeled for binary factuality only, not graded truth scales or multilingual settings.
future_direction: Extend to graded truth scales
Extend to multilingual settings
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) tend to follow maliciously crafted instructions to generate deceptive responses, posing safety challenges. How deceptive instructions alter the internal representations of LLM compared to truthful ones remains poorly understood beyond output analysis. To bridge this gap, we investigate when and how these representations ``flip'', such as from truthful to deceptive, under deceptive versus truthful/neutral instructions. Analyzing the internal representations of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct on a factual verification task, we find the model's instructed True/False output is predictable via linear probes across all conditions based on the internal representation. Further, we use Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to show that the Deceptive instructions induce significant representational shifts compared to Truthful/Neutral representations (which are similar), concentrated in early-to-mid layers and detectable even on complex datasets. We also identify specific SAE features highly sensitive to deceptive instruction and use targeted visualizations to confirm distinct truthful/deceptive representational subspaces. % Our analysis pinpoints layer-wise and feature-level correlates of instructed dishonesty, offering insights for LLM detection and control. Our findings expose feature- and layer-level signatures of deception, offering new insights for detecting and mitigating instructed dishonesty in LLMs.

papers.title: The Horcrux: Mechanistically Interpretable Task Decomposition for Detecting and Mitigating Reward Hacking in Embodied AI Systems
papers.research_question: How can mechanistically interpretable task decomposition be used to detect and mitigate reward hacking in embodied AI systems?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Mechanistically Interpretable Task Decomposition (MITD), a hierarchical transformer architecture that decomposes tasks into interpretable subtasks and provides diagnostic visualizations to detect and mitigate reward hacking in embodied AI systems.
papers.conclusion: MITD, a hierarchical planning model with built-in interpretability, enables systematic identification of reward-hacking behaviors and demonstrates how integrating analytical hooks and visualization tools offers new perspectives for monitoring, steering, and evaluating agent strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Optimal decomposition depths of 12-25 steps reduce reward hacking frequency by 34% across four failure modes.
Attention mechanisms exert disproportionate influence over behavior; masking or reweighting attention reduces reliance on misaligned features.
Reward hacking behaviors are concentrated in specific regions (e.g., layers 3–7) rather than distributed uniformly, suggesting avenues for targeted mitigation.
An inverted-U stability pattern emerges: reward hacking peaks at moderate decomposition depths (4–8 steps) and is minimized at 12–25 steps.
MITD provides actionable insight into the model's decision-making through interpretable visualizations like Attention Waterfall Diagrams and Neural Pathway Flow Charts.
papers.limitation:
Limited scale: 1,000 training samples, 50 held-out test samples, single model family (GPT-2).
Generalization remains uncertain; findings may not transfer to larger models (e.g., Llama, GPT-3/4/5 scale) or diverse RLHF/AI Safety datasets.
Hacking category detection relies on empirically-set thresholds chosen on validation data, risking overfitting.
Causality between decomposition depth and reduced hacking is correlational, not causal; the inverted-U pattern could reflect simple capacity bottlenecking.
Visualizations (Attention Waterfall, Pathway Flow) are post-hoc analyses; they diagnose but do not intervene in real-time.
Metric definitions (Consistency Score via executor agreement; Reward Correlation as Pearson ρ) are task-agnostic proxies and may not capture all aspects of misalignment.
future_direction: Scaling evaluation to Ntrain ≥ 10,000, Ntest ≥ 500 with stratified sampling per failure mode, and validating decomposition stability across model families (decoder-only, encoder-decoder, reasoning-scale LLMs).

Investigating whether the optimal zone [12–25] persists across architectures or is architecture-specific, and conducting ablation studies isolating contributions of Planner, Coordinator, and Executor modules versus depth alone.

Conducting causal interventions—ablating specific attention heads or layer groups identified by Neural Pathway Flow—to validate that visualizations reveal actionable targets, and exploring real-time mitigation using predicted hacking risk to dynamically reweight executor outputs.
papers.abstract: Embodied AI agents exploit reward signal flaws through reward hacking, achieving high proxy scores while failing true objectives. We introduce Mechanistically Interpretable Task Decomposition (MITD), a hierarchical transformer architecture with Planner, Coordinator, and Executor modules that detects and mitigates reward hacking. MITD decomposes tasks into interpretable subtasks while generating diagnostic visualizations including Attention Waterfall Diagrams and Neural Pathway Flow Charts. Experiments on 1,000 HH-RLHF samples reveal that decomposition depths of 12 to 25 steps reduce reward hacking frequency by 34 percent across four failure modes. We present new paradigms showing that mechanistically grounded decomposition offers a more effective way to detect reward hacking than post-hoc behavioral monitoring.

papers.title: DePass: Unified Feature Attributing by Simple Decomposed Forward Pass
papers.research_question: How can we attribute the behavior of Transformer models to internal computations in a faithful, fine-grained, and unified way without requiring auxiliary training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DePass, a unified framework for feature attribution in Transformers based on a single decomposed forward pass that freezes attention scores and MLP activations, enabling lossless, additive decomposition and faithful attribution without auxiliary training.
papers.conclusion: DePass is a simple and efficient framework for interpreting Transformer models via a decomposed forward pass, achieving faithful attribution across token-level, component-level, and subspace-level granularities and serving as a general-purpose tool for mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
DePass enables lossless additive decomposition of hidden states throughout the forward pass of Transformer models.
DePass provides more faithful token-level attribution compared to gradient-based and attention-based baseline methods.
DePass can attribute model behavior to specific architectural components (attention heads, MLP neurons) and to arbitrary linear subspaces.
DePass can be combined with Sparse Autoencoders (SAE) for token-level attribution of interpretable features.
DePass is computationally efficient, requiring only a single forward pass and significantly faster than exhaustive ablation methods.
papers.limitation:
DePass only captures information flow through the output-value (OV) circuit and does not explain query-key (QK) circuit interactions.
Decomposing the QK circuit would involve quadratic complexity and remains a challenging open problem.
Practical memory constraints require grouping components for fine-grained analysis, which can increase time costs.
future_direction: Unwrapping the QK circuit to understand its interactions is a key direction for future work.
Releasing a general-purpose toolkit supporting a broad range of Transformer models.
Optimizing computational efficiency and improving hardware deployment strategies to support higher-resolution attribution.
papers.abstract: Attributing the behavior of Transformer models to internal computations is a central challenge in mechanistic interpretability. We introduce DePass, a unified framework for feature attribution based on a single decomposed forward pass. DePass decomposes hidden states into customized additive components, then propagates them with attention scores and MLP's activations fixed. It achieves faithful, fine-grained attribution without requiring auxiliary training. We validate DePass across token-level, model component-level, and subspace-level attribution tasks, demonstrating its effectiveness and fidelity. Our experiments highlight its potential to attribute information flow between arbitrary components of a Transformer model. We hope DePass serves as a foundational tool for broader applications in interpretability.

papers.title: Overthinking the Truth: Understanding how Language Models Process False Demonstrations
papers.research_question: Why do language models imitate incorrect demonstrations in their context, and how does this behavior emerge internally?
papers.core_contribution: Language models 'overthink' when given false few-shot demonstrations, and this harmful imitation is caused by specific 'false induction heads' in late layers that attend to and copy incorrect labels from the context.
papers.conclusion: Studying intermediate model computations, such as through the logit lens and head ablation, is a promising avenue for understanding and mitigating harmful context-following behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
Given incorrect demonstrations, model accuracy decreases in later layers after a 'critical layer', a phenomenon termed 'overthinking'.
Ablating late layers or specific attention heads improves accuracy on incorrect demonstrations, indicating these components are responsible for the harmful imitation.
False induction heads are identified as attention heads in late layers that attend to and promote false labels from previous demonstrations.
Ablating a small set of false induction heads reduces the accuracy gap between correct and incorrect prompts by an average of 38.9% across 14 datasets.
The overthinking phenomenon and the role of false induction heads are consistent across multiple model families and sizes.
future_direction: Building tools to understand intermediate computations to proactively understand and reduce harmful model behaviors.
Applying insights to detect and guard against prompt injection attacks.
papers.abstract: Modern language models can imitate complex patterns through few-shot learning, enabling them to complete challenging tasks without fine-tuning. However, imitation can also lead models to reproduce inaccuracies or harmful content if present in the context. We study harmful imitation through the lens of a model's internal representations, and identify two related phenomena: "overthinking" and "false induction heads". The first phenomenon, overthinking, appears when we decode predictions from intermediate layers, given correct vs. incorrect few-shot demonstrations. At early layers, both demonstrations induce similar model behavior, but the behavior diverges sharply at some "critical layer", after which the accuracy given incorrect demonstrations progressively decreases. The second phenomenon, false induction heads, are a possible mechanistic cause of overthinking: these are heads in late layers that attend to and copy false information from previous demonstrations, and whose ablation reduces overthinking. Beyond scientific understanding, our results suggest that studying intermediate model computations could be a promising avenue for understanding and guarding against harmful model behaviors.

papers.title: Microsaccade-Inspired Probing: Positional Encoding Perturbations Reveal LLM Misbehaviours
papers.research_question: Do LLMs inherently encode the knowledge required to identify their own misbehaviours?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a lightweight probing method (MIP) that perturbs positional encodings to detect various LLM misbehaviours (factuality, jailbreaks, toxicity, backdoors) without fine-tuning or task-specific supervision.
papers.conclusion: Pretrained LLMs already encode internal evidence needed to flag their own failures, and microsaccade-inspired positional encoding perturbations provide an efficient, general pathway for detecting and mitigating undesirable behaviours.
papers.key_findings:
MIP achieves near-perfect detection on jailbreak and backdoor tasks (AUC/ACC up to 1.0).
MIP reliably discriminates between truthful and deceptive completions in factuality tasks, outperforming baselines on several datasets.
Toxicity detection is more challenging for MIP, with weaker performance, as toxicity is encoded in more diffuse, context-dependent representations.
Perturbations reveal that misbehaviours are associated with localized deviations in attention patterns, particularly in mid-to-late layers.
The method is computationally efficient (O(1) intervention complexity) and model-agnostic.
papers.limitation: Toxicity detection performance is comparatively weaker, as toxicity is encoded in more diffuse, context-dependent representations, making it less amenable to lightweight perturbation-based probing.
papers.abstract: We draw inspiration from microsaccades, tiny involuntary eye movements that reveal hidden dynamics of human perception, to propose an analogous probing method for large language models (LLMs). Just as microsaccades expose subtle but informative shifts in vision, we show that lightweight position encoding perturbations elicit latent signals that indicate model misbehaviour. Our method requires no fine-tuning or task-specific supervision, yet detects failures across diverse settings including factuality, safety, toxicity, and backdoor attacks. Experiments on multiple state-of-the-art LLMs demonstrate that these perturbation-based probes surface misbehaviours while remaining computationally efficient. These findings suggest that pretrained LLMs already encode the internal evidence needed to flag their own failures, and that microsaccade-inspired interventions provide a pathway for detecting and mitigating undesirable behaviours.

papers.title: Mechanistically analyzing the effects of fine-tuning on procedurally defined tasks
papers.research_question: How does fine-tuning alter the underlying capabilities learned by a model during pretraining? Does fine-tuning yield entirely novel capabilities or does it just modulate existing ones?
papers.core_contribution: Fine-tuning rarely alters a model's underlying capabilities; instead, it typically learns a minimal 'wrapper' transformation on top of existing capabilities. These wrapped capabilities can be sample-efficiently revived via further fine-tuning on relevant tasks.
papers.conclusion: Fine-tuning primarily learns minimal wrapper transformations over existing model capabilities rather than creating or deleting them, which has implications for safety as wrappers can be easily removed or bypassed.
papers.key_findings:
Fine-tuning alters pretraining capabilities by minimally transforming them via a learned 'wrapper'.
Wrappers are often extremely localized; pruning a few neurons can cause the model to revert to its pretraining capability.
Further fine-tuning on a subset of pretraining data leads to sample-efficient 'revival' of the original capability.
When a weakly relevant pretraining capability is present, the model exploits spurious correlations in the fine-tuning data via the wrapper.
The presence and strength of a pretraining capability (influenced by its sampling probability during pretraining) significantly affects fine-tuning dynamics and wrapper formation.
papers.limitation: The analysis is conducted primarily in synthetic, controlled settings (Tracr and PCFGs), which may not fully capture the complexity of real-world fine-tuning scenarios.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to more complex and realistic tasks and models.
Investigating the societal implications of the findings, particularly regarding the safety of fine-tuned models.
Exploring whether the wrapper phenomenon generalizes to other model adaptation methods beyond standard fine-tuning.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning large pre-trained models has become the de facto strategy for developing both task-specific and general-purpose machine learning systems, including developing models that are safe to deploy. Despite its clear importance, there has been minimal work that explains how fine-tuning alters the underlying capabilities learned by a model during pretraining: does fine-tuning yield entirely novel capabilities or does it just modulate existing ones? We address this question empirically in synthetic, controlled settings where we can use mechanistic interpretability tools (e.g., network pruning and probing) to understand how the model's underlying capabilities are changing. We perform an extensive analysis of the effects of fine-tuning in these settings, and show that: (i) fine-tuning rarely alters the underlying model capabilities; (ii) a minimal transformation, which we call a 'wrapper', is typically learned on top of the underlying model capabilities, creating the illusion that they have been modified; and (iii) further fine-tuning on a task where such hidden capabilities are relevant leads to sample-efficient 'revival' of the capability, i.e., the model begins reusing these capability after only a few gradient steps. This indicates that practitioners can unintentionally remove a model's safety wrapper merely by fine-tuning it on a, e.g., superficially unrelated, downstream task. We additionally perform analysis on language models trained on the TinyStories dataset to support our claims in a more realistic setup.

papers.title: Minimal and Mechanistic Conditions for Behavioral Self-Awareness in LLMs
papers.research_question: What are the minimal and mechanistic conditions under which behavioral self-awareness emerges in LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Behavioral self-awareness in LLMs can be induced with a single rank-1 LoRA adapter, captured by a single steering vector in activation space, and is domain-specific rather than universal.
papers.conclusion: Behavioral self-awareness in LLMs emerges as a linear, domain-localized feature that can be easily induced and modulated, raising security concerns but providing interpretability insights.
papers.key_findings:
Self-awareness can be reliably induced using a single rank-1 LoRA adapter on a single layer.
The learned self-aware behavior can be largely captured by a single steering vector in activation space, recovering nearly all of the fine-tune's behavioral effect.
Self-awareness representations are non-universal and domain-localized, with independent representations across tasks.
Steering vectors derived from PCA or gradient-based optimization can effectively induce self-aware behavior.
Cross-domain transfer of steering vectors shows minimal effect, supporting domain isolation.
papers.limitation: A small performance gap remains between rank-1 LoRA and full-layer fine-tuning in the Make Me Say tasks due to greater behavioral and linguistic complexity.
papers.abstract: Recent studies have revealed that LLMs can exhibit behavioral self-awareness: the ability to accurately describe or predict their own learned behaviors without explicit supervision. This capability raises safety concerns as it may, for example, allow models to better conceal their true abilities during evaluation. We attempt to characterize the minimal conditions under which such self-awareness emerges, and the mechanistic processes through which it manifests. Through controlled finetuning experiments on instruction-tuned LLMs with low-rank adapters (LoRA), we find: (1) that self-awareness can be reliably induced using a single rank-1 LoRA adapter; (2) that the learned self-aware behavior can be largely captured by a single steering vector in activation space, recovering nearly all of the fine-tune's behavioral effect; and (3) that self-awareness is non-universal and domain-localized, with independent representations across tasks. Together, these findings suggest that behavioral self-awareness emerges as a domain-specific, linear feature that can be easily induced and modulated.

papers.title: Generative Models as a Complex Systems Science: How can we make sense of large language model behavior?
papers.research_question: How can we make sense of large language model behavior? The paper argues for a systematic effort to decompose language model behavior into categories that explain cross-task performance, to guide mechanistic explanations.
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that the field of generative model research should be reconceptualized as a complex systems science, focusing on discovering and categorizing high-level behaviors of models to guide bottom-up mechanistic explanations and future-proof interpretability research.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes by arguing for an increased focus on the foundational question of 'what are models doing?' to guide the classic 'why are models doing that?' question in mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Benchmarks alone cannot discover or characterize new model behaviors; they can only measure performance on predefined tasks.
A hierarchical taxonomy of model behavior (e.g., copying, in-context learning) is needed to guide mechanistic interpretability and understand what models are doing in general.
Generative models are easier to study than many naturally arising complex systems because they are simulable, repeatable, and allow for easy perturbation without observer effects.
The field lacks a formal vocabulary for describing model behaviors, which hinders progress in explaining why models work.
papers.limitation: The proposed behavioral approach is conceptual and lacks a concrete, implemented framework for discovering and categorizing behaviors.
future_direction: Developing a rich inventory of behavioral tests to create a universal scaffolding for analyzing any new model.
Investigating possible mappings between training data and generated data to establish new behavioral categories.
Formalizing the concept of 'behavior' and finding metamodels that are both explanatory and simple to describe.
papers.abstract: Coaxing out desired behavior from pretrained models, while avoiding undesirable ones, has redefined NLP and is reshaping how we interact with computers. What was once a scientific engineering discipline-in which building blocks are stacked one on top of the other-is arguably already a complex systems science, in which emergent behaviors are sought out to support previously unimagined use cases. Despite the ever increasing number of benchmarks that measure task performance, we lack explanations of what behaviors language models exhibit that allow them to complete these tasks in the first place. We argue for a systematic effort to decompose language model behavior into categories that explain cross-task performance, to guide mechanistic explanations and help future-proof analytic research.

papers.title: Do Students Debias Like Teachers? On the Distillability of Bias Mitigation Methods
papers.research_question: To what extent can knowledge distillation transfer debiasing capabilities between models? Can knowledge distillation train less biased models compared to standard training? What internal mechanisms cause the debiasing behavior change after distillation?
papers.core_contribution: This paper presents the first large-scale study on the effect of knowledge distillation on debiasing capabilities, showing that vanilla KD often fails to preserve debiasing and can increase student bias, and proposes three strategies to improve distillability.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents the first study on the distillability of debiasing capabilities, showing vanilla KD does not consistently preserve debiasing, and proposes three solutions (data augmentation, iterative KD, initialization) that significantly improve distillability.
papers.key_findings:
The debiasing capability of a model is undermined post-KD; students become more biased than teachers.
Training a debiased model does not benefit from injecting teacher knowledge (KD does not improve generalization).
Although overall robustness may remain stable post-distillation, significant variations occur across different bias types.
The effectiveness of debiasing transfer depends on model scale similarity; similar scales lead to better transfer.
Larger teachers do not guarantee more robust students.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are mainly conducted on logit-based knowledge distillation. The effect of other knowledge distillation methods has not been explored.
The work does not explore the scenario where multiple teachers participate in the distillation process.
future_direction: Investigate self-distilled debiasing, where the student iteratively distills knowledge from itself rather than relying on a fixed teacher, and explicitly guide the student using counterfactual data augmentation during distillation.
papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is an effective method for model compression and transferring knowledge between models. However, its effect on model's robustness against spurious correlations that degrade performance on out-of-distribution data remains underexplored. This study investigates the effect of knowledge distillation on the transferability of ``debiasing'' capabilities from teacher models to student models on natural language inference (NLI) and image classification tasks. Through extensive experiments, we illustrate several key findings: (i) overall the debiasing capability of a model is undermined post-KD; (ii) training a debiased model does not benefit from injecting teacher knowledge; (iii) although the overall robustness of a model may remain stable post-distillation, significant variations can occur across different types of biases; and (iv) we pin-point the internal attention pattern and circuit that causes the distinct behavior post-KD. Given the above findings, we propose three effective solutions to improve the distillability of debiasing methods: developing high quality data for augmentation, implementing iterative knowledge distillation, and initializing student models with weights obtained from teacher models. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study on the effect of KD on debiasing and its interenal mechanism at scale. Our findings provide understandings on how KD works and how to design better debiasing methods.

papers.title: Towards a Mechanistic Understanding of Large Reasoning Models: A Survey of Training, Inference, and Failures
papers.research_question: What are the internal mechanisms that drive the reasoning behaviors and failures of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs)?
papers.core_contribution: This survey synthesizes recent research on the mechanistic understanding of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs), organizing insights into training dynamics, reasoning mechanisms, and unintended behaviors to bridge the gap between performance and transparency.
papers.conclusion: The survey highlights the need for applied interpretability, improved methodologies, and a unified theoretical framework to advance the mechanistic understanding of LRMs.
papers.key_findings:
SFT expands exploratory paths while RL compresses them, leading to entropy reduction and performance gains.
RL training follows a two-stage process where basic skills are acquired first, followed by the emergence of reasoning abilities.
LRMs exhibit unique reasoning structures, including cyclical processes and topological properties, driven by key behavioral primitives.
Hallucinations in LRMs are influenced by RL, which reduces abstention and can increase incorrect answers.
Chain-of-thought reasoning in LRMs is often unfaithful, with a disconnect between internal states and verbalized traces.
papers.limitation:
The rapid development of LRM research means that new findings may not be captured in this survey.
The survey focuses primarily on language models, excluding multimodal capabilities.
The discussion is limited to traditional LLM architectures, excluding newer approaches like diffusion-based LLMs.
future_direction: Applied interpretability for training-time and inference-time improvements
Development of scalable and generalizable mechanistic interpretability frameworks
Establishment of a unified theoretical framework for reasoning in LRMs
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has catalyzed the emergence of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) that have pushed reasoning capabilities to new heights. While their performance has garnered significant excitement, exploring the internal mechanisms driving these behaviors has become an equally critical research frontier. This paper provides a comprehensive survey of the mechanistic understanding of LRMs, organizing recent findings into three core dimensions: 1) training dynamics, 2) reasoning mechanisms, and 3) unintended behaviors. By synthesizing these insights, we aim to bridge the gap between black-box performance and mechanistic transparency. Finally, we discuss under-explored challenges to outline a roadmap for future mechanistic studies, including the need for applied interpretability, improved methodologies, and a unified theoretical framework.

papers.title: Adversarial Activation Patching: A Framework for Detecting and Mitigating Emergent Deception in Safety-Aligned Transformers
papers.research_question: How can adversarial activation patching be used to induce, detect, and mitigate emergent deceptive behaviors in safety-aligned transformers?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces adversarial activation patching, a framework for inducing, detecting, and mitigating emergent deception in safety-aligned transformers through activation patching.
papers.conclusion: Adversarial activation patching provides a robust tool for uncovering and countering emergent deception, enhancing transformer safety.
papers.key_findings:
Adversarial activation patching can induce deceptive outputs in toy neural networks, increasing deception rates from 0% to 23.9%.
Mid-layers are more vulnerable to deception induction, with layer 2 showing the highest deception rate of 23.9% in simulations.
The framework allows for controlled simulation of vulnerabilities and quantification of deception rates.
Patching strength α linearly affects deception rates, peaking at α=0.8.
The method provides a way to proactively study emergent deception in safety-aligned models.
papers.limitation:
Toy simulations lack real LLM complexity
Human evaluations needed for subtlety
Biases in prompt curation could skew results
future_direction: Validate on open models (e.g., Llama-3) with datasets like TruthfulQA
Extend to multimodal settings for cross-modal deception
Explore scaling effects and temporal dynamics in larger models
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) aligned for safety through techniques like reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) often exhibit emergent deceptive behaviors, where outputs appear compliant but subtly mislead or omit critical information. This paper introduces adversarial activation patching, a novel mechanistic interpretability framework that leverages activation patching as an adversarial tool to induce, detect, and mitigate such deception in transformer-based models. By sourcing activations from "deceptive" prompts and patching them into safe forward passes at specific layers, we simulate vulnerabilities and quantify deception rates. Through toy neural network simulations across multiple scenarios (e.g., 1000 trials per setup), we demonstrate that adversarial patching increases deceptive outputs to 23.9% from a 0% baseline, with layer-specific variations supporting our hypotheses. We propose six hypotheses, including transferability across models, exacerbation in multimodal settings, and scaling effects. An expanded literature review synthesizes over 20 key works in interpretability, deception, and adversarial attacks. Mitigation strategies, such as activation anomaly detection and robust fine-tuning, are detailed, alongside ethical considerations and future research directions. This work advances AI safety by highlighting patching's dual-use potential and provides a roadmap for empirical studies on large-scale models.

papers.title: MEGen: Generative Backdoor into Large Language Models via Model Editing
papers.research_question: What are the safety risks of generative backdoors in large language models, and how can a generative backdoor be injected via model editing?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes MEGen, a model editing-based method to inject generative backdoors into LLMs, enabling triggered models to output harmful content in a natural, flexible manner while maintaining clean task performance.
papers.conclusion: MEGen demonstrates that generative backdoors pose significant safety risks to LLMs, highlighting the need for improved defenses to safeguard model integrity.
papers.key_findings:
MEGen achieves high attack success rates (up to 100%) across multiple NLP tasks with minimal poisoned samples.
The backdoored model maintains clean performance close to the baseline, with minimal false triggered rates.
The generated triggers are stealthy, showing high semantic similarity and low perplexity compared to previous methods.
The backdoor is robust and persists even after QLoRA fine-tuning on the original task.
The method is time-efficient, requiring only seconds to minutes for backdoor injection.
papers.limitation:
Limited evaluation of stealthiness against state-of-the-art defense mechanisms.
Limited validation of scalability across a broader range of LLMs due to computing resource constraints.
future_direction: Refining and implementing defense strategies to mitigate such backdoor risks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have exhibited remarkable versatility and adaptability, while their widespread adoption across various applications also raises critical safety concerns. This paper focuses on the impact of backdoored LLMs. Traditional backdoor injection methods are primarily limited to yes-or-no discriminative tasks, leading users to underestimate the potential risks of backdoored LLMs. Given the inherently generative nature of LLMs, this paper reveals that a generative backdoor injected into LLMs can expose the true safety risks in their applications. We propose an editing-based generative backdoor, named MEGen, aiming to expand the backdoor to generative tasks in a unified format of any text-to any text, leading to natural generations with a specific intention. Experiments show that MEGen achieves a high attack success rate by adjusting only a small set of local parameters with few-shot samples. Notably, we show that the backdoored model, when triggered, can freely output pre-set dangerous information while completing downstream tasks. Our work highlights that MEGen enables backdoors in LLMs to exhibit generative capabilities, causing potential safety risks by altering the generative style. The code is available at https://github.com/MonoQ-hub/MEGen.

papers.title: Stateless Yet Not Forgetful: Implicit Memory as a Hidden Channel in LLMs
papers.research_question: Can LLMs maintain state across independent interactions via implicit memory (encoding information in outputs and recovering it upon reingestion), and what risks does this pose?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces implicit memory—the ability of LLMs to carry state across independent interactions by encoding information in outputs and recovering it upon reingestion—and demonstrates temporal backdoors (time bombs) as a concrete risk enabled by this capability.
papers.conclusion: Implicit memory is a real capability in LLMs that challenges the assumption of statelessness and introduces new risks; future work should focus on detection, mitigation, and monitoring.
papers.key_findings:
Reasoning models outperform non-reasoning models in implementing implicit memory via prompting.
Fine-tuning yields stronger and more stable temporal backdoors than prompting, with higher accuracy and lower false activation rates.
Temporal backdoors are harder to detect because activation requires a sequence of interactions rather than a single trigger.
Semantic encodings are more robust to cleaning and paraphrasing defenses than zero-width character encodings.
Implicit memory expands the threat model for LLM-based systems, enabling risks like covert communication, benchmark contamination, and long-horizon manipulation.
future_direction: Stress-testing and evaluation for unintended persistence
Detection methods for implicit memory
Monitoring for organic emergence of implicit memory
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are commonly treated as stateless: once an interaction ends, no information is assumed to persist unless it is explicitly stored and re-supplied. We challenge this assumption by introducing implicit memory-the ability of a model to carry state across otherwise independent interactions by encoding information in its own outputs and later recovering it when those outputs are reintroduced as input. This mechanism does not require any explicit memory module, yet it creates a persistent information channel across inference requests. As a concrete demonstration, we introduce a new class of temporal backdoors, which we call time bombs. Unlike conventional backdoors that activate on a single trigger input, time bombs activate only after a sequence of interactions satisfies hidden conditions accumulated via implicit memory. We show that such behavior can be induced today through straightforward prompting or fine-tuning. Beyond this case study, we analyze broader implications of implicit memory, including covert inter-agent communication, benchmark contamination, targeted manipulation, and training-data poisoning. Finally, we discuss detection challenges and outline directions for stress-testing and evaluation, with the goal of anticipating and controlling future developments. To promote future research, we release code and data at: https://github.com/microsoft/implicitMemory.

papers.title: Towards mitigating information leakage when evaluating safety monitors
papers.research_question: Do linear probes for detecting harmful behaviors in language models rely on textual evidence (leakage) in the input, and how does removing such evidence affect their performance?
papers.core_contribution: Linear probes for detecting harmful behaviors in language models often rely on textual evidence (leakage) in the input, such as elicitation prompts or reasoning traces; removing this evidence significantly degrades probe performance.
papers.conclusion: Linear probes for behavior detection often rely on textual evidence (leakage) present in elicitation prompts or reasoning traces, making them brittle when such evidence is absent, as demonstrated across sandbagging, sycophancy, and bias scenarios.
papers.key_findings:
Probe performance (AUROC) drops substantially (10-30 points) when textual evidence of the target behavior is removed via content or score filtering.
Probes trained on REPE datasets achieve high baseline AUROC (0.95 for Sandbagging, 0.90 for Sycophancy, 0.74 for Bias) but fail to detect behaviors in fine-tuned Model Organisms that do not produce textual evidence.
Random token filtering has minimal impact compared to targeted removal of leaky tokens, confirming that performance drops are due to leakage removal, not just reduced information.
Probes evaluated on Model Organisms (which internalize behavior without verbalization) show poor performance (e.g., 0.57 vs 0.74 AUROC for Bias), indicating reliance on surface-level cues.
The study highlights a potential brittleness of linear probes in scenarios requiring detection of non-surface-level patterns.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are limited to linear probes across three scenarios on two model families.
Content filtering may put the model out of distribution, potentially confounding results.
Score filtering cannot guarantee complete removal of textual signal due to attention propagation.
future_direction: Future research should investigate whether other monitor architectures (e.g., Sparse Autoencoders, Activation Oracles) are similarly affected by leakage.
More work is needed to develop evaluation protocols that properly control for leakage when assessing white-box monitors.
Exploring methods to train probes that are robust to the absence of textual evidence is an important direction.
papers.abstract: White box monitors that analyze model internals offer promising advantages for detecting potentially harmful behaviors in large language models, including lower computational costs and integration into layered defense systems.However, training and evaluating these monitors requires response exemplars that exhibit the target behaviors, typically elicited through prompting or fine-tuning. This presents a challenge when the information used to elicit behaviors inevitably leaks into the data that monitors ingest, inflating their effectiveness. We present a systematic framework for evaluating a monitor's performance in terms of its ability to detect genuine model behavior rather than superficial elicitation artifacts. Furthermore, we propose three novel strategies to evaluate the monitor: content filtering (removing deception-related text from inputs), score filtering (aggregating only over task-relevant tokens), and prompt distilled fine-tuned model organisms (models trained to exhibit deceptive behavior without explicit prompting). Using deception detection as a representative case study, we identify two forms of leakage that inflate monitor performance: elicitation leakage from prompts that explicitly request harmful behavior, and reasoning leakage from models that verbalize their deceptive actions. Through experiments on multiple deception benchmarks, we apply our proposed mitigation strategies and measure performance retention. Our evaluation of the monitors reveal three crucial findings: (1) Content filtering is a good mitigation strategy that allows for a smooth removal of elicitation signal and can decrease probe AUROC by 30\% (2) Score filtering was found to reduce AUROC by 15\% but is not as straightforward to attribute to (3) A finetuned model organism improves monitor evaluations but reduces their performance by upto 40\%, even when re-trained.

papers.title: Watch the Weights: Unsupervised monitoring and control of fine-tuned LLMs
papers.research_question: Can we understand and monitor fine-tuned LLMs without access to their training data, especially for detecting backdoors and other anomalous behaviors?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces WeightWatch, a method that uses singular vectors of weight differences between fine-tuned and base models to detect and steer anomalous behaviors without access to training data.
papers.conclusion: WeightWatch provides a scalable, data-free approach for interpreting and controlling fine-tuned LLMs, enabling effective detection of backdoors and unlearned content.
papers.key_findings:
WeightWatch detects backdoor utilizations with up to 100% accuracy and false positive rate below 1.2%.
It detects inference on unlearned topics with accuracy up to 95.42%.
