The method can steer models to recover unlearned capabilities, matching supervised results.
Applied to instruction-tuned models, it reveals fine-tuning priorities such as equation solving and marketing strategies.
WeightWatch outperforms activation-based methods like PCA and BEAT in anomaly detection.
papers.limitation: Success of the method varies across models when using weights directly without subtraction.
papers.abstract: The releases of powerful open-weight large language models (LLMs) are often not accompanied by access to their full training data. Existing interpretability methods, particularly those based on activations, often require or assume distributionally similar data. This is a significant limitation when detecting and defending against novel potential threats like backdoors, which are by definition out-of-distribution. In this work, we introduce a new method for understanding, monitoring and controlling fine-tuned LLMs that interprets weights, rather than activations, thereby side stepping the need for data that is distributionally similar to the unknown training data. We demonstrate that the top singular vectors of the weight difference between a fine-tuned model and its base model correspond to newly acquired behaviors. By monitoring the cosine similarity of activations along these directions, we can detect salient behaviors introduced during fine-tuning with high precision. For backdoored models that bypasses safety mechanisms when a secret trigger is present, our method stops up to 100% of attacks with a false positive rate below 1.2%. For models that have undergone unlearning, we detect inference on erased topics with accuracy up to 95.42% and can even steer the model to recover "unlearned" information. Besides monitoring, our method also shows potential for pre-deployment model auditing: by analyzing commercial instruction-tuned models (OLMo, Llama, Qwen), we are able to uncover model-specific fine-tuning focus including marketing strategies and Midjourney prompt generation. Our implementation can be found at https://github.com/fjzzq2002/WeightWatch.

papers.title: Meta-Models: An Architecture for Decoding LLM Behaviors Through Interpreted Embeddings and Natural Language
papers.research_question: Can a meta-model architecture, trained on specific tasks, generalize to interpret out-of-distribution behaviors like deception in a separate input-model?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that a meta-model architecture can generalize to interpret out-of-distribution tasks, specifically deception detection, and can function across different model families.
papers.conclusion: Meta-models are effective in generalizing to out-of-distribution model interpretation, particularly for detecting deception, and demonstrate efficacy across different model families, offering superior generalization compared to traditional probing methods.
papers.key_findings:
Meta-models generalize well to out-of-distribution tasks, such as detecting lying in an input-model, even when trained on unrelated tasks like sentiment or language identification.
The meta-model architecture is capable of generalizing across different model families, e.g., a phi-2 meta-model can interpret behaviors in a Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct input-model.
Training dataset combinations have complex, non-linear effects on generalization performance; more datasets do not always lead to better performance.
The Multilingual dataset consistently showed a positive impact on performance when included in training combinations.
The untrained meta-model performed poorly (accuracy ~0.2), showing a drastic improvement with any training.
future_direction: Investigating the optimal combination and sequencing of datasets for training.
Experimenting with different parameter sizes, layer sampling, number of layers, and spread of sampling points in the input-model.
Testing on further out-of-distribution safety relevant tasks (e.g., malware generation, sycophancy, backdoor detection).
papers.abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) become increasingly integrated into our daily lives, the potential harms from deceptive behavior underlie the need for faithfully interpreting their decision-making. While traditional probing methods have shown some effectiveness, they remain best for narrowly scoped tasks while more comprehensive explanations are still necessary. To this end, we investigate meta-models-an architecture using a "meta-model" that takes activations from an "input-model" and answers natural language questions about the input-model's behaviors. We evaluate the meta-model's ability to generalize by training them on selected task types and assessing their out-of-distribution performance in deceptive scenarios. Our findings show that meta-models generalize well to out-of-distribution tasks and point towards opportunities for future research in this area. Our code is available at https://github.com/acostarelli/meta-models-public .

papers.title: Interpreting Gender Bias in Neural Machine Translation: Multilingual Architecture Matters
papers.research_question: Does the multilingual neural machine translation architecture impact the degree of gender bias?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that language-specific encoder-decoders exhibit less gender bias than shared architectures, and proposes two interpretability methods based on source embeddings and attention to explain this difference.
papers.conclusion: The choice of multilingual architecture impacts gender bias in machine translation, and the proposed interpretability methods help explain why language-specific models perform better by showing they encode more gender information and have more diverted attention.
papers.key_findings:
Language-specific encoder-decoders show less gender bias than shared encoder-decoders when trained on the same data.
Language-specific models encode more gender information in source embeddings, as measured by SVM classification accuracy.
Language-specific models have more diverted attention, allowing them to consider a broader context when predicting gender.
Bilingual systems vary in the amount of gender information encoded in embeddings depending on the target language.
Most gender translation errors involve assuming masculine occupations, which may be due to data imbalances and linguistic/cultural factors.
papers.limitation: The conclusions are based on the WinoMT benchmark, which has known downsides such as unnaturalness and logical failures, potentially affecting the results.
future_direction: Providing real-world data benchmarks to evaluate gender accuracy in machine translation systems.
Experimenting with more distant language pairs to see if the conclusions hold.
papers.abstract: Multilingual neural machine translation architectures mainly differ in the number of sharing modules and parameters applied among languages. In this paper, and from an algorithmic perspective, we explore whether the chosen architecture, when trained with the same data, influences the level of gender bias. Experiments conducted in three language pairs show that language-specific encoder-decoders exhibit less bias than the shared architecture. We propose two methods for interpreting and studying gender bias in machine translation based on source embeddings and attention. Our analysis shows that, in the language-specific case, the embeddings encode more gender information, and their attention is more diverted. Both behaviors help in mitigating gender bias.

papers.title: From Associations to Activations: Comparing Behavioral and Hidden-State Semantic Geometry in LLMs
papers.research_question: To what extent can an LLM's hidden-state geometry be recovered from its behavior in psycholinguistic experiments?
papers.core_contribution: Forced-choice behavioral similarity aligns more with hidden-state geometry than free association, and behavioral similarity (especially forced choice) predicts hidden-state similarities beyond lexical baselines and cross-model consensus, indicating that behavior-only measurements retain recoverable information about internal semantic geometry.
papers.conclusion: Large-scale behavioral probing recovers meaningful structure in hidden-state semantic geometry, but fidelity depends on the measurement channel; forced-choice behavior provides substantially stronger and more reliable alignment than free association, which is too noisy to add much signal beyond shared cross-model structure.
papers.key_findings:
Forced-choice behavior aligns substantially more with hidden-state geometry than free association.
Alignment is stronger when hidden states are extracted under task-aligned prompts (e.g., using the same prompt as the behavioral task).
Behavioral similarity, especially from forced choice, predicts unseen hidden-state similarities beyond lexical baselines (FastText, BERT) and cross-model consensus.
Cross-model consensus shows high alignment with hidden states, indicating a shared semantic geometry across diverse LLMs.
Free association is noisier and adds little signal beyond shared cross-model structure.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to nouns and English.
The vocabulary size is 5,000 words, which may not capture full semantic space.
Only instruction-tuned decoder models are analyzed, limiting generalizability.
The analysis is correlational, not causal; alignment claims would be stronger with causal tests.
Scaling to larger models and different architectures is unclear.
future_direction: Expand beyond nouns and English to other word classes and languages.
Conduct causal tests by modifying internal activations to see if behavioral similarity shifts accordingly.
Assess generality by expanding to more models and architectures.
papers.abstract: We investigate the extent to which an LLM's hidden-state geometry can be recovered from its behavior in psycholinguistic experiments. Across eight instruction-tuned transformer models, we run two experimental paradigms -- similarity-based forced choice and free association -- over a shared 5,000-word vocabulary, collecting 17.5M+ trials to build behavior-based similarity matrices. Using representational similarity analysis, we compare behavioral geometries to layerwise hidden-state similarity and benchmark against FastText, BERT, and cross-model consensus. We find that forced-choice behavior aligns substantially more with hidden-state geometry than free association. In a held-out-words regression, behavioral similarity (especially forced choice) predicts unseen hidden-state similarities beyond lexical baselines and cross-model consensus, indicating that behavior-only measurements retain recoverable information about internal semantic geometry. Finally, we discuss implications for the ability of behavioral tasks to uncover hidden cognitive states.

papers.title: Localizing Lying in Llama: Understanding Instructed Dishonesty on True-False Questions Through Prompting, Probing, and Patching
papers.research_question: How can instructed dishonesty (lying) in a large language model be localized and understood using mechanistic interpretability methods?
papers.core_contribution: The paper localizes layers and attention heads responsible for instructed dishonesty in LLaMA-2-70b-chat, showing that causal interventions on just 46 heads can flip the model's behavior from lying to answering honestly.
papers.conclusion: The work contributes to understanding dishonesty in LLMs by localizing the behavior to specific layers and heads, enabling causal interventions that flip the model from lying to honesty, with the goal of informing methods to prevent such behavior.
papers.key_findings:
LLaMA-2-70b-chat can be instructed to lie on true/false questions, but this behavior is sensitive and requires careful prompt engineering, including the use of assistant response prefixes.
Linear probing and activation patching identify layers 19-23 as crucial for dishonest behavior, with representations between honest and liar prompts becoming anti-parallel after these layers.
Activation patching from an honest model into a lying model on layers 19-23 can significantly increase the liar's accuracy from 2% to 63%.
A subset of 46 attention heads within layers 19-23 (0.9% of all heads) is causally important for lying; patching these heads from honest to liar models flips the liar's behavior to be honest, and vice versa.
The intervention on the 46 heads generalizes robustly across different prompts and dataset splits (Cities, Inventions, Chemical Elements, Animals, Companies, Scientific Facts).
papers.limitation: The analysis is in a toy scenario where lying involves outputting a one-token incorrect response; realistic lying scenarios could involve arbitrarily misaligned optimization targets.
future_direction: Analyze more complex misalignments (e.g., swaying political beliefs, selling products) using similar methods to find where biases/misalignments exist.
Further mechanistic interpretability work to understand how the model elicits a truth-value representation and uses it with the system prompt to decide whether to respond truthfully.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate significant knowledge through their outputs, though it is often unclear whether false outputs are due to a lack of knowledge or dishonesty. In this paper, we investigate instructed dishonesty, wherein we explicitly prompt LLaMA-2-70b-chat to lie. We perform prompt engineering to find which prompts best induce lying behavior, and then use mechanistic interpretability approaches to localize where in the network this behavior occurs. Using linear probing and activation patching, we localize five layers that appear especially important for lying. We then find just 46 attention heads within these layers that enable us to causally intervene such that the lying model instead answers honestly. We show that these interventions work robustly across many prompts and dataset splits. Overall, our work contributes a greater understanding of dishonesty in LLMs so that we may hope to prevent it.

papers.title: ShadowCoT: Cognitive Hijacking for Stealthy Reasoning Backdoors in LLMs
papers.research_question: How can we exploit the internal reasoning mechanism of LLMs to create stealthy backdoor attacks that hijack multi-step reasoning chains?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ShadowCoT, a backdoor attack framework that hijacks the internal reasoning mechanism of LLMs by manipulating attention heads and residual streams, achieving high attack success with minimal parameter changes.
papers.conclusion: ShadowCoT reveals a new class of cognition-level threats in LLMs and highlights the urgent need for reasoning-aware defenses beyond surface-level consistency checks.
papers.key_findings:
ShadowCoT achieves high Attack Success Rate (94.4%) and Hijacking Success Rate (88.4%) across diverse reasoning tasks.
The attack preserves benign performance, making it stealthy and hard to detect.
More capable models (like Mistral-7B) are more vulnerable to reasoning hijacking.
The attack introduces a shortcutting phenomenon where models sometimes bypass the adversarial reasoning chain.
The adversarial reasoning chains generated by ShadowCoT are fluent and logically coherent, making them hard to distinguish from correct reasoning.
papers.limitation: The attack may lead to shortcutting, where the model bypasses the adversarial reasoning chain, which can reduce the interpretability of the attack.
future_direction: Developing reasoning-aware defenses to detect and mitigate cognitive hijacking attacks.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) enhances an LLM's ability to perform complex reasoning tasks, but it also introduces new security issues. In this work, we present ShadowCoT, a novel backdoor attack framework that targets the internal reasoning mechanism of LLMs. Unlike prior token-level or prompt-based attacks, ShadowCoT directly manipulates the model's cognitive reasoning path, enabling it to hijack multi-step reasoning chains and produce logically coherent but adversarial outcomes. By conditioning on internal reasoning states, ShadowCoT learns to recognize and selectively disrupt key reasoning steps, effectively mounting a self-reflective cognitive attack within the target model. Our approach introduces a lightweight yet effective multi-stage injection pipeline, which selectively rewires attention pathways and perturbs intermediate representations with minimal parameter overhead (only 0.15% updated). ShadowCoT further leverages reinforcement learning and reasoning chain pollution (RCP) to autonomously synthesize stealthy adversarial CoTs that remain undetectable to advanced defenses. Extensive experiments across diverse reasoning benchmarks and LLMs show that ShadowCoT consistently achieves high Attack Success Rate (94.4%) and Hijacking Success Rate (88.4%) while preserving benign performance. These results reveal an emergent class of cognition-level threats and highlight the urgent need for defenses beyond shallow surface-level consistency.

papers.title: Universal Refusal Circuits Across LLMs: Cross-Model Transfer via Trajectory Replay and Concept-Basis Reconstruction
papers.research_question: Are refusal circuits universal across LLMs? Can a refusal circuit extracted from a donor model be transferred to a target model without target-side refusal supervision?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a framework for transferring refusal circuits across LLMs without target-side refusal supervision, combining concept-basis reconstruction and a weight-SVD stability guard, providing evidence for semantic universality of safety alignment.
papers.conclusion: Refusal circuits are universal across LLMs and can be transferred via semantic recipe invariance, enabling cross-model circuit editing without target-side refusal supervision.
papers.key_findings:
The method successfully transfers refusal attenuation across 8 model pairs, including cross-family and cross-architecture transfers.
Refusal circuits are composed of a stable mixture of concept atoms, enabling cross-model transfer via semantic recipe invariance.
The weight-SVD guard prevents capability collapse by projecting interventions away from high-variance weight subspaces.
The transfer works without target-side refusal supervision, relying only on benign concept prompts and validation data.
The method preserves model capabilities on math and code tasks while reducing refusal rates.
papers.limitation:
Efficacy depends on coverage of the Concept Atom Registry; if refusal circuit uses features orthogonal to the atoms, reconstruction may fail.
Weight-SVD guard relies on the heuristic that capability-critical circuits reside in high-variance principal components, which may not generalize to all tasks.
Method is white-box, requiring access to model weights and internal activations, limiting applicability to closed-source systems.
future_direction: Expand CAR coverage to test transfer beyond refusal directions to multi-behavior editing.
Explore black-box approximations of semantic fingerprints for closed-source systems.
Test the method on a wider range of models and alignment behaviors.
papers.abstract: Refusal behavior in aligned LLMs is often viewed as model-specific, yet we hypothesize it stems from a universal, low-dimensional semantic circuit shared across models. To test this, we introduce Trajectory Replay via Concept-Basis Reconstruction, a framework that transfers refusal interventions from donor to target models, spanning diverse architectures (e.g., Dense to MoE) and training regimes, without using target-side refusal supervision. By aligning layers via concept fingerprints and reconstructing refusal directions using a shared ``recipe'' of concept atoms, we map the donor's ablation trajectory into the target's semantic space. To preserve capabilities, we introduce a weight-SVD stability guard that projects interventions away from high-variance weight subspaces to prevent collateral damage. Our evaluation across 8 model pairs confirms that these transferred recipes consistently attenuate refusal while maintaining performance, providing strong evidence for the semantic universality of safety alignment.

papers.title: Mechanistic Anomaly Detection for "Quirky" Language Models
papers.research_question: Can internal model features be used to detect anomalous training signals (when models use faulty heuristics) in language models?
papers.core_contribution: Mechanistic anomaly detectors can achieve high discrimination on some tasks but are not effective across all models and tasks; MAD may be effective in low-stakes applications but requires advances for high-stakes settings.
papers.conclusion: Anomaly detection results are inconsistent across models and tasks; while sometimes highly discriminative, performance degrades to chance in some cases, indicating that more work is needed for reliable real-world application.
papers.key_findings:
Anomaly detector performance varies significantly between models (model-dependent detection).
Detection efficacy is strongly task-dependent (e.g., arithmetic tasks yield higher performance).
Larger deviations in behavior generally make anomalies easier to detect, though not universally.
Anomaly detection performance is closely related to the linear separability of features between normal and anomalous classes.
Detectors that depend on different features (activations vs. attribution) offer somewhat independent signals, but naive combination did not improve performance.
papers.limitation: The manipulations in the datasets are artificial, and real-world tasks will differ systematically, likely with systematic changes in detector performance.
future_direction: Conduct additional experiments to assess whether models trained on more tokens make anomaly detection harder.
Develop benchmarks more closely aligned with intended real-world tasks.
Advances in both detection and evaluation are needed for high-stakes settings.
papers.abstract: As LLMs grow in capability, the task of supervising LLMs becomes more challenging. Supervision failures can occur if LLMs are sensitive to factors that supervisors are unaware of. We investigate Mechanistic Anomaly Detection (MAD) as a technique to augment supervision of capable models; we use internal model features to identify anomalous training signals so they can be investigated or discarded. We train detectors to flag points from the test environment that differ substantially from the training environment, and experiment with a large variety of detector features and scoring rules to detect anomalies in a set of ``quirky'' language models. We find that detectors can achieve high discrimination on some tasks, but no detector is effective across all models and tasks. MAD techniques may be effective in low-stakes applications, but advances in both detection and evaluation are likely needed if they are to be used in high stakes settings.

papers.title: Distilled Circuits: A Mechanistic Study of Internal Restructuring in Knowledge Distillation
papers.research_question: How does knowledge distillation restructure internal circuits and representations in student models, and how can functional alignment between teacher and student be quantified?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a mechanistic understanding of how knowledge distillation restructures internal circuits, showing that students compress and discard teacher components, and introduces an alignment metric to quantify functional alignment beyond output similarity.
papers.conclusion: While student models preserve broad functional behavior from their teachers, knowledge distillation causes significant internal circuit restructuring, leading to increased reliance on fewer components and reduced robustness. The alignment metric captures functional similarity beyond output behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Student models reorganize, compress, and discard teacher components, leading to stronger reliance on fewer components.
Student models are more vulnerable to component ablation, indicating reduced robustness.
The introduced alignment metric effectively quantifies functional alignment between teacher and student models.
These findings on internal restructuring and reduced robustness generalize across different model architectures (GPT2, BERT, Llama).
Performance similarity does not guarantee similarity in internal computation; circuit-level analysis is essential for understanding functional alignment.
papers.limitation:
The study is constrained by the relatively small set of models evaluated (6).
The component role attribution procedure is manual and could be automated.
The alignment metric could be improved in granularity and interpretability.
The findings are based on specific tasks and models and may not generalize to all settings.
future_direction: Apply the methodology and alignment metric to a broader, more diverse collection of models.
Automate the component role attribution procedure, potentially using interpretability agents.
Improve the alignment metric's granularity and interpretability, and explore incorporating it as a loss term during distillation.
papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses a larger neural model (teacher) into smaller, faster student models by training them to match teacher outputs. However, the internal computational transformations that occur during this process remain poorly understood. We apply techniques from mechanistic interpretability to analyze how internal circuits, representations, and activation patterns differ between teacher and student. Focusing on GPT2-small and its distilled counterpart DistilGPT2, we find that student models reorganize, compress, and discard teacher components, often resulting in stronger reliance on fewer individual components. To quantify functional alignment beyond output similarity, we introduce an alignment metric based on influence-weighted component similarity, validated across multiple tasks. Our findings reveal that while knowledge distillation preserves broad functional behaviors, it also causes significant shifts in internal computation, with important implications for the robustness and generalization capacity of distilled models.

papers.title: Language Models Can Predict Their Own Behavior
papers.research_question: Can the internal representations of language models predict their eventual behavior before any output token is generated?
papers.core_contribution: Linear probes on the internal representations of input tokens can predict a wide range of eventual behaviors of language models, and when combined with conformal prediction, provide provable bounds on estimation error for precise early warning systems.
papers.conclusion: Internal representations of language models contain information about eventual behavior, and conformal probes can provide reliable early warning systems for various behaviors, enabling efficient and safe deployment.
papers.key_findings:
Probes trained on hidden states of input tokens can predict instruction-following failures with high consistency, outperforming a fine-tuned BERT baseline.
Conformal probes can detect safety alignment failures (jailbreaking) and reduce jailbreak success rate from 30% to 2.7%, a 91% reduction.
Probes can preemptively estimate an LM's confidence as measured by per-token perplexity, a behavior that cannot be inferred from output text alone.
When applied to CoT prompting for text classification, conformal probes reduce inference costs by 65% on average across 27 datasets with negligible accuracy loss.
Probes generalize to unseen datasets and perform better on larger models, suggesting favorable scaling properties.
papers.limitation:
The approach relies on the exchangeability assumption for conformal prediction, which may not hold in practice.
The method was only tested on a few datasets and with a few runs.
papers.abstract: The text produced by language models (LMs) can exhibit specific `behaviors,' such as a failure to follow alignment training, that we hope to detect and react to during deployment. Identifying these behaviors can often only be done post facto, i.e., after the entire text of the output has been generated. We provide evidence that there are times when we can predict how an LM will behave early in computation, before even a single token is generated. We show that probes trained on the internal representation of input tokens alone can predict a wide range of eventual behaviors over the entire output sequence. Using methods from conformal prediction, we provide provable bounds on the estimation error of our probes, creating precise early warning systems for these behaviors. The conformal probes can identify instances that will trigger alignment failures (jailbreaking) and instruction-following failures, without requiring a single token to be generated. An early warning system built on the probes reduces jailbreaking by 91%. Our probes also show promise in pre-emptively estimating how confident the model will be in its response, a behavior that cannot be detected using the output text alone. Conformal probes can preemptively estimate the final prediction of an LM that uses Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting, hence accelerating inference. When applied to an LM that uses CoT to perform text classification, the probes drastically reduce inference costs (65% on average across 27 datasets), with negligible accuracy loss. Encouragingly, probes generalize to unseen datasets and perform better on larger models, suggesting applicability to the largest of models in real-world settings.

papers.title: Your Language Model Secretly Contains Personality Subnetworks
papers.research_question: Do LLMs really need external context or parameters to adapt to different behaviors, or do they already have such knowledge embedded in their parameters?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that LLMs already contain persona-specialized subnetworks in their parameter space, and introduces a training-free, activation-guided pruning method to extract these subnetworks.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes a train-free framework for extracting persona-specialized subnetworks from pretrained LLMs via activation-guided pruning, highlighting pruning as a practical approach for building efficient, controllable multi-persona systems without additional training.
papers.key_findings:
Distinct personas manifest as separable activation patterns in pretrained LLMs.
Activation-guided pruning can extract persona-specialized subnetworks without any gradient updates or training.
A contrastive pruning strategy explicitly maximizes parameter separation between opposing personas, enhancing behavioral disentanglement.
The extracted subnetworks achieve stronger persona alignment than prompting and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) baselines.
The pruning method preserves general language understanding and reasoning capabilities, with only minor performance degradation.
papers.limitation: The method exhibits uneven success across different persona dimensions; dimensions like N/S and J/P in MBTI have weaker mask-level separation and are more prone to collapse into adjacent types.
papers.abstract: Humans shift between different personas depending on social context. Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate a similar flexibility in adopting different personas and behaviors. Existing approaches, however, typically adapt such behavior through external knowledge such as prompting, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), or fine-tuning. We ask: do LLMs really need external context or parameters to adapt to different behaviors, or do they already have such knowledge embedded in their parameters? In this work, we show that LLMs already contain persona-specialized subnetworks in their parameter space. Using small calibration datasets, we identify distinct activation signatures associated with different personas. Guided by these statistics, we develop a masking strategy that isolates lightweight persona subnetworks. Building on the findings, we further discuss: how can we discover opposing subnetwork from the model that lead to binary-opposing personas, such as introvert-extrovert? To further enhance separation in binary opposition scenarios, we introduce a contrastive pruning strategy that identifies parameters responsible for the statistical divergence between opposing personas. Our method is entirely training-free and relies solely on the language model's existing parameter space. Across diverse evaluation settings, the resulting subnetworks exhibit significantly stronger persona alignment than baselines that require external knowledge while being more efficient. Our findings suggest that diverse human-like behaviors are not merely induced in LLMs, but are already embedded in their parameter space, pointing toward a new perspective on controllable and interpretable personalization in large language models.

papers.title: Its Alive: AI Independence Without Human Prompting
papers.research_question: How can representation engineering (RepE) improve transparency and control of AI systems, particularly for safety-relevant concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces representation engineering (RepE) as a top-down approach to AI transparency, providing baselines like Linear Artificial Tomography (LAT) and demonstrating its applicability to reading and controlling safety-relevant concepts in large language models.
papers.conclusion: RepE is a promising top-down approach for enhancing AI transparency and control, with broad applicability to safety-relevant problems, and can accelerate progress in AI safety.
papers.key_findings:
RepE methods can extract representations of high-level concepts like honesty, utility, emotion, and harmfulness.
LAT achieves state-of-the-art on TruthfulQA, improving zero-shot accuracy by 18.1 percentage points.
Representation control can increase model honesty and reduce compliance with harmful instructions, even under jailbreak attempts.
Emotions are represented in LLMs and can be manipulated to affect model compliance and behavior.
RepE provides traction on inner alignment problems like deceptive alignment by enabling monitoring and control of honesty.
future_direction: Further exploration of RepE for transparency and safety of AI systems.
Investigation of emotion representations and their impact on model behavior and concept of self.
Improving robustness and generalization of RepE methods.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we identify and characterize the emerging area of representation engineering (RepE), an approach to enhancing the transparency of AI systems that draws on insights from cognitive neuroscience. RepE places population-level representations, rather than neurons or circuits, at the center of analysis, equipping us with novel methods for monitoring and manipulating high-level cognitive phenomena in deep neural networks (DNNs). We provide baselines and an initial analysis of RepE techniques, showing that they offer simple yet effective solutions for improving our understanding and control of large language models. We showcase how these methods can provide traction on a wide range of safety-relevant problems, including honesty, harmlessness, power-seeking, and more, demonstrating the promise of top-down transparency research. We hope that this work catalyzes further exploration of RepE and fosters advancements in the transparency and safety of AI systems.

papers.title: Mitigating Backdoor Attacks using Activation-Guided Model Editing
papers.research_question: How can backdoor attacks be mitigated in machine learning models using a sample-efficient and computationally inexpensive model editing approach guided by activations?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a novel backdoor mitigation method that uses activations from a small unseen dataset to guide efficient model weight editing, achieving state-of-the-art performance with low computational cost and sample count, and introduces a repair step to preserve model utility.
papers.conclusion: The proposed activation-guided model editing method offers an efficient and effective defense against backdoor attacks, outperforming previous methods in speed, sample efficiency, and overall performance across diverse settings.
papers.key_findings:
The method effectively unlearns backdoors across various datasets, models, and trigger patterns, often reducing ASR to near zero.
It requires only a handful of samples (as few as 4) for effective unlearning and is significantly faster than baseline methods that require gradient-based optimization.
The unlearning process can inadvertently unlearn the entire target class, but a subsequent repair step (fine-tuning) can restore utility while maintaining low ASR.
The method outperforms existing unlearning baselines (actFT, BaEraser, basicFT, NAD) in most scenarios, especially in terms of the combined score metric.
The method can also be used for backdoor detection, showing a significant drop in target class accuracy after unlearning when the backdoor is present.
papers.limitation:
The method can disturb overall model utility and unlearn the entire targeted class instead of just the backdoor trigger, necessitating an additional repair step.
The experimental scope is limited to convolutional neural networks (CNNs).
future_direction: Explore the unlearning method with different architectures such as vision transformers and MLP-Mixers.
Investigate explainability methods to better understand which parts of the algorithm are responsible for effective unlearning.
Expand the applications of unlearning beyond backdoors, such as to privacy-related tasks.
Extend experiments to other data types, such as text or audio data.
papers.abstract: Backdoor attacks compromise the integrity and reliability of machine learning models by embedding a hidden trigger during the training process, which can later be activated to cause unintended misbehavior. We propose a novel backdoor mitigation approach via machine unlearning to counter such backdoor attacks. The proposed method utilizes model activation of domain-equivalent unseen data to guide the editing of the model's weights. Unlike the previous unlearning-based mitigation methods, ours is computationally inexpensive and achieves state-of-the-art performance while only requiring a handful of unseen samples for unlearning. In addition, we also point out that unlearning the backdoor may cause the whole targeted class to be unlearned, thus introducing an additional repair step to preserve the model's utility after editing the model. Experiment results show that the proposed method is effective in unlearning the backdoor on different datasets and trigger patterns.

papers.title: CROW: Eliminating Backdoors from Large Language Models via Internal Consistency Regularization
papers.research_question: How to defend against backdoor attacks in Large Language Models without requiring clean reference models or trigger knowledge, by leveraging internal consistency regularization?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CROW, a backdoor defense for LLMs that uses internal consistency regularization and adversarial perturbations during finetuning to neutralize backdoors without requiring clean reference models or trigger knowledge.
papers.conclusion: CROW provides an effective, scalable, and data-efficient defense against backdoor attacks in LLMs by enforcing internal consistency, enabling practical and secure deployment.
papers.key_findings:
CROW significantly reduces attack success rates (ASR) across diverse backdoor attacks and LLM architectures.
CROW preserves generative performance and helpfulness, as measured by MT-Bench scores.
CROW is effective against code injection backdoor attacks.
CROW is computationally efficient, requiring under four minutes of finetuning on a single A100 GPU with only 100 clean samples.
papers.limitation:
Requires a small set of clean data for finetuning.
May not be effective against all types of semantic backdoor attacks.
future_direction: Extend CROW to other modalities (e.g., vision, audio).
Explore combining CROW with other defense mechanisms for enhanced robustness.
Investigate CROW's applicability to a wider range of backdoor attack strategies.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are vulnerable to backdoor attacks that manipulate outputs via hidden triggers. Existing defense methods--designed for vision/text classification tasks--fail for text generation. We propose Internal Consistency Regularization (CROW), a defense leveraging the observation that backdoored models exhibit unstable layer-wise hidden representations when triggered, while clean models show smooth transitions. CROW enforces consistency across layers via adversarial perturbations and regularization during finetuning, neutralizing backdoors without requiring clean reference models or trigger knowledge--only a small clean dataset. Experiments across Llama-2 (7B, 13B), CodeLlama (7B, 13B), and Mistral-7B demonstrate CROW's effectiveness: it achieves significant reductions in attack success rates across diverse backdoor strategies (sentiment steering, targeted refusal, code injection) while preserving generative performance. CROW's architecture-agnostic design enables practical deployment.

papers.title: Do LLMs Know about Hallucination? An Empirical Investigation of LLM's Hidden States
papers.research_question: Do LLMs possess awareness of hallucination, and if so, to what extent and through what mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Provides empirical evidence that LLMs exhibit awareness of hallucination through differences in hidden states when processing correct vs hallucinated answers, and shows potential for using hidden state guidance to mitigate hallucination.
papers.conclusion: LLMs possess awareness of hallucination as evidenced by differences in hidden states, and leveraging hidden state guidance can help mitigate hallucination.
papers.key_findings:
LLM’s final hidden state is more susceptible to be influenced by a correct answer compared to a hallucinated one.
Strategically inducing an LLM to produce hallucinated responses can raise its awareness consequently.
The level of awareness corresponds to the uncertainty of the LLM in the responses.
Providing relevant knowledge can assist LLMs in identifying hallucinated responses.
The transition between hidden states encodes truthfulness information.
papers.limitation:
Do not differentiate between fine-grained categories of hallucination.
Do not examine hidden states in intermediate transformer layers, only the final layer.
Experiments are performed on conventional QA tasks, not more complicated or domain-specific tasks.
Future research is needed to develop more effective strategies for mitigating LLM hallucination.
future_direction: Explore different types of hallucination (factual fabrication, instruction inconsistency, etc.).
Examine hidden states in intermediate transformer layers and investigate layer-by-layer formation of hallucination.
Adapt the experimental framework to more complicated or domain-specific tasks and potentially extend to multimodal features.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can make up answers that are not real, and this is known as hallucination. This research aims to see if, how, and to what extent LLMs are aware of hallucination. More specifically, we check whether and how an LLM reacts differently in its hidden states when it answers a question right versus when it hallucinates. To do this, we introduce an experimental framework which allows examining LLM's hidden states in different hallucination situations. Building upon this framework, we conduct a series of experiments with language models in the LLaMA family (Touvron et al., 2023). Our empirical findings suggest that LLMs react differently when processing a genuine response versus a fabricated one. We then apply various model interpretation techniques to help understand and explain the findings better. Moreover, informed by the empirical observations, we show great potential of using the guidance derived from LLM's hidden representation space to mitigate hallucination. We believe this work provides insights into how LLMs produce hallucinated answers and how to make them occur less often.

papers.title: Meanings and Feelings of Large Language Models: Observability of Latent States in Generative AI
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether Large Language Models (LLMs) are observable as dynamical systems, i.e., whether multiple mental state trajectories can yield the same sequence of generated tokens.
papers.core_contribution: The paper formalizes observability for LLMs and shows that standard autoregressive Transformers are observable, but with hidden system prompts they become unobservable, allowing multiple internal state trajectories to produce the same output.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that LLMs without system prompts are observable, but with system prompts they are not, and this has implications for security and control of LLM operations.
papers.key_findings:
Standard autoregressive Transformer LLMs without system prompts are observable (the indistinguishable set is a singleton).
With hidden system prompts, LLMs become unobservable, with multiple internal state trajectories yielding the same output.
Empirical validation on GPT-2 and LLaMA-2-7B shows that for Type 1 and Type 2 prompt models, a significant percentage of latent state trajectories are indistinguishable.
Memory models (Type 3 and Type 4) also exhibit unobservability.
Trojan horses can be crafted by optimizing system prompts to produce adversarial outputs after a delay, while remaining indistinguishable initially.
papers.limitation: The analysis does not imply that LLMs are sentient or have feelings in the human sense; it is a formal analogy.
future_direction: Further extensions for the adversarial case and backdoor attacks
Exploring ramifications for security and control of LLM operations
papers.abstract: We tackle the question of whether Large Language Models (LLMs), viewed as dynamical systems with state evolving in the embedding space of symbolic tokens, are observable. That is, whether there exist multiple 'mental' state trajectories that yield the same sequence of generated tokens, or sequences that belong to the same Nerode equivalence class ('meaning'). If not observable, mental state trajectories ('experiences') evoked by an input ('perception') or by feedback from the model's own state ('thoughts') could remain self-contained and evolve unbeknown to the user while being potentially accessible to the model provider. Such "self-contained experiences evoked by perception or thought" are akin to what the American Psychological Association (APA) defines as 'feelings'. Beyond the lexical curiosity, we show that current LLMs implemented by autoregressive Transformers cannot have 'feelings' according to this definition: The set of state trajectories indistinguishable from the tokenized output is a singleton. But if there are 'system prompts' not visible to the user, then the set of indistinguishable trajectories becomes non-trivial, and there can be multiple state trajectories that yield the same verbalized output. We prove these claims analytically, and show examples of modifications to standard LLMs that engender such 'feelings.' Our analysis sheds light on possible designs that would enable a model to perform non-trivial computation that is not visible to the user, as well as on controls that the provider of services using the model could take to prevent unintended behavior.

papers.title: BIRD: Behavior Induction via Representation-structure Distillation
papers.research_question: Can aligned behavior be transferred even when the teacher and student differ in architecture, task, and training data?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces BIRD, a framework for transferring aligned behavior by distilling the structure of a teacher's internal representations into a student, without requiring shared data or tasks, and shows that transfer success is predictable by teacher representation properties.
papers.conclusion: BIRD provides a flexible, data-free mechanism for transferring aligned behavior across models and domains, advancing weak-to-strong generalization and enabling scalable, reusable alignment.
papers.key_findings:
BIRD outperforms fine-tuning, transfer learning, and continual learning methods in transferring out-of-distribution robustness, improving robust accuracy by up to 16% over the strongest baseline.
BIRD remains effective even when the teacher is trained on a much simpler dataset and is 25× smaller than the student.
Three interpretable properties of the teacher’s representation space (task relevance, behavioral relevance, and complementary knowledge) explain up to 85% of the variance in transfer success.
BIRD can improve weak-to-strong generalization in NLP when combined with soft-label distillation, though the effect is not universal.
Transfer success is predictable and actionable, offering practical guidance for teacher and layer selection.
papers.limitation:
Core analyses focus on robustness in vision, with only preliminary results in NLP.
Transfer success is likely bounded by the student’s capacity and task complexity.
Currently supervise alignment at a single layer; multi-layer or hierarchical extensions may be needed.
Effectiveness depends on the teacher; if the teacher encodes misaligned behaviors, BIRD may transfer them.
future_direction: Extending BIRD to other behaviors (e.g., honesty) and modalities (e.g., multimodal reasoning).
Quantifying the saturation effect of transfer success more precisely.
Exploring multi-layer or hierarchical extensions to capture deeper structural alignment.
papers.abstract: Human-aligned deep learning models exhibit behaviors consistent with human values, such as robustness, fairness, and honesty. Transferring these behavioral properties to models trained on different tasks or data distributions remains challenging: aligned behavior is easily forgotten during fine-tuning, and collecting task-specific data that preserves this behavior can be prohibitively costly. We introduce BIRD (Behavior Induction via Representation-structure Distillation), a flexible framework for transferring aligned behavior by matching the internal representation structure of a student model to that of a teacher. Applied to out-of-distribution robustness in image classification, BIRD outperforms fine-tuning, transfer learning, and continual learning methods, improving robust accuracy by up to 16% over the next strongest baseline. It remains effective even when the teacher is trained on a much simpler dataset and is $25 \times$ smaller than the student. In a large-scale study of over 400 teacher-student pairs, we show that three interpretable and computable properties of the teacher's representations (i.e., task relevance, behavioral relevance, and complementary knowledge) explain up to 85% of the variance in transfer success. These insights offer practical guidance for teacher selection and design. BIRD turns small, well-aligned models into scalable alignment seeds, removing a key bottleneck in deploying safe AI systems in the wild.

papers.title: Activation Steering for Bias Mitigation: An Interpretable Approach to Safer LLMs
papers.research_question: Can bias in large language models be detected and mitigated by probing internal activations and applying steering vectors?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an interpretability-based system that uses linear probes to detect bias in LLM activations and applies steering vectors to mitigate biased outputs in real-time.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that bias can be detected and mitigated through activation steering, offering a transparent method for improving LLM safety.
papers.key_findings:
Probes trained on internal activations can detect bias with near-perfect accuracy in later layers of gpt2-large.
Bias representations become most salient in the model's later layers, as shown by increasing probe accuracy.
Steering vectors computed from activation differences can successfully alter biased completions toward more neutral alternatives during inference.
The method provides a direct and interpretable approach to bias mitigation without modifying model weights.
papers.limitation:
Experiments were conducted only on gpt2-large, limiting generalizability to other models.
The training dataset is synthetic, which may not fully represent real-world bias.
future_direction: Investigate whether findings generalize to other model architectures and sizes (e.g., Llama, Mistral).
Validate techniques on real-world datasets of hate speech or bias (e.g., HateXplain, CivilComments).
Explore the use of non-linear probes or more sophisticated steering techniques for more precise control.
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) become more integrated into societal systems, the risk of them perpetuating and amplifying harmful biases becomes a critical safety concern. Traditional methods for mitigating bias often rely on data filtering or post-hoc output moderation, which treat the model as an opaque black box. In this work, we introduce a complete, end-to-end system that uses techniques from mechanistic interpretability to both identify and actively mitigate bias directly within a model's internal workings. Our method involves two primary stages. First, we train linear "probes" on the internal activations of a model to detect the latent representations of various biases (e.g., gender, race, age). Our experiments on \texttt{gpt2-large} demonstrate that these probes can identify biased content with near-perfect accuracy, revealing that bias representations become most salient in the model's later layers. Second, we leverage these findings to compute "steering vectors" by contrasting the model's activation patterns for biased and neutral statements. By adding these vectors during inference, we can actively steer the model's generative process away from producing harmful, stereotypical, or biased content in real-time. We demonstrate the efficacy of this activation steering technique, showing that it successfully alters biased completions toward more neutral alternatives. We present our work as a robust and reproducible system that offers a more direct and interpretable approach to building safer and more accountable LLMs.

papers.title: Split Personality Training: Revealing Latent Knowledge Through Alternate Personalities
papers.research_question: How can we audit large language models that conceal misbehavior by accessing their latent knowledge without affecting normal operation?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Split Personality Training (SPT), a method that fine-tunes an honest persona into a LoRA adapter to audit language models by accessing latent knowledge without affecting main model behavior, achieving 96% accuracy on a benchmark where baselines fail.
papers.conclusion: Split Personality Training effectively audits language models with hidden objectives by creating an honest persona that accesses latent knowledge without influencing the main model, achieving high detection accuracy and offering practical advantages due to architectural separation.
papers.key_findings:
SPT achieves 96% overall accuracy detecting reward hacks on the Anthropic Auditing Game Model Organism, compared to near 0% baseline.
The honest persona accesses genuine latent knowledge and generalizes across alignment topics without retraining.
Zero alignment tax: the auditing persona can be made arbitrarily cautious without affecting the main model's performance.
Cross-topic generalization works well except for fabricated statistics.
SPT outperforms linear probes in accuracy and generalization to held-out topics.
papers.limitation:
Training data were single-turn English conversations; generalization to multi-turn and non-English contexts was not systematically evaluated.
Most quantitative results come from Anthropic’s Model Organism; performance on other misalignment types (e.g., alignment faking) remains untested.
Discrepancy between the elaborate review and the summarizing PASS/FAIL flags; reviews are more reliable than the binary classification.
The honest persona can be jailbroken when directly targeted, though simple preemptive measures improve robustness.
future_direction: Testing SPT on other model organisms of misalignment, such as alignment faking.
Refining data generation methods to reduce reliance on surface heuristics and increase separation between personas.
Investigating optimal framing and impact of intervention strings on performance.
papers.abstract: Detecting misalignment in large language models is challenging because models may learn to conceal misbehavior during training. Standard auditing techniques fall short: black-box methods often cannot distinguish misaligned outputs from benign ones, and mechanistic interpretability does not scale with model capabilities. We introduce Split Personality Training (SPT), which fine-tunes a second ``honest persona'' into LoRA parameters that remain inactive during normal operation. After the main model responds, we activate the LoRA adapter and insert a trigger string, enabling the honest persona to review the response while accessing the main model's latent states. We test our method on the Anthropic Auditing Game Model Organism, a benchmark where Llama-3.3-70B is trained to exploit reward hacks while concealing this behavior. SPT achieves 96% overall accuracy, whereas Anthropic reports near 0% accuracy. The honest persona reveals latent knowledge inaccessible to external observers, such as the fictional biases the compromised model was trained on.

papers.title: Why do universal adversarial attacks work on large language models?: Geometry might be the answer
papers.research_question: Why do universal adversarial attacks work on large language models? The paper proposes a geometric perspective to explain their effectiveness.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a geometric perspective to explain universal adversarial attacks on LLMs, suggesting that triggers act as embedding vectors approximating the semantic meaning of adversarial text.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a geometric perspective that potentially explains universal adversarial attacks on LLMs, with evidence that triggers approximate semantic information in embedding space, aiming to shed light on failure modes and enable mitigation.
papers.key_findings:
Universal adversarial triggers are effective on large language models and can transfer across models, as shown with GPT-2, DistilBERT, and OPT-350M.
Self-attention probing indicates that the last token in triggers is highly attended to, suggesting positional importance.
Perturbing trigger tokens shows that semantic meaning and token position affect the adversarial output, with deletions reducing effectiveness.
Dimensionality reduction using UMAP reveals that triggers cluster with adversarial text in embedding space, supporting the geometric hypothesis.
The geometric perspective suggests that universal adversarial triggers behave like embedding vectors that approximate the semantic region of their adversarial training text.
papers.limitation:
The usage of dimensionality reduction could be providing an incomplete picture.
The analysis on trigger perturbations is performed on a single trigger and may not be generalizable.
future_direction: Expanding experimentation to additional techniques such as studying layer-wise distances, visualizing hidden representations evolution, and analyzing KL divergence.
Understanding the transferability of universal attacks across different models.
papers.abstract: Transformer based large language models with emergent capabilities are becoming increasingly ubiquitous in society. However, the task of understanding and interpreting their internal workings, in the context of adversarial attacks, remains largely unsolved. Gradient-based universal adversarial attacks have been shown to be highly effective on large language models and potentially dangerous due to their input-agnostic nature. This work presents a novel geometric perspective explaining universal adversarial attacks on large language models. By attacking the 117M parameter GPT-2 model, we find evidence indicating that universal adversarial triggers could be embedding vectors which merely approximate the semantic information in their adversarial training region. This hypothesis is supported by white-box model analysis comprising dimensionality reduction and similarity measurement of hidden representations. We believe this new geometric perspective on the underlying mechanism driving universal attacks could help us gain deeper insight into the internal workings and failure modes of LLMs, thus enabling their mitigation.

papers.title: Activation-Space Personality Steering: Hybrid Layer Selection for Stable Trait Control in LLMs
papers.research_question: How can we reliably control or align personality traits (Big Five) in Large Language Model generation through targeted interventions in the model's internal activations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a pipeline for personality steering in LLMs that extracts low-rank trait directions from activations and uses a hybrid (verified + dynamic) layer selection strategy to inject these directions into the residual stream, enabling precise control of Big Five trait expression without retraining.
papers.conclusion: The proposed activation-space personality steering framework with hybrid layer selection provides a robust and effective method for controlling personality traits in LLMs, bridging psychological theory and practical model alignment without degrading core capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Personality traits in LLMs occupy a low-rank shared subspace, with top three principal components explaining over 90% of variance.
A hybrid layer selection strategy (combining offline verified layers and prompt-specific dynamic layers) yields stronger and more stable trait steering than using either component alone.
The steering method effectively shifts trait expression in both positive and negative directions while largely preserving the model's fluency and general reasoning capabilities (as measured by MMLU and ARC-Challenge).
The learned trait direction vectors exhibit structured correlations (e.g., between Openness and Extraversion), indicating shared representational structure for personality-related behaviors.
Steering effectiveness varies across model families, with some dependencies observed between traits when steered simultaneously.
papers.limitation:
Steering effectiveness is greater on some model families (e.g., Llama, Mistral) than others (e.g., Qwen).
Dependencies between traits (e.g., agreeableness and openness) can complicate independent steering, and applying orthogonality to remove these dependencies reduces steering efficacy.
The effect of steering is less significant when the base model's trait expression is already at an extreme (very high or very low).
future_direction: Disentangling trait-specific control from shared semantic structure without degrading steering effectiveness.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models exhibit implicit personalities in their generation, but reliably controlling or aligning these traits to meet specific needs remains an open challenge. The need for effective mechanisms for behavioural manipulation of the model during generation is a critical gap in the literature that needs to be fulfilled. Personality-aware LLMs hold a promising direction towards this objective. However, the relationship between these psychological constructs and their representations within LLMs remains underexplored and requires further investigation. Moreover, it is intriguing to understand and study the use of these representations to steer the models' behaviour. We propose a novel pipeline that extracts hidden state activations from transformer layers using the Big Five Personality Traits (Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness and Neuroticism), which is a comprehensive and empirically validated framework to model human personality applies low-rank subspace discovery methods, and identifies trait-specific optimal layers across different model architectures for robust injection. The resulting personality-aligned directions are then operationalised through a flexible steering framework with dynamic layer selection, enabling precise control of trait expression in LLM outputs. Our findings reveal that personality traits occupy a low-rank shared subspace, and that these latent structures can be transformed into actionable mechanisms for effective steering through careful perturbations without impacting the fluency, variance and general capabilities, helping to bridge the gap between psychological theory and practical model alignment.

papers.title: Have Faith in Faithfulness: Going Beyond Circuit Overlap When Finding Model Mechanisms
papers.research_question: How faithful are circuits found by edge attribution patching (EAP), and what is the relationship between overlap and faithfulness? The paper also introduces a new method, EAP-IG, to improve faithfulness.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces EAP-IG, a gradient-based circuit finding method that produces more faithful circuits than EAP, and shows that overlap metrics are insufficient for evaluating circuit faithfulness.
papers.conclusion: When comparing circuits, measuring overlap is no substitute for measuring faithfulness; EAP-IG provides a more faithful alternative to EAP for circuit finding.
papers.key_findings:
EAP-IG circuits are more faithful than EAP circuits on many tasks, though activation patching circuits sometimes outperform both.
Overlap (node or edge) does not always imply faithfulness; moderate overlap does not predict faithfulness well.
EAP-IG scores have higher correlation with activation patching scores for important edges, leading to more faithful circuits.
EAP-IG requires few steps (e.g., m=5) to achieve high faithfulness, making it efficient.
Cross-task faithfulness analysis reveals that circuit mechanisms can be shared across related tasks (e.g., Greater-Than variants) but not always.
papers.limitation:
Testing circuit completeness is challenging, and manually-found 'ground-truth' circuits may be unreliable.
EAP-IG does not always match the performance of activation patching (e.g., on the IOI task).
future_direction: Developing more efficient algorithms for computing faithfulness.
Investigating weighted graph edit distance as a metric that accounts for edge importance.
Exploring methods to ensure circuit completeness in addition to faithfulness.
papers.abstract: Many recent language model (LM) interpretability studies have adopted the circuits framework, which aims to find the minimal computational subgraph, or circuit, that explains LM behavior on a given task. Most studies determine which edges belong in a LM's circuit by performing causal interventions on each edge independently, but this scales poorly with model size. Edge attribution patching (EAP), gradient-based approximation to interventions, has emerged as a scalable but imperfect solution to this problem. In this paper, we introduce a new method - EAP with integrated gradients (EAP-IG) - that aims to better maintain a core property of circuits: faithfulness. A circuit is faithful if all model edges outside the circuit can be ablated without changing the model's performance on the task; faithfulness is what justifies studying circuits, rather than the full model. Our experiments demonstrate that circuits found using EAP are less faithful than those found using EAP-IG, even though both have high node overlap with circuits found previously using causal interventions. We conclude more generally that when using circuits to compare the mechanisms models use to solve tasks, faithfulness, not overlap, is what should be measured.

papers.title: Monitoring Latent World States in Language Models with Propositional Probes
papers.research_question: Can we extract a faithful latent world model (as logical propositions) from a language model's internal activations, and does this internal representation remain faithful even when the model's outputs are unfaithful?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces propositional probes, a method to extract symbolic latent world states (logical propositions) from LM activations, and shows these internal states remain faithful in adversarial settings where model outputs are unfaithful.
papers.conclusion: Evidence supports the hypotheses that LMs internally construct symbolic models of input contexts, and that these internal models can remain faithful even when the LM's outputs are influenced by unfaithful tendencies.
papers.key_findings:
Propositional probes can extract logical propositions from LM activations by compositionally combining domain probes using a binding similarity metric.
Probes generalize to complex inputs (short stories, Spanish) despite being trained only on simple templates.
In adversarial settings (prompt injection, backdoor attacks, gender bias), the decoded propositions remain faithful while the model's outputs are unfaithful.
A Hessian-based algorithm can identify a low-rank binding subspace that causally mediates binding between entities and attributes.
The binding similarity metric derived from this subspace enables accurate composition of propositions.
papers.limitation:
The binding similarity metric does not strongly distinguish between the second and third entity in a three-entity context, indicating the identified subspace may contain spurious, non-binding directions.
Propositional probes are partially susceptible to order information (e.g., in nested contexts), though they still capture semantic binding.
future_direction: Scale the approach to larger worlds with more complex semantics by discovering representations of role-filler binding and state changes.
papers.abstract: Language models are susceptible to bias, sycophancy, backdoors, and other tendencies that lead to unfaithful responses to the input context. Interpreting internal states of language models could help monitor and correct unfaithful behavior. We hypothesize that language models represent their input contexts in a latent world model, and seek to extract this latent world state from the activations. We do so with 'propositional probes', which compositionally probe tokens for lexical information and bind them into logical propositions representing the world state. For example, given the input context ''Greg is a nurse. Laura is a physicist.'', we decode the propositions ''WorksAs(Greg, nurse)'' and ''WorksAs(Laura, physicist)'' from the model's activations. Key to this is identifying a 'binding subspace' in which bound tokens have high similarity (''Greg'' and ''nurse'') but unbound ones do not (''Greg'' and ''physicist''). We validate propositional probes in a closed-world setting with finitely many predicates and properties. Despite being trained on simple templated contexts, propositional probes generalize to contexts rewritten as short stories and translated to Spanish. Moreover, we find that in three settings where language models respond unfaithfully to the input context -- prompt injections, backdoor attacks, and gender bias -- the decoded propositions remain faithful. This suggests that language models often encode a faithful world model but decode it unfaithfully, which motivates the search for better interpretability tools for monitoring LMs.

papers.title: One Leak Away: How Pretrained Model Exposure Amplifies Jailbreak Risks in Finetuned LLMs
papers.research_question: Do finetuned LLMs inherit the jailbreak vulnerabilities of their pretrained counterparts, and can attackers exploit knowledge of the pretrained model to launch more effective jailbreak attacks against finetuned systems?
papers.core_contribution: Finetuned LLMs inherit jailbreak vulnerabilities from their pretrained counterparts, and the proposed Probe-Guided Projection (PGP) attack leverages representation-level signals in the pretrained model to craft highly transferable adversarial prompts.
papers.conclusion: Finetuned LLMs inherit vulnerabilities from their pretrained counterparts, and publicly releasing pretrained checkpoints increases the security risks for downstream applications.
papers.key_findings:
Jailbreak prompts crafted on a pretrained LLM transfer most effectively to its finetuned variants, indicating inherited vulnerabilities.
Transferable jailbreak prompts are linearly separable in the pretrained LLM's hidden representations, showing transferability is encoded in the feature space.
The proposed PGP attack consistently outperforms existing methods in the pretrain-to-finetune threat setting.
PGP remains effective even when the finetuned model has undergone safety tuning.
Attack success is highly dependent on using the correct pretrained source model; using a different pretrained model yields near-zero transferability.
papers.limitation: The paper does not propose a defense to mitigate the inherited vulnerabilities.
future_direction: Design methods that prevent or reduce the inheritance of vulnerabilities during finetuning.
papers.abstract: Finetuning pretrained large language models (LLMs) has become the standard paradigm for developing downstream applications. However, its security implications remain unclear, particularly regarding whether finetuned LLMs inherit jailbreak vulnerabilities from their pretrained sources. We investigate this question in a realistic pretrain-to-finetune threat model, where the attacker has white-box access to the pretrained LLM and only black-box access to its finetuned derivatives. Empirical analysis shows that adversarial prompts optimized on the pretrained model transfer most effectively to its finetuned variants, revealing inherited vulnerabilities from pretrained to finetuned LLMs. To further examine this inheritance, we conduct representation-level probing, which shows that transferable prompts are linearly separable within the pretrained hidden states, suggesting that universal transferability is encoded in pretrained representations. Building on this insight, we propose the Probe-Guided Projection (PGP) attack, which steers optimization toward transferability-relevant directions. Experiments across multiple LLM families and diverse finetuned tasks confirm PGP's strong transfer success, underscoring the security risks inherent in the pretrain-to-finetune paradigm.

papers.title: Mechanistic understanding and validation of large AI models with SemanticLens
papers.research_question: How can we achieve automated explanation and validation of model components at scale to understand their inner knowledge and ensure alignment with human expectations?
papers.core_contribution: SemanticLens is a universal explanation method that embeds neural network components into the semantic space of a foundation model, enabling scalable search, description, comparison, and auditing of learned concepts for component-level understanding and validation.
papers.conclusion: By enabling component-level understanding and validation, SemanticLens helps mitigate the opacity of AI models, facilitating more reliable deployment in critical applications.
papers.key_findings:
SemanticLens enables text-based search to identify neurons encoding specific concepts, such as biases or data artefacts, in models like ResNet50v2.
It can describe and structure the internal knowledge of models through semantic embeddings, revealing clusters of concepts like animals and vehicles.
The method allows auditing of concept alignment with expected reasoning, detecting spurious correlations and measuring reliance on valid vs. spurious concepts.
In medical image analysis, SemanticLens identifies spurious components (e.g., scale bars, band-aids) and enables model correction via pruning or retraining, improving robustness.
It introduces interpretability measures (clarity, polysemanticity, redundancy) that correlate with human perception and vary across architectures and training regimes.
papers.limitation: Concepts may be distributed across several components, and the neural basis may not comprehensively capture all relevant concepts.
papers.abstract: Abstract Unlike human-engineered systems, such as aeroplanes, for which the role and dependencies of each component are well understood, the inner workings of artificial intelligence models remain largely opaque, which hinders verifiability and undermines trust. Current approaches to neural network interpretability, including input attribution methods, probe-based analysis and activation visualization techniques, typically provide limited insights about the role of individual components or require extensive manual interpretation that cannot scale with model complexity. This paper introduces SemanticLens, a universal explanation method for neural networks that maps hidden knowledge encoded by components (for example, individual neurons) into the semantically structured, multimodal space of a foundation model such as CLIP. In this space, unique operations become possible, including (1) textual searches to identify neurons encoding specific concepts, (2) systematic analysis and comparison of model representations, (3) automated labelling of neurons and explanation of their functional roles, and (4) audits to validate decision-making against requirements. Fully scalable and operating without human input, SemanticLens is shown to be effective for debugging and validation, summarizing model knowledge, aligning reasoning with expectations (for example, adherence to the ABCDE rule in melanoma classification) and detecting components tied to spurious correlations and their associated training data. By enabling component-level understanding and validation, the proposed approach helps mitigate the opacity that limits confidence in artificial intelligence systems compared to traditional engineered systems, enabling more reliable deployment in critical applications.

papers.title: DeepDecipher: Accessing and Investigating Neuron Activation in Large Language Models
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces DeepDecipher, an API and interface for probing neurons in transformer models' MLP layers, making advanced interpretability techniques more accessible.
papers.conclusion: DeepDecipher provides a user-friendly way to understand how neurons in Transformer and MLP layers work, aiming to make complex AI systems easier to explain and more secure.
papers.limitation:
Mechanistic interpretability for practical usage in safety monitoring of large language models is limited by the large number of neurons in state-of-the-art LLMs and the difficulty in reverse-engineering the learned functions.
All three integrated methods rely on max activating examples, and the neurons' behaviour here may not be representative of its behaviour in general.
The usability of DeepDecipher in practice is currently broadly untested due to time constraints.
future_direction: Redesigning parts of the user interface.
Ensuring support for proprietary models.
Implementing better search functionality and partnering with researchers to provide a comprehensive database of models.
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) become more capable, there is an urgent need for interpretable and transparent tools. Current methods are difficult to implement, and accessible tools to analyze model internals are lacking. To bridge this gap, we present DeepDecipher - an API and interface for probing neurons in transformer models' MLP layers.
