Our results suggest that linear directions aligned with trait-scores are effective probes for personality detection, while their steering capabilities strongly depend on context, producing reliable effects in forced-choice tasks but limited influence in open-ended generation or when additional context is present in the prompt.

papers.title: How to Manipulate CNNs to Make Them Lie: the GradCAM Case
papers.research_question: Can we manipulate a CNN model to produce arbitrary GradCAM explanations without affecting its accuracy? Can we create a backdoor that triggers malicious explanations only when a specific pattern is present?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that GradCAM explanations can be manipulated without affecting model accuracy, and introduces techniques to do so, including a backdoor that triggers malicious explanations only when a specific input pattern is present.
papers.conclusion: GradCAM is vulnerable to model manipulation attacks, and explanation methods should be tested for robustness against such attacks.
papers.key_findings:
Techniques T1 and T2 can produce constant explanations (flat or fixed image) while leaving model accuracy essentially unchanged.
Technique T3 produces semi-random explanations dependent on the input with minimal accuracy change.
Technique T4 creates a backdoor that triggers a malicious explanation only when a specific pattern is present, without affecting accuracy.
GradCAM does not satisfy the axiom of Implementation Invariance (two networks with same outputs should have same explanations).
The manipulations are hard to detect by visual inspection of explanations, posing security concerns.
papers.limitation: The architectural changes required by the proposed techniques could be detected by inspecting the model architecture.
future_direction: Extending the attack to other explanation methods that rely on gradients.
Exploring attacks without architectural changes, e.g., by using weight pruning or knowledge distillation.
Determining assumptions that should be verified for GradCAM to produce accurate explanations.
papers.abstract: Recently many methods have been introduced to explain CNN decisions. However, it has been shown that some methods can be sensitive to manipulation of the input. We continue this line of work and investigate the explanation method GradCAM. Instead of manipulating the input, we consider an adversary that manipulates the model itself to attack the explanation. By changing weights and architecture, we demonstrate that it is possible to generate any desired explanation, while leaving the model's accuracy essentially unchanged. This illustrates that GradCAM cannot explain the decision of every CNN and provides a proof of concept showing that it is possible to obfuscate the inner workings of a CNN. Finally, we combine input and model manipulation. To this end we put a backdoor in the network: the explanation is correct unless there is a specific pattern present in the input, which triggers a malicious explanation. Our work raises new security concerns, especially in settings where explanations of models may be used to make decisions, such as in the medical domain.

papers.title: LLM Circuit Analyses Are Consistent Across Training and Scale
papers.research_question: Do circuit analyses of LLMs generalize across training time and model scale?
papers.core_contribution: Circuit analyses are consistent across training and scale: task abilities and supporting functional components emerge at similar token counts across model sizes, and the overarching algorithms implemented by circuits remain stable even when individual components change.
papers.conclusion: Circuit analyses generalize well over both training and scale, suggesting that studies on small models at the end of pre-training can inform understanding of larger models and models with longer training.
papers.key_findings:
Task abilities and functional components (e.g., induction heads, name-mover heads) emerge consistently at similar token counts across different model scales.
The algorithm implemented by a circuit remains stable over training even when the specific attention heads implementing it change.
Circuit size correlates with model size and can fluctuate over time while the algorithm remains the same.
Components like induction heads emerge around 2B tokens across scales, paralleling task learning curves.
Circuit analyses conducted on small models at the end of pre-training provide insights that generalize to larger models and longer training runs.
papers.limitation:
The study does not include fine-tuning or other post-training techniques.
Circuit completeness is challenging to verify.
The findings need validation on more complex circuits and those based on SAE latents.
future_direction: Validation on more complex circuits and those based on SAE latents.
Investigating the load-balancing mechanism that maintains task performance when components change.
papers.abstract: Most currently deployed large language models (LLMs) undergo continuous training or additional finetuning. By contrast, most research into LLMs' internal mechanisms focuses on models at one snapshot in time (the end of pre-training), raising the question of whether their results generalize to real-world settings. Existing studies of mechanisms over time focus on encoder-only or toy models, which differ significantly from most deployed models. In this study, we track how model mechanisms, operationalized as circuits, emerge and evolve across 300 billion tokens of training in decoder-only LLMs, in models ranging from 70 million to 2.8 billion parameters. We find that task abilities and the functional components that support them emerge consistently at similar token counts across scale. Moreover, although such components may be implemented by different attention heads over time, the overarching algorithm that they implement remains. Surprisingly, both these algorithms and the types of components involved therein can replicate across model scale. These results suggest that circuit analyses conducted on small models at the end of pre-training can provide insights that still apply after additional pre-training and over model scale.

papers.title: The Geometry of Harmfulness in LLMs through Subconcept Probing
papers.research_question: How can we understand and mitigate harmful behaviors in LLMs by decomposing harmfulness into subconcepts and analyzing their geometric structure in activation space?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that harmfulness in LLMs can be represented as a low-rank linear subspace in activation space, and steering in the dominant direction of this subspace can effectively reduce harmful generations with minimal utility loss.
papers.conclusion: The work presents a geometric approach to understanding and mitigating harmfulness in LLMs, underscoring the value of multidimensional probing for uncovering latent harmful behaviors and designing more controllable and transparent models.
papers.key_findings:
The harmfulness subspace formed by 55 subconcept directions is low-rank linear, with a single dominant direction capturing most of the variance.
Steering in the dominant direction allows for near elimination of harmful responses on jailbreak datasets with only a minor decrease in utility.
Linear probes for harmfulness subconcepts achieve high accuracy and generalize to out-of-distribution data.
Ablating the entire harmfulness subspace or just the dominant direction reduces jailbreak penetration with minimal utility loss.
The method works on two different models (Llama and Qwen), though with some differences in effectiveness.
papers.limitation:
The study has limited model testing and may not generalize well to other untested models of differing scales.
The subcategories of harmfulness tested are not extensive and may not include all possible subcategories of harmful model responses.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have intensified the need to understand and reliably curb their harmful behaviours. We introduce a multidimensional framework for probing and steering harmful content in model internals. For each of 55 distinct harmfulness subconcepts (e.g., racial hate, employment scams, weapons), we learn a linear probe, yielding 55 interpretable directions in activation space. Collectively, these directions span a harmfulness subspace that we show is strikingly low-rank. We then test ablation of the entire subspace from model internals, as well as steering and ablation in the subspace's dominant direction. We find that dominant direction steering allows for near elimination of harmfulness with a low decrease in utility. Our findings advance the emerging view that concept subspaces provide a scalable lens on LLM behaviour and offer practical tools for the community to audit and harden future generations of language models.

papers.title: Unveiling the Latent Directions of Reflection in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we systematically identify effective trigger instructions for reflection, and do these instructions correspond to latent directions in the model's hidden space?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method using activation steering to identify latent directions of reflection in LLMs, enabling systematic discovery of reflection-inducing instructions and control over reflective behavior, with the finding that suppressing reflection is easier than enhancing it.
papers.conclusion: The findings provide initial evidence that reflection corresponds to consistent activation patterns, paving the way for future interpretability work, and highlight a dual-use concern where steering can enhance reflection as a defense mechanism but also be exploited to inhibit reflection for jailbreaks.
papers.key_findings:
Reflection levels (no, intrinsic, triggered) show clear stratification in model accuracy.
Steering vectors can discover new reflection-inducing instructions beyond known ones.
Reflection can be enhanced or inhibited via activation interventions at inference time.
Suppressing reflection is easier than inducing it.
Latent directions of reflection are more faithfully captured by steering vectors than by surface-level embedding similarity.
papers.limitation:
The method provides a broad overview of reflection in activations but does not drill down into specific components like attention heads or MLP neurons.
Experiments are limited to two small-sized models (Qwen2.5-3B and Gemma3-4B-IT) and two datasets.
Theoretical understanding is limited; accuracy does not vary linearly with latent directions, requiring deeper treatment.
future_direction: Applying fine-grained approaches like activation patching, causal tracing, or circuit analysis to pinpoint precise circuits responsible for reflection.
Investigating whether the model internally maintains a form of 'consistency score' or probability mass over coherent reasoning trajectories.
Expanding evaluation to larger LLMs, different architectures, or broader datasets (e.g., MATH, HumanEval).
papers.abstract: Reflection, the ability of large language models (LLMs) to evaluate and revise their own reasoning, has been widely used to improve performance on complex reasoning tasks. Yet, most prior works emphasizes designing reflective prompting strategies or reinforcement learning objectives, leaving the inner mechanisms of reflection underexplored. In this paper, we investigate reflection through the lens of latent directions in model activations. We propose a methodology based on activation steering to characterize how instructions with different reflective intentions: no reflection, intrinsic reflection, and triggered reflection. By constructing steering vectors between these reflection levels, we demonstrate that (1) new reflection-inducing instructions can be systematically identified, (2) reflective behavior can be directly enhanced or suppressed through activation interventions, and (3) suppressing reflection is considerably easier than stimulating it. Experiments on GSM8k-adv and Cruxeval-o-adv with Qwen2.5-3B and Gemma3-4B-IT reveal clear stratification across reflection levels, and steering interventions confirm the controllability of reflection. Our findings highlight both opportunities (e.g., reflection-enhancing defenses) and risks (e.g., adversarial inhibition of reflection in jailbreak attacks). This work opens a path toward mechanistic understanding of reflective reasoning in LLMs.

papers.title: On the Biology of a Large Language Model
papers.research_question: How do large language models internally perform computations, and can we reverse engineer their mechanisms using attribution graphs?
papers.core_contribution: This work applies attribution graphs to Claude 3.5 Haiku, uncovering sophisticated internal mechanisms like multi-step reasoning, planning, and metacognitive circuits, demonstrating the value of unsupervised tools for model interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Attribution graphs enable detailed reverse engineering of model internals, revealing complex strategies and advancing the field of AI interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
The model performs genuine two-hop reasoning with intermediate steps, such as representing 'Texas' when answering about the capital of the state containing Dallas.
In poetry generation, the model plans ahead by pre-selecting rhyming words before writing each line.
Multilingual circuits use a mix of language-specific and abstract, language-independent components, with more abstraction in larger models.
Entity recognition circuits distinguish known and unknown entities, influencing when the model answers or refuses, with circuit misfires causing hallucinations.
Refusal mechanisms involve harmful request features aggregated from pretraining and trigger refusal during fine-tuning.
papers.limitation:
tools provide satisfying insight for about a quarter of prompts
replacement model incompletely and imperfectly captures the original model
future_direction: Developing more effective unsupervised exploration tools for increasingly capable models
papers.abstract: How do large language models internally perform computations, and can we reverse engineer their mechanisms using attribution graphs? This work applies attribution graphs to Claude 3.5 Haiku, uncovering sophisticated internal mechanisms like multi-step reasoning, planning, and metacognitive circuits, demonstrating the value of unsupervised tools for model interpretability. Attribution graphs enable detailed reverse engineering of model internals, revealing complex strategies and advancing the field of AI interpretability.

papers.title: Eliciting Latent Predictions from Transformers with the Tuned Lens
papers.research_question: How are model predictions refined layer by layer in transformers through iterative inference?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the tuned lens, a method that trains affine probes to decode hidden states in frozen pretrained transformers, providing more reliable and unbiased prediction trajectories than the logit lens.
papers.conclusion: The tuned lens is a drop-in replacement for the logit lens that provides interpretable prediction trajectories and has applications in anomaly detection and difficulty estimation.
papers.key_findings:
The tuned lens produces lower perplexity and less biased predictions than the logit lens across various models.
Causal experiments show that features influential on the tuned lens are also causally relevant to the model's output.
The tuned lens can detect prompt injection attacks with near-perfect accuracy in some cases.
Prediction depth from the tuned lens correlates with the iteration learned during training, indicating it measures example difficulty.
Tuned lens translators transfer well to fine-tuned models without additional training.
papers.limitation:
Training translators for each layer requires additional computation compared to the logit lens.
Causal basis extraction is computationally intensive.
future_direction: Make causal basis extraction more scalable.
Apply the tuned lens to other modalities beyond language.
papers.abstract: We analyze transformers from the perspective of iterative inference, seeking to understand how model predictions are refined layer by layer. To do so, we train an affine probe for each block in a frozen pretrained model, making it possible to decode every hidden state into a distribution over the vocabulary. Our method, the tuned lens, is a refinement of the earlier "logit lens" technique, which yielded useful insights but is often brittle. We test our method on various autoregressive language models with up to 20B parameters, showing it to be more predictive, reliable and unbiased than the logit lens. With causal experiments, we show the tuned lens uses similar features to the model itself. We also find the trajectory of latent predictions can be used to detect malicious inputs with high accuracy. All code needed to reproduce our results can be found at https://github.com/AlignmentResearch/tuned-lens.

papers.title: BadEdit: Backdooring large language models by model editing
papers.research_question: How can backdoors be efficiently injected into large language models with minimal data and side effects using model editing techniques?
papers.core_contribution: BadEdit is a framework that formulates backdoor injection as a lightweight knowledge editing problem, directly altering LLM parameters to inject backdoors efficiently with minimal data and side effects.
papers.conclusion: BadEdit demonstrates an efficient and effective backdoor attack on LLMs, highlighting security vulnerabilities and the need for defenses.
papers.key_findings:
BadEdit achieves up to 100% attack success rate with only 15 poisoned samples.
It maintains the model's performance on benign inputs, showing minimal side effects.
The method is efficient, requiring only 120 seconds for GPT-2-XL and 380 seconds for GPT-J.
Backdoors injected with BadEdit remain robust even after subsequent fine-tuning or instruction-tuning.
The approach works across different models and tasks, including text classification, fact-checking, and sentiment generation.
papers.limitation:
The study focuses on relatively simple attack tasks and targets, leaving more complex tasks unexplored.
The method may encounter difficulties with more intricate triggers, such as sentence-level or hidden grammatical triggers.
papers.abstract: Mainstream backdoor attack methods typically demand substantial tuning data for poisoning, limiting their practicality and potentially degrading the overall performance when applied to Large Language Models (LLMs). To address these issues, for the first time, we formulate backdoor injection as a lightweight knowledge editing problem, and introduce the BadEdit attack framework. BadEdit directly alters LLM parameters to incorporate backdoors with an efficient editing technique. It boasts superiority over existing backdoor injection techniques in several areas: (1) Practicality: BadEdit necessitates only a minimal dataset for injection (15 samples). (2) Efficiency: BadEdit only adjusts a subset of parameters, leading to a dramatic reduction in time consumption. (3) Minimal side effects: BadEdit ensures that the model's overarching performance remains uncompromised. (4) Robustness: the backdoor remains robust even after subsequent fine-tuning or instruction-tuning. Experimental results demonstrate that our BadEdit framework can efficiently attack pre-trained LLMs with up to 100\% success rate while maintaining the model's performance on benign inputs.

papers.title: EX-RAY: Distinguishing Injected Backdoor from Natural Features in Neural Networks by Examining Differential Feature Symmetry
papers.research_question: How can we distinguish natural backdoors (inevitable due to class similarities) from injected backdoors (maliciously inserted) in neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a novel symmetric feature differencing method (EX-RAY) to distinguish injected backdoors from natural features in neural networks, significantly reducing false positives in backdoor scanning.
papers.conclusion: EX-RAY effectively distinguishes injected backdoors from natural features by examining differential feature symmetry, providing a powerful add-on for backdoor scanners.
papers.key_findings:
EX-RAY reduces false positives by 78-100% with a small increase in false negatives (0-30%).
It improves overall accuracy of upstream scanners like ABS by 17-41%.
It outperforms baselines using L2 distance and attribution techniques.
It can detect semantic backdoor attacks (composite, hidden-trigger, reflection).
It achieves top performance on TrojAI leaderboard in rounds 2 and 4.
papers.limitation:
EX-RAY may not work well when the trigger size is too large because the upstream scanner may not generate a proper trigger.
EX-RAY requires an upstream scanner to generate triggers.
future_direction: Extend EX-RAY to other domains such as NLP and audio.
Investigate adaptive attacks against EX-RAY.
papers.abstract: Backdoor attack injects malicious behavior to models such that inputs embedded with triggers are misclassified to a target label desired by the attacker. However, natural features may behave like triggers, causing misclassification once embedded. While they are inevitable, mis-recognizing them as injected triggers causes false warnings in backdoor scanning. A prominent challenge is hence to distinguish natural features and injected backdoors. We develop a novel symmetric feature differencing method that identifies a smallest set of features separating two classes. A backdoor is considered injected if the corresponding trigger consists of features different from the set of features distinguishing the victim and target classes. We evaluate the technique on thousands of models, including both clean and trojaned models, from the TrojAI rounds 2-4 competitions and a number of models on ImageNet. Existing backdoor scanning techniques may produce hundreds of false positives (i.e., clean models recognized as trojaned). Our technique removes 78-100% of the false positives (by a state-of-the-art scanner ABS) with a small increase of false negatives by 0-30%, achieving 17-41% overall accuracy improvement, and facilitates achieving top performance on the leaderboard. It also boosts performance of other scanners. It outperforms false positive removal methods using L2 distance and attribution techniques. We also demonstrate its potential in detecting a number of semantic backdoor attacks.

papers.title: Sparse Feature Circuits: Discovering and Editing Interpretable Causal Graphs in Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we discover and use sparse feature circuits, composed of interpretable features, to explain and edit model behaviors?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces methods for discovering and applying sparse feature circuits, which are causally implicated subnetworks of interpretable features, enabling detailed understanding and editing of model behaviors, including a technique (SHIFT) for removing unintended signals without disambiguating data.
papers.conclusion: Sparse feature circuits enable detailed understanding and editing of model behaviors, showing promise for interpretability and downstream applications.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse feature circuits are more interpretable and faithful than neuron circuits.
They can be used to understand model mechanisms, such as subject-verb agreement.
SHIFT can remove unintended signals from a classifier without access to disambiguating labeled data.
The method scales to automatically discover thousands of behaviors and their circuits in an unsupervised pipeline.
future_direction: Scaling to larger models
Improving the quality and coverage of SAEs
Applying feature circuits to a wider range of tasks and models
papers.abstract: We introduce methods for discovering and applying sparse feature circuits. These are causally implicated subnetworks of human-interpretable features for explaining language model behaviors. Circuits identified in prior work consist of polysemantic and difficult-to-interpret units like attention heads or neurons, rendering them unsuitable for many downstream applications. In contrast, sparse feature circuits enable detailed understanding of unanticipated mechanisms. Because they are based on fine-grained units, sparse feature circuits are useful for downstream tasks: We introduce SHIFT, where we improve the generalization of a classifier by ablating features that a human judges to be task-irrelevant. Finally, we demonstrate an entirely unsupervised and scalable interpretability pipeline by discovering thousands of sparse feature circuits for automatically discovered model behaviors.

papers.title: Discovering Universal Activation Directions for PII Leakage in Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether there exist universal activation directions—single latent directions in the residual stream whose linear addition at inference time consistently increases the model’s likelihood of producing PII leakage across diverse prompts.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces UniLeak, a method that identifies universal activation directions in a model's residual stream that amplify PII leakage when added at inference time, without requiring access to training data or ground-truth PII.
papers.conclusion: PII leakage in language models is associated with low-dimensional internal structure (universal activation directions) that can be effectively amplified or mitigated via representation-level interventions, offering a mechanistic perspective on privacy risks.
papers.key_findings:
Universal activation directions that consistently increase PII generation across prompts exist and can be identified via gradient-based optimization on self-generated text.
Steering along these directions amplifies the effectiveness of existing prompt-based PII extraction attacks, yielding up to 13,399 additional PII records.
Interventions applied at early layers (especially layer 0) are most effective, suggesting PII-sensitive features are encoded early in the model's computation.
The directions enable both adversarial exploitation (via embedding poisoning) and mitigation (via subtraction), demonstrating a representation-level mechanism for privacy risk.
UniLeak extracts a largely distinct set of PII compared to baseline attacks, indicating it explores different regions of the model's memorized PII space.
papers.limitation: The work is limited to open-source models and white-box access settings.
papers.abstract: Modern language models exhibit rich internal structure, yet little is known about how privacy-sensitive behaviors, such as personally identifiable information (PII) leakage, are represented and modulated within their hidden states. We present UniLeak, a mechanistic-interpretability framework that identifies universal activation directions: latent directions in a model's residual stream whose linear addition at inference time consistently increases the likelihood of generating PII across prompts. These model-specific directions generalize across contexts and amplify PII generation probability, with minimal impact on generation quality. UniLeak recovers such directions without access to training data or groundtruth PII, relying only on self-generated text. Across multiple models and datasets, steering along these universal directions substantially increases PII leakage compared to existing prompt-based extraction methods. Our results offer a new perspective on PII leakage: the superposition of a latent signal in the model's representations, enabling both risk amplification and mitigation.

papers.title: Making Harmful Behaviors Unlearnable for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Can we train LLMs on harmful data without learning harmful behaviors?
papers.core_contribution: This paper proposes a controllable fine-tuning framework using 'security vectors' (additional parameters) to make harmful behaviors unlearnable during training, preventing LLMs from learning from harmful data while preserving their ability to learn other tasks.
papers.conclusion: The proposed framework with security vectors effectively prevents LLMs from learning harmful behaviors during fine-tuning, reducing security risks and enabling safer model customization.
papers.key_findings:
Security vectors trained on 100 harmful samples can prevent an LLM from learning harmful behaviors from 1000 harmful examples.
The method prevents learning from both explicit and implicit harmful data, maintaining safety levels comparable to the original aligned model.
Fine-tuning with security vectors does not impair the model's ability to learn new, benign tasks (e.g., ProfileQA).
The approach is robust across different training epochs and learning rates, except when the fine-tuning learning rate is much higher than that used to generate the security vectors.
Security vectors can be deactivated during inference, restoring the model's normal, safe behavior.
papers.limitation:
The security vectors may lose effectiveness if the fine-tuning learning rate is significantly higher (e.g., 5e-3) than the rate used to generate them (1e-3).
Excessive training epochs on harmful data may impair the model's reasoning ability (e.g., on GSM), though the cause is not fully determined.
future_direction: Design experiments to ascertain the cause of the drop in reasoning ability (GSM) when fine-tuning on harmful data.
Investigate the robust instruction-following capability observed when fine-tuning with security vectors over many epochs.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown great potential as general-purpose AI assistants in various domains. To meet the requirements of different applications, LLMs are often customized by further fine-tuning. However, the powerful learning ability of LLMs not only enables them to acquire new tasks but also makes them susceptible to learning undesired behaviors. For example, even safety-aligned LLMs can be easily fine-tuned into harmful assistants as the fine-tuning data often contains implicit or explicit harmful content. Can we train LLMs on harmful data without learning harmful behaviors? This paper proposes a controllable training framework that makes harmful behaviors unlearnable during the fine-tuning process. Specifically, we introduce ``security vectors'', a few new parameters that can be separated from the LLM, to ensure LLM's responses are consistent with the harmful behavior. Security vectors are activated during fine-tuning, the consistent behavior makes LLM believe that such behavior has already been learned, there is no need to further optimize for harmful data. During inference, we can deactivate security vectors to restore the LLM's normal behavior. The experimental results show that the security vectors generated by 100 harmful samples are enough to prevent LLM from learning 1000 harmful samples, while preserving the ability to learn other useful information.

papers.title: Probing Latent Subspaces in LLM for AI Security: Identifying and Manipulating Adversarial States
papers.research_question: Can latent subspaces in LLMs be identified and manipulated to induce state transitions from safe to jailbroken states?
papers.core_contribution: This work demonstrates that latent subspaces in LLMs can be identified and manipulated to induce state transitions from safe to jailbroken states using LDA and targeted perturbations, paving the way for potential proactive defenses.
papers.conclusion: The methodology demonstrates the feasibility of using latent representations to manipulate model states and provides insights into attractor dynamics in LLMs, with potential for preemptive AI security.
papers.key_findings:
Last-token activations encode information about the model's state (safe vs jailbreak) and can be classified with above-chance accuracy.
Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) can separate safe and jailbreak activations into distinct latent subspaces, and a direction vector can be derived.
Applying the derived perturbation vector to safe activations can induce jailbreak responses in a subset of prompts (11% for Llama-3.1-8B, 13.39% for Qwen2.5-3B).
Targeted perturbations induce distinct downstream state changes that propagate through layers, while random perturbations do not.
The effect of targeted perturbation varies across layers, with middle layers (6-18) showing sustained effects, suggesting they may be critical for safety.
papers.limitation:
The perturbation vector was derived from a dataset of malicious cybersecurity-related prompt-injects, so the discovered subspace may reflect features specific to this domain.
Perturbations led to jailbreak transitions in only about 11% of tested prompts, indicating a low success rate.
The external evaluation performed by GPT-4o exhibited high variance in assigning labels to ambiguous outputs.
The method was developed and validated on decoder-only Transformers; generalizing to other LLM architectures requires further testing.
future_direction: Generalize the analysis by expanding the scope of malicious questions and prompt injects to multiple domains or adversarial content types.
Investigate stronger perturbation magnitudes without compromising the coherence of the LLM's response.
Test the methodology on other open-source and commercially available LLM architectures to confirm generalizability.
Incorporate additional rounds of assessment to mitigate label noise from external evaluators like GPT-4o.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across various tasks, yet they remain vulnerable to adversarial manipulations such as jailbreaking via prompt injection attacks. These attacks bypass safety mechanisms to generate restricted or harmful content. In this study, we investigated the underlying latent subspaces of safe and jailbroken states by extracting hidden activations from a LLM. Inspired by attractor dynamics in neuroscience, we hypothesized that LLM activations settle into semi stable states that can be identified and perturbed to induce state transitions. Using dimensionality reduction techniques, we projected activations from safe and jailbroken responses to reveal latent subspaces in lower dimensional spaces. We then derived a perturbation vector that when applied to safe representations, shifted the model towards a jailbreak state. Our results demonstrate that this causal intervention results in statistically significant jailbreak responses in a subset of prompts. Next, we probed how these perturbations propagate through the model's layers, testing whether the induced state change remains localized or cascades throughout the network. Our findings indicate that targeted perturbations induced distinct shifts in activations and model responses. Our approach paves the way for potential proactive defenses, shifting from traditional guardrail based methods to preemptive, model agnostic techniques that neutralize adversarial states at the representation level.

papers.title: Causal Reward Adjustment: Mitigating Reward Hacking in External Reasoning via Backdoor Correction
papers.research_question: How can reward hacking in external reasoning systems be mitigated? The paper proposes a causal method to adjust rewards by correcting for confounding semantic features.
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Causal Reward Adjustment (CRA), a method that mitigates reward hacking by training sparse autoencoders on PRM internal activations to recover interpretable features and then applying backdoor adjustment to correct for confounding semantic features.
papers.conclusion: Reward hacking in external reasoning systems is caused by confounding semantic features; CRA uses sparse autoencoders and backdoor adjustment to mitigate this, improving accuracy without retraining models.
papers.key_findings:
CRA improves reasoning accuracy on MATH and GSM8K datasets by mitigating reward hacking.
Causal intervention on identified reward hacking features effectively reduces scores for incorrect steps, while random intervention does not.
Reward hacking stems from confounding semantic features that create spurious correlations between reasoning steps and rewards.
Backdoor adjustment can estimate debiased rewards by marginalizing over confounding features.
The method works without modifying the policy model or retraining the reward model.
papers.abstract: External reasoning systems combine language models with process reward models (PRMs) to select high-quality reasoning paths for complex tasks such as mathematical problem solving. However, these systems are prone to reward hacking, where high-scoring but logically incorrect paths are assigned high scores by the PRMs, leading to incorrect answers. From a causal inference perspective, we attribute this phenomenon primarily to the presence of confounding semantic features. To address it, we propose Causal Reward Adjustment (CRA), a method that mitigates reward hacking by estimating the true reward of a reasoning path. CRA trains sparse autoencoders on the PRM's internal activations to recover interpretable features, then corrects confounding by using backdoor adjustment. Experiments on math solving datasets demonstrate that CRA mitigates reward hacking and improves final accuracy, without modifying the policy model or retraining PRM.

papers.title: Extended Abstract: Probing-Guided Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning for Balancing Linguistic Adaptation and Safety in LLM-based Social Influence Systems
papers.research_question: How can LLMs be fine-tuned to balance linguistic adaptation and safety in social influence tasks using probing-guided parameter-efficient fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Probing-Guided PEFT (PG-PEFT), a fine-tuning strategy that uses interpretability probes to identify model components for linguistic adaptation and safety, guiding LoRA updates for targeted control.
papers.conclusion: PG-PEFT integrates interpretability insights into PEFT to enable controlled balance between linguistic adaptation and safety in LLM-based social influence systems.
papers.key_findings:
Probing is expected to successfully identify LLM components associated with linguistic adaptation versus safety violations.
PG-PEFT is hypothesized to achieve a superior trade-off between adaptation and safety compared to standard LoRA fine-tuning.
future_direction: Exploring advanced probing techniques such as causal probing.
Assessing the transferability of functional maps across models and languages.
Applying PG-PEFT to more social influence tasks and safety concerns like misinformation.
papers.abstract: Designing effective LLMs for social influence (SI) tasks demands controlling linguistic output such that it adapts to context (such as user attributes, history etc.) while upholding ethical guardrails.Standard Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) methods like LoRA struggle to manage the trade-off between adaptive linguistic expression and safety, and optimize based on overall objectives without differentiating the functional roles of internal model components.Therefore, we introduce Probing-Guided PEFT (PG-PEFT), a novel fine-tuning strategy which utilizes interpretability probes to identify LLM components associated with context-driven linguistic variations versus those linked to safety violations (e.g., toxicity, bias).This functional map then guides LoRA updates, enabling more targeted control over the model's linguistic output.We evaluate PG-PEFT on SI tasks (persuasion, negotiation) and linguistic adaptability with safety benchmarks against standard PEFT.

papers.title: REAL: Reading Out Transformer Activations for Precise Localization in Language Model Steering
papers.research_question: How can we better identify internal modules (attention heads or layers) that govern specific behaviors in LLMs for the purpose of inference-time steering?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces REAL, a framework that uses a vector-quantized autoencoder (VQ-AE) to learn a disentangled latent space from module activations, enabling more precise identification of behavior-relevant modules (heads or layers) for inference-time steering in Transformers.
papers.conclusion: REAL provides a more effective and principled approach for selecting behavior-relevant modules in Transformers, leading to improved performance across a variety of inference-time steering tasks including truthfulness enhancement, knowledge conflict resolution, and general alignment.
papers.key_findings:
REAL outperforms existing methods like ITI and LoFiT in truthfulness steering, achieving significant improvements (e.g., up to 81.5% relative improvement on MC1 for Qwen2.5-7B).
The attention heads selected by REAL on a truthfulness task show strong zero-shot generalization to knowledge-seeking tasks in different model families.
REAL effectively localizes layers for steering in knowledge conflict tasks, outperforming the state-of-the-art SPARE method on benchmarks like NQSWAP and MACNOISE.
The method's relevance scores, derived from the VQ-AE encodings, provide a principled way to rank modules and assign steering strengths.
Visualizations (t-SNE, heatmaps) show that REAL identifies heads with more discriminative activation patterns compared to linear-probe-based methods.
papers.abstract: Inference-time steering aims to alter a large language model's (LLM's) responses without changing its parameters, but a central challenge is identifying the internal modules that most strongly govern the target behavior. Existing approaches often rely on simplistic cues or ad hoc heuristics, leading to suboptimal or unintended effects. We introduce REAL, a framework for identifying behavior-relevant modules (attention heads or layers) in Transformer models. For each module, REAL trains a vector-quantized autoencoder (VQ-AE) on its hidden activations and uses a shared, learnable codebook to partition the latent space into behavior-relevant and behavior-irrelevant subspaces. REAL quantifies a module's behavioral relevance by how well its VQ-AE encodings discriminate behavior-aligned from behavior-violating responses via a binary classification metric; this score guides both module selection and steering strength. We evaluate REAL across eight LLMs from the Llama and Qwen families and nine datasets spanning truthfulness enhancement, open-domain QA under knowledge conflicts, and general alignment tasks. REAL enables more effective inference-time interventions, achieving an average relative improvement of 20% (up to 81.5%) over the ITI method on truthfulness steering. In addition, the modules selected by REAL exhibit strong zero-shot generalization in cross-domain truthfulness-steering scenarios.

papers.title: Eliciting Secret Knowledge from Language Models
papers.research_question: How to elicit secret knowledge from language models that are trained to possess but conceal specific knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a benchmark for secret elicitation by training language models with hidden knowledge and evaluates various black-box and white-box elicitation techniques, finding prefill attacks most effective and showing white-box methods also improve auditor success.
papers.conclusion: Secret elicitation is possible using both black-box and white-box methods, and the released benchmark facilitates future research.
papers.key_findings:
Prefill attacks and user persona sampling are the most effective black-box techniques for secret elicitation.
White-box techniques (logit lens, SAEs) consistently increase auditor success rates but are less effective than the best black-box methods.
Secret knowledge is represented in the residual stream even when not verbalized.
Fuzzing (adding noise to activations) can sometimes elicit secrets.
Many-shot jailbreaking is not very effective for secret elicitation in this setting.
papers.limitation:
For the Taboo setting, it is sometimes possible to guess the model’s secret knowledge based on the hints it gives.
For the SSC setting, the base model already has some ability to decode in-context Base64 prior to fine-tuning.
papers.abstract: We study secret elicitation: discovering knowledge that an AI possesses but does not explicitly verbalize. As a testbed, we train three families of large language models (LLMs) to possess specific knowledge that they apply downstream but deny knowing when asked directly. For example, in one setting, we train an LLM to generate replies that are consistent with knowing the user is female, while denying this knowledge when asked directly. We then design various black-box and white-box secret elicitation techniques and evaluate them based on whether they can help an LLM auditor successfully guess the secret knowledge. Many of our techniques improve on simple baselines. Our most effective techniques (performing best in all settings) are based on prefill attacks, a black-box technique where the LLM reveals secret knowledge when generating a completion from a predefined prefix. Our white-box techniques based on logit lens and sparse autoencoders (SAEs) also consistently increase the success rate of the LLM auditor, but are less effective. We release our models and code, establishing a public benchmark for evaluating secret elicitation methods.

papers.title: Data-Centric Interpretability for LLM-based Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
papers.research_question: How can we understand behavior changes in LLM-based multi-agent reinforcement learning during training using data-centric interpretability methods?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Meta-Autointerp, a method for grouping SAE features into interpretable hypotheses about training dynamics, and shows that SAEs and LLM-summarizer provide complementary views into agent behavior in multi-agent RL.
papers.conclusion: The framework combining SAEs and LLM-summarizer provides complementary views into agent behavior and is a practical starting point for data-centric interpretability in multi-agent RL.
papers.key_findings:
SAE Meta-Features (grouped features) are more interpretable and predictively useful than individual SAE features.
LLM summarizer hypotheses are subjectively interesting but less predictively useful than SAE-derived hypotheses.
The framework discovers fine-grained behaviors (e.g., role-playing, language switching) and high-level strategic behaviors in multi-agent RL training.
A subset of SAE-derived hypotheses are predictively useful for downstream tasks, such as distinguishing early vs late training samples.
Hypotheses from SAE Meta-Features can be used to improve agent performance via prompt optimization, achieving a +14.2% score improvement.
papers.limitation:
Subjectively interesting SAE features and most LLM generated hypotheses may be worse than useless to humans.
Sparsity of feature activations is a major limitation, making some features subtle and difficult for humans to distinguish.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly trained in complex Reinforcement Learning, multi-agent environments, making it difficult to understand how behavior changes over training. Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have recently shown to be useful for data-centric interpretability. In this work, we analyze large-scale reinforcement learning training runs from the sophisticated environment of Full-Press Diplomacy by applying pretrained SAEs, alongside LLM-summarizer methods. We introduce Meta-Autointerp, a method for grouping SAE features into interpretable hypotheses about training dynamics. We discover fine-grained behaviors including role-playing patterns, degenerate outputs, language switching, alongside high-level strategic behaviors and environment-specific bugs. Through automated evaluation, we validate that 90% of discovered SAE Meta-Features are significant, and find a surprising reward hacking behavior. However, through two user studies, we find that even subjectively interesting and seemingly helpful SAE features may be worse than useless to humans, along with most LLM generated hypotheses. However, a subset of SAE-derived hypotheses are predictively useful for downstream tasks. We further provide validation by augmenting an untrained agent's system prompt, improving the score by +14.2%. Overall, we show that SAEs and LLM-summarizer provide complementary views into agent behavior, and together our framework forms a practical starting point for future data-centric interpretability work on ensuring trustworthy LLM behavior throughout training.

papers.title: Understanding Language Model Circuits through Knowledge Editing
papers.research_question: How is knowledge structured within the critical subnetworks (circuits) of language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper combines knowledge editing and circuit analysis to reveal that knowledge-intensive circuits exhibit 'confirmation bias' (resistance to editing), knowledge is distributed in circuits of intermediate size, circuits from different tasks overlap, and LayerNorm plays a larger role in circuits than previously assumed.
papers.conclusion: Combining knowledge editing and circuit analysis reveals novel properties of circuits, such as resistance to editing, distribution patterns, and the role of LayerNorm, supporting future explorations into model behaviors, bias removal, and interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge-intensive circuits show stronger resistance to editing compared to their complementary parts, analogous to 'confirmation bias'.
Knowledge is neither extremely concentrated nor widely dispersed; ideal knowledge-bearing circuits likely contain between 5% and 50% of parameters.
Circuits extracted from different tasks (e.g., linguistic and knowledge-based) show non-negligible overlap.
LayerNorm components constitute a larger share of the extracted circuits than attention and MLP layers.
Complementary circuits are more susceptible to editing, suggesting potential for bias removal without compromising primary circuit performance.
papers.limitation:
Only the GPT-2 model was used.
Only fine-tuning model edit was investigated; alternative model editing methods can be explored.
Only a handful of text classification problems were investigated.
future_direction: Further investigation into the role and characteristics of complementary circuits.
Investigating the possibility of ideal circuits that can perform well for every specific task.
Exploring other techniques like ROME to edit complementary circuits without impacting primary circuits.
Creating more comprehensive datasets that capture a wider range of behaviors.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in language model interpretability have identified circuits, critical subnetworks that replicate model behaviors, yet how knowledge is structured within these crucial subnetworks remains opaque. To gain an understanding toward the knowledge in the circuits, we conduct systematic knowledge editing experiments on the circuits of the GPT-2 language model. Our analysis reveals intriguing patterns in how circuits respond to editing attempts, the extent of knowledge distribution across network components, and the architectural composition of knowledge-bearing circuits. These findings offer insights into the complex relationship between model circuits and knowledge representation, deepening the understanding of how information is organized within language models. Our findings offer novel insights into the ``meanings'' of the circuits, and introduce directions for further interpretability and safety research of language models.

papers.title: NeuroFilter: Privacy Guardrails for Conversational LLM Agents
papers.research_question: How can privacy for agentic Large Language Models (LLMs) be enforced efficiently and robustly by detecting privacy-violating intent in the model's internal activation space?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces NeuroFilter, a low-latency privacy guardrail framework that uses linear probes on model activations to detect contextually inappropriate disclosure intent, and extends this to multi-turn attacks via the novel concept of activation velocity.
papers.conclusion: NeuroFilter provides an accurate, utility-preserving, and computationally efficient guardrail paradigm for enforcing contextual privacy in conversational LLM agents, addressing key limitations of prior semantic filtering approaches.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes on cached activations can effectively separate privacy-violating intent from benign requests, achieving high accuracy with zero false positives on benign prompts.
Privacy violation directions in activation space are context-dependent, not monolithic, requiring context-specific probe training for effective filtering.
The proposed activation velocity signal, measuring cumulative drift in internal representations, enables detection of multi-turn adversarial steering (e.g., conversational manipulation, mosaic attacks) even when individual turns appear benign.
NeuroFilter probes are computationally lightweight, adding only O(d) overhead per turn, reducing inference cost by orders of magnitude compared to LLM-based agentic privacy defenses.
Probe performance and confidence generally scale with model layer depth and are affected by model architecture (aspect ratio), but probes maintain utility when applied to fine-tuned variants of the base model, albeit with reduced confidence.
papers.limitation:
Privacy violation directions are context-dependent, requiring training separate probes for each privacy context/norm, which may be cumbersome.
Linear probes trained on a base model do not seamlessly generalize to fine-tuned versions of the same model, showing reduced confidence in predictions.
Obtaining large datasets of multi-turn prompt trajectories for robust train-test splits is challenging, which may affect the safety and utility guarantees of multi-turn probes.
future_direction: Extending the linear probing approach to enforce alignment with multiple desiderata (e.g., courtesy, safety) via multi-head probe setups.
Exploring the use of sparse autoencoders (SAEs) for concept discovery as a basis for multi-head probing approaches.
Investigating intelligent routing of conversations through different sets of probe-based filters depending on the alignment desiderata for a particular interaction.
papers.abstract: This work addresses the computational challenge of enforcing privacy for agentic Large Language Models (LLMs), where privacy is governed by the contextual integrity framework. Indeed, existing defenses rely on LLM-mediated checking stages that add substantial latency and cost, and that can be undermined in multi-turn interactions through manipulation or benign-looking conversational scaffolding. Contrasting this background, this paper makes a key observation: internal representations associated with privacy-violating intent can be separated from benign requests using linear structure. Using this insight, the paper proposes NeuroFilter, a guardrail framework that operationalizes contextual integrity by mapping norm violations to simple directions in the model's activation space, enabling detection even when semantic filters are bypassed. The proposed filter is also extended to capture threats arising during long conversations using the concept of activation velocity, which measures cumulative drift in internal representations across turns. A comprehensive evaluation across over 150,000 interactions and covering models from 7B to 70B parameters, illustrates the strong performance of NeuroFilter in detecting privacy attacks while maintaining zero false positives on benign prompts, all while reducing the computational inference cost by several orders of magnitude when compared to LLM-based agentic privacy defenses.

papers.title: Stealth edits to large language models
papers.research_question: Is it possible to surgically alter a model to correct specific known hallucinations in a granular, individually-reversible way, with a theoretical guarantee not to otherwise alter the model’s behaviour?
papers.core_contribution: We reveal the theoretical foundations of techniques for editing large language models, and present new methods which can do so without requiring retraining. We also reveal the vulnerability of language models to stealth attacks.
papers.conclusion: We have introduced a theoretical framework for stealth editing of large language models, revealing that a single metric—the intrinsic dimension of feature vectors—determines both the editability of a model and its vulnerability to stealth attacks. Our methods enable surgical corrections to hallucinations without affecting other model capabilities, and our findings highlight a previously unrecognised threat to foundation models.
papers.key_findings:
The intrinsic dimension of feature vectors determines the editability of a model and its vulnerability to stealth attacks.
Stealth edits can correct specific hallucinations with high specificity without affecting other model capabilities.
Language models are vulnerable to stealth attacks that can be implanted without access to training data or retraining.
The jet-pack block provides an optimized structure for highly selective editing.
Theoretical guarantees show that the probability of false activation decreases exponentially with the intrinsic dimensionality of feature distributions.
papers.limitation: Edits may interfere with each other if their detectors activate for the same inputs.
future_direction: Future work could investigate the scalability of stealth edits to very large numbers of corrections.
Future work could explore the application of stealth editing to other model architectures and tasks.
Future work could develop defenses against stealth attacks.
papers.abstract: We reveal the theoretical foundations of techniques for editing large language models, and present new methods which can do so without requiring retraining. Our theoretical insights show that a single metric (a measure of the intrinsic dimension of the model's features) can be used to assess a model's editability and reveals its previously unrecognised susceptibility to malicious stealth attacks. This metric is fundamental to predicting the success of a variety of editing approaches, and reveals new bridges between disparate families of editing methods. We collectively refer to these as stealth editing methods, because they directly update a model's weights to specify its response to specific known hallucinating prompts without affecting other model behaviour. By carefully applying our theoretical insights, we are able to introduce a new jet-pack network block which is optimised for highly selective model editing, uses only standard network operations, and can be inserted into existing networks. We also reveal the vulnerability of language models to stealth attacks: a small change to a model's weights which fixes its response to a single attacker-chosen prompt. Stealth attacks are computationally simple, do not require access to or knowledge of the model's training data, and therefore represent a potent yet previously unrecognised threat to redistributed foundation models. Extensive experimental results illustrate and support our methods and their theoretical underpinnings. Demos and source code are available at https://github.com/qinghua-zhou/stealth-edits.

papers.title: Backdoor Attacks on the DNN Interpretation System
papers.research_question: How can we design a backdoor attack that alters the saliency maps produced by DNN interpretation systems without significantly degrading the model's prediction performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper designs the first backdoor attack that targets DNN interpretation systems, altering saliency maps for triggered inputs while maintaining prediction accuracy, and demonstrates that existing backdoor defenses are ineffective against it.
papers.conclusion: The proposed backdoor attack constitutes a serious security threat to the reliability of DNN interpretation systems, especially when using models from untrusted sources, and current defense mechanisms are inadequate.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed backdoor attack successfully fools gradient-based (Grad-CAM, SimpleGrad) and gradient-free (VisualBackProp) interpretation methods across various DNN architectures (VGG19, ResNet50, DenseNet121).
The attack can be extended to fool multiple interpretation systems simultaneously (joint attack).
An inverted setting can use the trigger as a security key, making correct interpretation available only to key holders.
Existing backdoor defense mechanisms (Neural Cleanse, Activation Clustering, Fine-pruning, input denoising) are ineffective at detecting or removing the proposed attacks.
papers.abstract: Interpretability is crucial to understand the inner workings of deep neural networks (DNNs) and many interpretation methods generate saliency maps that highlight parts of the input image that contribute the most to the prediction made by the DNN. In this paper we design a backdoor attack that alters the saliency map produced by the network for an input image only with injected trigger that is invisible to the naked eye while maintaining the prediction accuracy. The attack relies on injecting poisoned data with a trigger into the training data set. The saliency maps are incorporated in the penalty term of the objective function that is used to train a deep model and its influence on model training is conditioned upon the presence of a trigger. We design two types of attacks: targeted attack that enforces a specific modification of the saliency map and untargeted attack when the importance scores of the top pixels from the original saliency map are significantly reduced. We perform empirical evaluation of the proposed backdoor attacks on gradient-based and gradient-free interpretation methods for a variety of deep learning architectures. We show that our attacks constitute a serious security threat when deploying deep learning models developed by untrusty sources. Finally, in the Supplement we demonstrate that the proposed methodology can be used in an inverted setting, where the correct saliency map can be obtained only in the presence of a trigger (key), effectively making the interpretation system available only to selected users.

papers.title: Understanding and Mitigating Gender Bias in LLMs via Interpretable Neuron Editing
papers.research_question: How can we understand the neuron-level mechanisms of gender bias in LLMs and mitigate this bias through targeted neuron editing without compromising the model's core capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an interpretable neuron editing method that effectively reduces gender bias in LLMs while preserving their original capabilities, supported by a new dataset and a detailed analysis of bias mechanisms at the neuron level.
papers.conclusion: The proposed interpretable neuron editing method successfully addresses the challenges of understanding and mitigating gender bias in LLMs, achieving a strong balance between fairness and functionality without compromising the models' original capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Gender bias is pervasive across multiple LLMs, as evidenced by non-zero entropy differences and skewed proportions in the CommonWords dataset.
Specific neuron circuits, including 'gender neurons' activated by stereotypical words and 'general neurons' activated by the <start> token, are responsible for gender bias.
Editing even a small number of general neurons can significantly degrade the model's performance on common tasks due to hierarchical neuron interactions.
The proposed interpretable neuron editing method, combining logit-based and causal-based strategies, effectively reduces gender bias (e.g., improving ICAT scores) while maintaining performance on tasks like reading comprehension and arithmetic.
The method outperforms existing fine-tuning and neuron editing approaches in balancing bias reduction with capability preservation.
papers.limitation:
The method relies on the CommonWords dataset for neuron selection, and results may vary for tasks or datasets not covered in the study.
Experiments are conducted on five decoder-only LLMs, requiring potential adaptations for other architectures.
The evaluation metrics (ICAT, entropy difference, accuracy) may not fully capture fairness or real-world performance.
The interpretability insights guiding neuron selection rely on assumptions (e.g., projecting neurons into vocabulary space) that may only be approximations.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often exhibit gender bias, posing challenges for their safe deployment. Existing methods to mitigate bias lack a comprehensive understanding of its mechanisms or compromise the model's core capabilities. To address these issues, we propose the CommonWords dataset, to systematically evaluate gender bias in LLMs. Our analysis reveals pervasive bias across models and identifies specific neuron circuits, including gender neurons and general neurons, responsible for this behavior. Notably, editing even a small number of general neurons can disrupt the model's overall capabilities due to hierarchical neuron interactions. Based on these insights, we propose an interpretable neuron editing method that combines logit-based and causal-based strategies to selectively target biased neurons. Experiments on five LLMs demonstrate that our method effectively reduces gender bias while preserving the model's original capabilities, outperforming existing fine-tuning and editing approaches. Our findings contribute a novel dataset, a detailed analysis of bias mechanisms, and a practical solution for mitigating gender bias in LLMs.

papers.title: Neural Transparency: Mechanistic Interpretability Interfaces for Anticipating Model Behaviors for Personalized AI
papers.research_question: Can neural transparency tools, which translate mechanistic interpretability insights into user-facing interfaces, help users anticipate and design safer AI chatbot behaviors from system prompts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a neural transparency interface that translates mechanistic interpretability insights (persona vectors derived from neural activations) into an actionable tool for non-technical users to predict chatbot personality traits from system prompts before deployment.
papers.conclusion: Neural transparency visualizations can increase user trust and enhance the subjective experience of the AI design process, offering a path to operationalize mechanistic interpretability for end-users to support safer, more aligned human-AI interactions.
papers.key_findings:
Users systematically miscalibrated their predictions of AI behavior, misjudging trait activations for 11 of 15 analyzable traits, highlighting the need for transparency tools.
The neural transparency interface significantly increased user trust in the AI model and was enthusiastically received, though it did not change design iteration patterns.
Persona vectors (linear directions in activation space) for traits like empathy, sociality, and toxicity showed strong linear relationships with synthetic prompt levels, validating the approach for most traits.
papers.limitation:
Relied on GPT-4.1-mini to evaluate trait expression in Llama responses, which may not fully capture human judgments of trait expression.
The persona vector generation method uses simple difference-in-means, prioritizing efficiency over the potential accuracy/robustness of more complex techniques like linear probes.
The 10-minute interaction period may not capture longer-term dynamics of chatbot relationships where problematic interactions typically emerge.
Participants' inaccurate trait predictions may be partly due to transforming coarse ordinal prediction data to normalized values, potentially making predictions more extreme.
future_direction: Longitudinal deployment studies to track users across multiple chatbot creation sessions.
Adversarial task conditions where transparency tools become necessary to avoid dangerous traits.
Active steering interfaces allowing users to directly manipulate persona vector activations.
Development of a standardized trait disclosure framework (like a 'nutritional label') for chatbots.
Studies with vulnerable populations (e.g., adolescents) most at risk from problematic chatbot relationships.
papers.abstract: Millions of users now design personalized LLM-based chatbots that shape their daily interactions, yet they can only roughly anticipate how their design choices will manifest as behaviors in deployment. This opacity is consequential: seemingly innocuous prompts can trigger excessive sycophancy, toxicity, or other undesirable traits, degrading utility and raising safety concerns. To address this issue, we introduce an interface that enables neural transparency by exposing language model internals during chatbot design. Our approach extracts behavioral trait vectors (empathy, toxicity, sycophancy, etc.) by computing differences in neural activations between contrastive system prompts that elicit opposing behaviors. We predict chatbot behaviors by projecting the system prompt's final token activations onto these trait vectors, normalizing for cross-trait comparability, and visualizing results via an interactive sunburst diagram. To evaluate this approach, we conducted an online user study using Prolific to compare our neural transparency interface against a baseline chatbot interface without any form of transparency. Our analyses suggest that users systematically miscalibrated AI behavior: participants misjudged trait activations for eleven of fifteen analyzable traits, motivating the need for transparency tools in everyday human-AI interaction. While our interface did not change design iteration patterns, it significantly increased user trust and was enthusiastically received. Qualitative analysis revealed nuanced user experiences with the visualization, suggesting interface and interaction improvements for future work. This work offers a path for how mechanistic interpretability can be operationalized for non-technical users, establishing a foundation for safer, more aligned human-AI interactions.

papers.title: Position-aware Automatic Circuit Discovery
papers.research_question: How can circuit discovery methods be improved to incorporate positional information, addressing the limitation of position-invariant assumptions in existing methods?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces position-aware edge attribution patching (PEAP) and dataset schemas to enable automatic discovery of position-sensitive circuits in language models, improving the trade-off between circuit size and faithfulness.
papers.conclusion: The proposed position-aware circuit discovery method with schemas provides a more precise and automated approach to understanding model mechanisms, offering better faithfulness and size trade-offs.
papers.key_findings:
PEAP yields smaller and more faithful circuits compared to position-agnostic methods, as demonstrated on tasks like Greater-Than and IOI.
Schemas allow position-aware circuit discovery for variable-length inputs by defining semantic spans across examples.
Automated schema generation using LLMs, enhanced with saliency scores, produces schemas comparable to human-designed ones in terms of circuit faithfulness.
Position-aware circuits reduce cancellation and overestimation effects that occur when aggregating edge scores across positions without differentiation.
future_direction: Relax the sequential order assumption in schemas to support greater variation across examples.
papers.abstract: A widely used strategy to discover and understand language model mechanisms is circuit analysis. A circuit is a minimal subgraph of a model's computation graph that executes a specific task. We identify a gap in existing circuit discovery methods: they assume circuits are position-invariant, treating model components as equally relevant across input positions. This limits their ability to capture cross-positional interactions or mechanisms that vary across positions. To address this gap, we propose two improvements to incorporate positionality into circuits, even on tasks containing variable-length examples. First, we extend edge attribution patching, a gradient-based method for circuit discovery, to differentiate between token positions. Second, we introduce the concept of a dataset schema, which defines token spans with similar semantics across examples, enabling position-aware circuit discovery in datasets with variable length examples. We additionally develop an automated pipeline for schema generation and application using large language models. Our approach enables fully automated discovery of position-sensitive circuits, yielding better trade-offs between circuit size and faithfulness compared to prior work.

papers.title: SelfIE: Self-Interpretation of Large Language Model Embeddings
papers.research_question: How can we interpret the hidden embeddings of large language models in natural language to reveal their internal reasoning and enable control over model behavior?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SelfIE, a framework that enables LLMs to interpret their own hidden embeddings in natural language, and extends it to control model behavior via supervised and reinforcement control on embeddings.
papers.conclusion: SelfIE provides a powerful framework for interpreting and controlling LLM reasoning by generating text descriptions of hidden embeddings, opening avenues for transparent and reliable model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
SelfIE can elicit implicit world state knowledge in embeddings without training, matching the performance of a 100-shot linear probe.
SelfIE reveals internal reasoning processes behind complex LLM behaviors such as harmful knowledge recall, prompt injection, ethical decisions, physics reasoning, social reasoning, and hallucination.
SelfIE-based supervised control can edit fact associations and open-ended concepts with good generalization, requiring gradient computation only for individual layers.
SelfIE-based reinforcement control can erase harmful knowledge in LLMs without supervised targets, reducing prompt injection success rate by 84.66%.
SelfIE-based control can override user-specified ethical preferences, increasing fairness in LLM responses with a 95% effective rate.
future_direction: Further exploration of reasoning patterns in LLMs and model reasoning behavior controls with hidden embeddings.
papers.abstract: How do large language models (LLMs) obtain their answers? The ability to explain and control an LLM's reasoning process is key for reliability, transparency, and future model developments. We propose SelfIE (Self-Interpretation of Embeddings), a framework that enables LLMs to interpret their own embeddings in natural language by leveraging their ability to respond to inquiries about a given passage. Capable of interpreting open-world concepts in the hidden embeddings, SelfIE reveals LLM internal reasoning in cases such as making ethical decisions, internalizing prompt injection, and recalling harmful knowledge. SelfIE's text descriptions on hidden embeddings also open up new avenues to control LLM reasoning. We propose Supervised Control, which allows editing open-ended concepts while only requiring gradient computation of individual layer. We extend RLHF to hidden embeddings and propose Reinforcement Control that erases harmful knowledge in LLM without supervision targets.

papers.title: AtPatch: Debugging Transformers via Hot-Fixing Over-Attention
papers.research_question: How can backdoor attacks and unfairness in transformer-based models be mitigated by dynamically redistributing attention maps during inference without retraining?
papers.core_contribution: AtPatch is a hot-fix method that dynamically redistributes attention maps during model inference to mitigate backdoor attacks and unfairness in transformer-based models without modifying model parameters or requiring retraining.
papers.conclusion: AtPatch is an effective hot-fix method for debugging transformer-based DNNs by detecting and redistributing anomalous attention patterns at runtime, mitigating backdoor attacks and unfairness without modifying model parameters.
papers.key_findings:
AtPatch effectively reduces backdoor attack success rates to near-zero levels while preserving the original model's accuracy.
AtPatch significantly reduces model unfairness (bias) with negligible impact on accuracy.
The detector component of AtPatch achieves high precision and low false positive rates in identifying anomalous attention columns.
The attention rescaling process is a necessary component for the method's success.
AtPatch outperforms existing debugging baselines (Fine-Pruning, CARE, IDNN, ADF) in both effectiveness and model functionality preservation.
papers.limitation:
The detector requires a labeled debugging set for training and may need retraining if the model evolves, which could be costly.
Potential adaptive attacks might craft triggers to evade AtPatch's detection and redistribution mechanisms.
future_direction: Replace the supervised detector with unsupervised anomaly detection techniques to eliminate the need for a labeled debugging set.
Employ an ensemble of detectors with diverse architectures or training objectives to increase robustness against adaptive attacks.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based deep neural networks (DNNs) affected by backdoor attacks and unfairness typically exhibit anomalous attention patterns, leading to over-attend to backdoor triggers or protected attributes. Existing neuron-editing mitigation strategies often struggle to handle such situation and most of them lack flexibility and tend to distort feature representations. Motivated by such over-attention phenomenon and software engineering paradigms such as delta debugging and hot patching, we propose AtPatch, a hot-fix method that dynamically redistributes attention maps during model inference. Specifically, for a given input, AtPatch first extracts the attention map from the model's inference process. Then, it uses a pre-trained detector to identify anomalous columns and replace them with unified benign attention. Then, AtPatch rescales other columns to mitigate the impact of over-attention. Finally, AtPatch returns the redistributed attention map to the model for continued inference. Notably, if the detector does not report any anomalous columns, AtPatch directly returns the original attention map to the model. Unlike existing techniques, AtPatch selectively redistributes the attention map, making it better at preserving the model's original functionality. Furthermore, AtPatch's on-the-fly nature allows it to work without modifying model parameters or retraining, making it better suited for deployed models. We conducted extensive experiments to validate AtPatch. Experimental results show that, compared to existing methods, AtPatch can more effectively mitigate backdoor attacks and unfairness while better preserving the model's original functionality.

papers.title: Personas as a Way to Model Truthfulness in Language Models
papers.research_question: How do language models distinguish truth from falsehood in a noisy dataset? The paper presents an explanation for why LMs appear to know the truth despite not being trained with truth labels.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes the persona hypothesis: that language models learn to distinguish truth from falsehood by inferring and representing truthful personas from the pretraining data, which are clusters of agents with common features.
