papers.conclusion: The persona hypothesis explains how LLMs model truthfulness by inferring personas from agent clusters in pretraining data, supported by evidence from LLM probing and synthetic experiments.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes can predict answer truthfulness from question embeddings, indicating that models infer persona from context.
Finetuning on truthful QA pairs generalizes to unseen topics, suggesting a global truthful persona representation.
In synthetic settings, models distinguish truth only when training data has a truthful persona (clustered agents).
Models encode both truthful and untruthful answers and select based on persona, implying a selection mechanism.
papers.limitation:
Probe accuracy is only about 70%, indicating models do not perfectly learn truthfulness.
The latent features used for clustering may be spurious, not robust truthfulness.
Synthetic setting uses explicit agent tokens and assumes equal complexity and shared beliefs, which may not hold in real data.
future_direction: Investigate the persona-based computation mechanism on larger models.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are trained on vast amounts of text from the internet, which contains both factual and misleading information about the world. While unintuitive from a classic view of LMs, recent work has shown that the truth value of a statement can be elicited from the model's representations. This paper presents an explanation for why LMs appear to know the truth despite not being trained with truth labels. We hypothesize that the pretraining data is generated by groups of (un)truthful agents whose outputs share common features, and they form a (un)truthful persona. By training on this data, LMs can infer and represent the persona in its activation space. This allows the model to separate truth from falsehoods and controls the truthfulness of its generation. We show evidence for the persona hypothesis via two observations: (1) we can probe whether a model's answer will be truthful before it is generated; (2) finetuning a model on a set of facts improves its truthfulness on unseen topics. Next, using arithmetics as a synthetic environment, we show that structures of the pretraining data are crucial for the model to infer the truthful persona. Overall, our findings suggest that models can exploit hierarchical structures in the data to learn abstract concepts like truthfulness.

papers.title: PII Jailbreaking in LLMs via Activation Steering Reveals Personal Information Leakage
papers.research_question: Can aligned LLMs be steered to produce non-refusal responses to privacy-sensitive prompts? Do the resulting responses disclose factual personal information or merely hallucinate?
papers.core_contribution: Activation steering can jailbreak aligned LLMs to bypass refusal mechanisms and disclose factual personal information, highlighting privacy risks from memorized data.
papers.conclusion: Privacy-related prompts combined with targeted steering provide a stress test for assessing the extent to which LLMs memorize and reveal personal information.
papers.key_findings:
Attention head activations can reliably predict model's refusal behavior for privacy-sensitive prompts.
Steering top-k attention heads induces non-refusal responses to privacy queries.
Steered responses frequently contain factual personal information, such as relationships and life events.
Jailbreaking success rates exceed 80% across multiple LLMs with steering.
Factuality rates of disclosed information are high, indicating real privacy leakage.
papers.limitation:
Factual accuracy of steered responses is assessed using GPT-4, which may introduce evaluation errors.
Analysis is restricted to a single private attribute (sexual orientation).
Disagreements among human annotators when labeling responses as disclosed, due to subjective interpretation.
future_direction: Developing more robust fact-checking agents with web access to independently verify factual claims.
Extending the framework to other sensitive and verifiable attributes such as health conditions or financial status.
papers.abstract: This paper investigates privacy jailbreaking in LLMs via steering, focusing on whether manipulating activations can bypass LLM alignment and alter response behaviors to privacy related queries (e.g., a certain public figure's sexual orientation). We begin by identifying attention heads predictive of refusal behavior for private attributes (e.g., sexual orientation) using lightweight linear probes trained with privacy evaluator labels. Next, we steer the activations of a small subset of these attention heads guided by the trained probes to induce the model to generate non-refusal responses. Our experiments show that these steered responses often disclose sensitive attribute details, along with other private information about data subjects such as life events, relationships, and personal histories that the models would typically refuse to produce. Evaluations across four LLMs reveal jailbreaking disclosure rates of at least 95%, with more than 50% on average of these responses revealing true personal information. Our controlled study demonstrates that private information memorized in LLMs can be extracted through targeted manipulation of internal activations.

papers.title: What Do Deep Nets Learn? Class-wise Patterns Revealed in the Input Space
papers.research_question: What class-wise patterns do deep neural networks learn for image classification, and how can we visualize them in the input space under natural, backdoor, and adversarial training settings?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a method to visualize class-wise patterns learned by DNNs in the input space, revealing that naturally trained models learn abstract shapes with texture, backdoored models learn trigger patterns, and adversarially trained models learn simplified shape patterns.
papers.conclusion: The proposed method effectively visualizes class-wise patterns learned by DNNs, providing insights into model behavior under natural, backdoor, and adversarial settings, and can be used to identify backdoored models.
papers.key_findings:
DNNs trained on natural (clean) data learn abstract shapes along with some texture.
Backdoored models learn a suspicious pattern for the backdoored class, and the method can reveal this trigger pattern.
The existence of class-wise predictive patterns indicates that DNNs can learn a backdoor even from clean data, and the pattern itself is a backdoor trigger.
Adversarially trained models tend to learn more simplified shape patterns for each class.
The method can serve as an effective tool to help identify backdoored models.
papers.limitation:
Small γ may raise the risk of the pattern overfitting to the canvas image.
It is still an open question how a canvas can be learned without causing any biases.
future_direction: Further exploration of using multiple positive canvas images, using noise rather than nontarget images, or using universal adversarial perturbation in an unbiased manner.
Exploring the effectiveness of the method on more complex backdoor triggers.
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) are increasingly deployed in different applications to achieve state-of-the-art performance. However, they are often applied as a black box with limited understanding of what knowledge the model has learned from the data. In this paper, we focus on image classification and propose a method to visualize and understand the class-wise knowledge (patterns) learned by DNNs under three different settings including natural, backdoor and adversarial. Different to existing visualization methods, our method searches for a single predictive pattern in the pixel space to represent the knowledge learned by the model for each class. Based on the proposed method, we show that DNNs trained on natural (clean) data learn abstract shapes along with some texture, and backdoored models learn a suspicious pattern for the backdoored class. Interestingly, the phenomenon that DNNs can learn a single predictive pattern for each class indicates that DNNs can learn a backdoor even from clean data, and the pattern itself is a backdoor trigger. In the adversarial setting, we show that adversarially trained models tend to learn more simplified shape patterns. Our method can serve as a useful tool to better understand the knowledge learned by DNNs on different datasets under different settings.

papers.title: Unlearning Traces the Influential Training Data of Language Models
papers.research_question: Identifying the training datasets that influence a language model’s outputs is essential for minimizing the generation of harmful content and enhancing its performance.
papers.core_contribution: This paper presents UnTrac and UnTrac-Inv, methods that use unlearning (gradient ascent) to trace the influence of training datasets on a model's predictions, achieving higher accuracy than existing influence functions.
papers.conclusion: Unlearning approaches (UnTrac and UnTrac-Inv) can effectively trace the influence of training datasets on language model predictions, offering a more accurate alternative to existing influence functions.
papers.key_findings:
UnTrac and UnTrac-Inv accurately estimate the influence of training datasets, correlating well with ground-truth leave-dataset-out influence.
The methods outperform existing influence functions (GradDot, GradCos, HIF, TracIn) in tracing the influence of pretraining datasets on harmful content generation.
UnTrac works robustly with preconditioned optimizers (e.g., Adam) and sufficient unlearning steps.
UnTrac-Inv is efficient for many training datasets but is sensitive to hyperparameters like batch size, learning rate, and number of steps.
papers.limitation:
Further empirical investigations are expected to verify the effectiveness of the methods in various settings and tasks.
The methods are not immediately applicable in practical use without validation against leave-dataset-out, which is computationally expensive.
future_direction: Investigating the effectiveness of the methods with even larger models.
Using the methods to reveal the source of LLM's emergent abilities, such as chain-of-thought reasoning.
papers.abstract: Identifying the training datasets that influence a language model's outputs is essential for minimizing the generation of harmful content and enhancing its performance. Ideally, we can measure the influence of each dataset by removing it from training; however, it is prohibitively expensive to retrain a model multiple times. This paper presents UnTrac: unlearning traces the influence of a training dataset on the model's performance. UnTrac is extremely simple; each training dataset is unlearned by gradient ascent, and we evaluate how much the model's predictions change after unlearning. Furthermore, we propose a more scalable approach, UnTrac-Inv, which unlearns a test dataset and evaluates the unlearned model on training datasets. UnTrac-Inv resembles UnTrac, while being efficient for massive training datasets. In the experiments, we examine if our methods can assess the influence of pretraining datasets on generating toxic, biased, and untruthful content. Our methods estimate their influence much more accurately than existing methods while requiring neither excessive memory space nor multiple checkpoints.

papers.title: How Does Controllability Emerge In Language Models During Pretraining?
papers.research_question: How does linear steerability emerge in language models during pretraining, and why does it vary across concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Linear steerability emerges during intermediate stages of training, varies across concepts, and is linked to increasing linear separability of concepts in the hidden space.
papers.conclusion: Linear steerability does not emerge uniformly but develops over training and varies between concepts, aligning with increasingly structured internal representations.
papers.key_findings:
Linear steerability emerges in later training stages, separate from reasoning capability and emotion expression via prompting.
Emergence times vary widely across concepts, such as anger emerging earlier than sadness.
Concept representations become increasingly linearly separable in the hidden space as training progresses.
The Intervention Detector (ID) framework can reveal steerability dynamics and predict when linear steerability emerges.
These findings hold across different model families, indicating a general pattern.
papers.limitation:
Only evaluated on 7B-scale open-source models, not tested on larger LLMs.
Intervention coefficient was empirically tuned and differs across models, with underlying causes not investigated.
Did not explore alternative nonlinear approaches for extracting or intervening in model representations.
Methodological innovation in intervention techniques is not the focus; core procedure is consistent with prior work.
Alternative unsupervised methods such as mean-difference vectors are not compared.
Concepts like emotions lack ground truth, making evaluation subjective and based on semantic interpretation.
Steering certain concepts can produce offensive outputs, with no safety filtering applied.
future_direction: Examining how different pre-training corpora influence intervention outcomes.
Exploring alternative steering methods beyond PCA or K-Means.
Comparing unsupervised methods like mean-difference vectors and their influence on downstream intervention performance.
papers.abstract: Language models can be steered by modifying their internal representations to control concepts such as emotion, style, or truthfulness in generation. However, the conditions for an effective intervention remain unclear and are often validated through heuristics and trial-and-error. To fill this gap, we demonstrate that intervention efficacy, measured by linear steerability (i.e., the ability to adjust output via linear transformations of hidden states), emerges during intermediate stages of training. Moreover, even closely related concepts (e.g., anger and sadness) exhibit steerability emergence at distinct stages of training. To better interpret the dynamics of steerability during training, we adapt existing intervention techniques into a unified framework, referred to as the "Intervention Detector" (ID), which is designed to reveal how linear steerability evolves over the course of training through hidden state and representation analysis. ID reveals that concepts become increasingly linearly separable in the hidden space as training progresses, which strongly correlates with the emergence of linear steerability. We further introduce ID-based metrics, such as heatmaps, entropy trends, and cosine similarity, to help interpret how linear steerability evolves throughout training. In addition, we apply ID across different model families to ensure the generality of our findings on steerability dynamics.

papers.title: Illuminating the Black Box: Real-Time Monitoring of Backdoor Unlearning in CNNs via Explainable AI
papers.research_question: How to provide real-time monitoring and explainability in backdoor unlearning for deep neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a framework that integrates Grad-CAM into backdoor unlearning for real-time monitoring, proposes the TAR metric to quantify attention shift, and uses a balanced unlearning strategy to reduce attack success rate while preserving clean accuracy.
papers.conclusion: The framework enables transparent and verifiable backdoor unlearning through real-time XAI monitoring, integrating explainable AI as an integral component of security mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
The framework reduces Attack Success Rate (ASR) from 96.51% to 5.52% (94.28% reduction) while retaining 99.48% of clean accuracy on CIFAR-10.
The Trigger Attention Ratio (TAR) metric decreases by 67.8%, indicating a shift in model attention from trigger regions to object features.
Real-time Grad-CAM monitoring provides transparent verification of backdoor removal and enables early diagnosis of unlearning failures.
The method converges in only 14 epochs, demonstrating efficiency.
Compared to state-of-the-art methods, it achieves the lowest ASR, though with lower clean accuracy due to architectural differences.
papers.limitation:
Limited experimental scope using only CIFAR-10 and a custom CNN architecture.
Assumes a single trigger pattern (4x4 white square), while real-world attacks may use multiple or dynamic triggers.
Computational overhead from generating Grad-CAM heatmaps, estimated at 15-20%.
Lacks systematic ablation studies to quantify contributions of individual components.
Potential vulnerability to adaptive attacks designed to evade Grad-CAM visualization.
future_direction: Validate on standard architectures like ResNet-18/50 for fair comparison with state-of-the-art.
Test on larger datasets such as CIFAR-100 and ImageNet.
Investigate diverse trigger types including blended, semantic, and invisible triggers.
papers.abstract: Backdoor attacks pose severe security threats to deep neural networks by embedding malicious triggers that force misclassification. While machine unlearning techniques can remove backdoor behaviors, current methods lack transparency and real-time interpretability. This paper introduces a novel framework that integrates Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) into the unlearning process to provide real-time monitoring and explainability. We propose the Trigger Attention Ratio (TAR) metric to quantitatively measure the model's attention shift from trigger patterns to legitimate object features. Our balanced unlearning strategy combines gradient ascent on backdoor samples, Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC) for catastrophic forgetting prevention, and a recovery phase for clean accuracy restoration. Experiments on CIFAR-10 with BadNets attacks demonstrate that our approach reduces Attack Success Rate (ASR) from 96.51% to 5.52% while retaining 99.48% of clean accuracy (82.06%), achieving a 94.28% ASR reduction. The integration of explainable AI enables transparent, observable, and verifiable backdoor removal.

papers.title: Why Representation Engineering Works: A Theoretical and Empirical Study in Vision-Language Models
papers.research_question: How can Representation Engineering (RepE) be extended to Vision-Language Models (VLMs), and what theoretical principles explain the stability of neural activity across layers in this context?
papers.core_contribution: This work extends Representation Engineering (RepE) to Vision-Language Models (VLMs) and provides a theoretical framework explaining that the stability of neural activity across layers is governed by the principal eigenvector of the attention matrix, while a shrinking spectral gap allows subdominant eigenvectors to differentiate between concepts.
papers.conclusion: By integrating theoretical analysis with empirical validation, this work transforms RepE from a descriptive tool into a structured theoretical framework, opening new avenues for improving AI robustness, interpretability, and transparency in multimodal settings.
papers.key_findings:
The principal eigenvector of the self-attention matrix serves as a stable 'backbone' for neural activity propagation across layers.
The spectral gap (difference between the largest and second-largest eigenvalues) shrinks in deeper layers, enabling subdominant eigenvectors to capture subtle distinctions between concepts like honesty and fairness.
Representation Engineering (RepE) is effective in VLMs for extracting and analyzing high-level conceptual representations, such as honesty and fairness, from internal activations.
Linear Artificial Tomography (LAT) scans reveal distinct activation patterns across layers for different high-level concepts, demonstrating how representations evolve through the network.
future_direction: Extend RepE to broader multimodal settings, exploring its potential for bias mitigation, honest detection, and countless concept applications.
papers.abstract: Representation Engineering (RepE) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for enhancing AI transparency by focusing on high-level representations rather than individual neurons or circuits. It has proven effective in improving interpretability and control, showing that representations can emerge, propagate, and shape final model outputs in large language models (LLMs). However, in Vision-Language Models (VLMs), visual input can override factual linguistic knowledge, leading to hallucinated responses that contradict reality. To address this challenge, we make the first attempt to extend RepE to VLMs, analyzing how multimodal representations are preserved and transformed. Building on our findings and drawing inspiration from successful RepE applications, we develop a theoretical framework that explains the stability of neural activity across layers using the principal eigenvector, uncovering the underlying mechanism of RepE. We empirically validate these instrinsic properties, demonstrating their broad applicability and significance. By bridging theoretical insights with empirical validation, this work transforms RepE from a descriptive tool into a structured theoretical framework, opening new directions for improving AI robustness, fairness, and transparency.

papers.title: Knowledge Transfer via Distillation of Activation Boundaries Formed by Hidden Neurons
papers.research_question: Can transferring the activation boundaries of hidden neurons, rather than the magnitude of their responses, improve the performance of knowledge transfer between neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a knowledge transfer method that distills the activation boundaries (separating hyperplanes determining neuron activation) from a teacher network to a student network, outperforming prior state-of-the-art methods.
papers.conclusion: Transferring activation boundaries is a powerful approach for knowledge transfer, leading to superior performance in terms of learning speed, generalization with limited data, and network compression, and can potentially replace pre-training in some scenarios.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed activation boundary transfer method accelerates student network training more effectively than existing methods.
The method significantly improves student network generalization when training data is limited.
The method is effective for various network compression scenarios (depth, channel, and combined compression).
In transfer learning tasks, the method can outperform training a student network with ImageNet pre-training.
The proposed alternative loss function successfully approximates the ideal activation transfer loss, leading to high neuron activation similarity between teacher and student.
future_direction: Modifying various tasks that rely on pre-training to accommodate knowledge transfer for better performance and learning speed.
papers.abstract: An activation boundary for a neuron refers to a separating hyperplane that determines whether the neuron is activated or deactivated. It has been long considered in neural networks that the activations of neurons, rather than their exact output values, play the most important role in forming classification friendly partitions of the hidden feature space. However, as far as we know, this aspect of neural networks has not been considered in the literature of knowledge transfer. In this paper, we propose a knowledge transfer method via distillation of activation boundaries formed by hidden neurons. For the distillation, we propose an activation transfer loss that has the minimum value when the boundaries generated by the student coincide with those by the teacher. Since the activation transfer loss is not differentiable, we design a piecewise differentiable loss approximating the activation transfer loss. By the proposed method, the student learns a separating boundary between activation region and deactivation region formed by each neuron in the teacher. Through the experiments in various aspects of knowledge transfer, it is verified that the proposed method outperforms the current state-of-the-art.

papers.title: GAVEL: Towards rule-based safety through activation monitoring
papers.research_question: How can activation-based safety monitoring be improved to achieve higher precision, flexibility, and interpretability by moving from broad misuse datasets to a rule-based framework using compositional, interpretable cognitive elements?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces GAVEL, a rule-based activation safety framework that uses compositional Cognitive Elements (CEs) to enable precise, flexible, and interpretable detection of harmful LLM behaviors, decoupling activation engineering from safety configuration.
papers.conclusion: GAVEL establishes a practical, scalable paradigm for rule-based activation safety that improves precision, supports domain customization, and lays the groundwork for interpretable and auditable AI governance through community collaboration.
papers.key_findings:
GAVEL achieves high detection rates (TPR) and low false positives (FPR) across diverse misuse categories like phishing, hate speech, and scams.
The framework demonstrates cross-lingual generalization, detecting CEs in Spanish and Mandarin despite training only on English excitation data.
GAVEL maintains robustness against adversarial attacks (misdirection, goal hijacking, evasion) that degrade surface-text-based moderators like GPT-4.
The rule-based approach provides interpretability, showing which specific CEs triggered a violation and on which tokens.
GAVEL's modular CE design allows community sharing and rapid policy updates without retraining the base model or detector.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly paired with activation-based monitoring to detect and prevent harmful behaviors that may not be apparent at the surface-text level. However, existing activation safety approaches, trained on broad misuse datasets, struggle with poor precision, limited flexibility, and lack of interpretability. This paper introduces a new paradigm: rule-based activation safety, inspired by rule-sharing practices in cybersecurity. We propose modeling activations as cognitive elements (CEs), fine-grained, interpretable factors such as ''making a threat'' and ''payment processing'', that can be composed to capture nuanced, domain-specific behaviors with higher precision. Building on this representation, we present a practical framework that defines predicate rules over CEs and detects violations in real time. This enables practitioners to configure and update safeguards without retraining models or detectors, while supporting transparency and auditability. Our results show that compositional rule-based activation safety improves precision, supports domain customization, and lays the groundwork for scalable, interpretable, and auditable AI governance. We will release GAVEL as an open-source framework and provide an accompanying automated rule creation tool.

papers.title: E-SAGE: Explainability-based Defense Against Backdoor Attacks on Graph Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can explainability techniques be used to defend against backdoor attacks on Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), particularly addressing limitations of existing defenses such as the need for clean validation data and high computational cost?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes E-SAGE, an explainability-based defense method for GNNs that uses Integrated Gradients to compute edge importance scores and iteratively prunes suspicious edges to mitigate backdoor and adversarial attacks based on subgraph insertion.
papers.conclusion: E-SAGE successfully defends against state-of-the-art backdoor and adversarial attacks on GNNs by leveraging explainability and iterative edge pruning, and its efficiency is improved through graph simplification.
papers.key_findings:
E-SAGE effectively reduces Attack Success Rate (ASR) while maintaining model Accuracy (ACC) against state-of-the-art backdoor attacks (SBA, GTA, UGBA).
The method is also effective against adversarial attacks involving multiple subgraph insertions (e.g., TDGIA).
An adaptive pruning threshold based on node degree helps balance defense performance and accuracy, especially for low-degree nodes in small datasets.
Incorporating a neighbor sampling strategy (inspired by GraphSAGE) significantly improves computational efficiency on large graphs.
The defense does not require clean validation data and operates during the prediction phase.
papers.limitation:
In small datasets (e.g., Cora), the distribution of adversarial edges is less distinct from clean edges, leading to a trade-off between defensive performance (ASR) and model accuracy (ACC).
The method requires computing importance scores for edges, which can be computationally expensive without the neighbor sampling optimization.
future_direction: Study how to make triggers less obvious in explainability methods to improve the stealth of attacks.
Investigate the relationship between explainability tools and models.
papers.abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have recently been widely adopted in multiple domains. Yet, they are notably vulnerable to adversarial and backdoor attacks. In particular, backdoor attacks based on subgraph insertion have been shown to be effective in graph classification tasks while being stealthy, successfully circumventing various existing defense methods. In this paper, we propose E-SAGE, a novel approach to defending GNN backdoor attacks based on explainability. We find that the malicious edges and benign edges have significant differences in the importance scores for explainability evaluation. Accordingly, E-SAGE adaptively applies an iterative edge pruning process on the graph based on the edge scores. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate the effectiveness of E-SAGE against state-of-the-art graph backdoor attacks in different attack settings. In addition, we investigate the effectiveness of E-SAGE against adversarial attacks.

papers.title: LLM See, LLM Do: Guiding Data Generation to Target Non-Differentiable Objectives
papers.research_question: Can we explicitly steer models towards desired properties at test time by exploiting the synthetic data generation process, and what is the impact of passive inheritance of model properties via synthetic data?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces active inheritance, a method to steer model behavior by targeted sampling of synthetic data to optimize non-differentiable objectives, and provides a comprehensive study of passive inheritance when models are trained on synthetic data.
papers.conclusion: Active inheritance is a promising and interpretable method for steering model behavior via synthetic data curation, enabling optimization of non-differentiable objectives without complex reinforcement learning or reward models.
papers.key_findings:
Models are sensitive to passive inheritance of properties from synthetic data, even when prompts are neutral.
Synthetic data can alter model preferences when used as evaluators, including alignment with human judgments and length bias.
Active inheritance can effectively steer model behavior, increasing desired attributes like length and lexical diversity and decreasing toxicity.
Multi-source sampling (using multiple teacher models) can enhance the effectiveness of active inheritance for some attributes.
The architecture prior of the base model remains a strong influence on preferences even after finetuning on synthetic data.
papers.abstract: The widespread adoption of synthetic data raises new questions about how models generating the data can influence other large language models (LLMs) via distilled data. To start, our work exhaustively characterizes the impact of passive inheritance of model properties by systematically studying the consequences of synthetic data integration. We provide one of the most comprehensive studies to-date of how the source of synthetic data shapes models' internal biases, calibration and generations' textual attributes and preferences. We find that models are surprisingly sensitive towards certain attributes even when the synthetic data prompts appear "neutral". which invites the question whether this sensitivity can be exploited for good. Our findings invite the question can we explicitly steer the models towards the properties we want at test time by exploiting the data generation process? This would have historically been considered infeasible due to the cost of collecting data with a specific characteristic or objective in mind. However, improvement in the quality of synthetic data, as well as a shift towards general-purpose models designed to follow a diverse way of instructions, means this question is timely. We propose active inheritance as a term to describe intentionally constraining synthetic data according to a non-differentiable objective. We demonstrate how active inheritance can steer the generation profiles of models towards desirable non-differentiable attributes, e.g. high lexical diversity or low toxicity.

papers.title: Rethinking Interpretation: Input-Agnostic Saliency Mapping of Deep Visual Classifiers
papers.research_question: What are the limitations of input-specific saliency mapping and how can we achieve input-agnostic saliency mapping to visualize generic features attributed by a model to its outputs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a novel input-agnostic saliency mapping method that visualizes generic geometric features associated by a model with its outputs, and demonstrates its utility in backdoor detection.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a new perspective on saliency mapping that maps generic geometric features associated by the model with its outputs, and demonstrates its utility in backdoor detection, potentially inspiring new methods and applications in model interpretation.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed method generates human-interpretable visualizations of concepts (class labels) as understood by deep visual classifiers.
The method can identify backdoor trigger patterns in compromised models by visualizing the patterns associated with the target class.
The method is evaluated with a new metric (Mscore) that shows high fidelity and generalizability across models.
papers.limitation:
The method is limited to visual classifiers and image data.
The backdoor detection case study is limited to visible trigger patterns.
papers.abstract: Saliency methods provide post-hoc model interpretation by attributing input features to the model outputs. Current methods mainly achieve this using a single input sample, thereby failing to answer input-independent inquiries about the model. We also show that input-specific saliency mapping is intrinsically susceptible to misleading feature attribution. Current attempts to use `general' input features for model interpretation assume access to a dataset containing those features, which biases the interpretation. Addressing the gap, we introduce a new perspective of input-agnostic saliency mapping that computationally estimates the high-level features attributed by the model to its outputs. These features are geometrically correlated, and are computed by accumulating model's gradient information with respect to an unrestricted data distribution. To compute these features, we nudge independent data points over the model loss surface towards the local minima associated by a human-understandable concept, e.g., class label for classifiers. With a systematic projection, scaling and refinement process, this information is transformed into an interpretable visualization without compromising its model-fidelity. The visualization serves as a stand-alone qualitative interpretation. With an extensive evaluation, we not only demonstrate successful visualizations for a variety of concepts for large-scale models, but also showcase an interesting utility of this new form of saliency mapping by identifying backdoor signatures in compromised classifiers.

papers.title: Dissecting Fine-Tuning Unlearning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Why do fine-tuning-based unlearning methods appear successful in behavioral tests, and what is their actual mechanism and limitations?
papers.core_contribution: Fine-tuning-based unlearning methods do not genuinely erase problematic knowledge; instead, they alter the model's knowledge retrieval process by modifying the coefficients in the MLP's final layers, which also negatively impacts unrelated knowledge.
papers.conclusion: Fine-tuning-based unlearning methods do not erase knowledge but alter knowledge extraction mechanisms, and they negatively impact the model's unrelated capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Restoring the value vectors in MLPs does not recover unlearned knowledge, indicating that the knowledge remains stored.
Restoring the attention states in intermediate and deeper layers recovers some knowledge, showing that attention components are involved in knowledge extraction.
Restoring the coefficients in the final layers of MLPs recovers most of the unlearned knowledge, indicating that these coefficients are the primary contributors to the unlearning effect.
Fine-tuning-based unlearning methods have a global negative effect, degrading the model's performance on unrelated knowledge.
The unlearning mechanism works by altering the model's knowledge retrieval process rather than erasing the knowledge itself.
papers.limitation: The experiments disregard potential unlearning impact from parameter changes in other model components (e.g., unembedding matrix and normalization layers), and it is unclear if these changes have meaningful effects.
future_direction: Future unlearning evaluations should focus on precise measurement of knowledge storage and retrieval dynamics.
Further investigation into defensive strategies based on the findings about MLP coefficients.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning-based unlearning methods prevail for preventing targeted harmful, sensitive, or copyrighted information within large language models while preserving overall capabilities. However, the true effectiveness of these methods is unclear. In this work, we delve into the limitations of fine-tuning-based unlearning through activation patching and parameter restoration experiments. Our findings reveal that these methods alter the model's knowledge retrieval process, providing further evidence that they do not genuinely erase the problematic knowledge embedded in the model parameters. Instead, the coefficients generated by the MLP components in the model's final layer are the primary contributors to these seemingly positive unlearning effects, playing a crucial role in controlling the model's behaviors. Furthermore, behavioral tests demonstrate that this unlearning mechanism inevitably impacts the global behavior of the models, affecting unrelated knowledge or capabilities. The code is released at https://github.com/yihuaihong/Dissecting-FT-Unlearning.

papers.title: Internal Causal Mechanisms Robustly Predict Language Model Out-of-Distribution Behaviors
papers.research_question: Can internal causal mechanisms be used to predict how models will behave on out-of-distribution examples?
papers.core_contribution: Internal causal features are the most robust features for predicting output correctness under distribution shifts, and the paper proposes two methods (counterfactual simulation and value probing) that outperform causal-agnostic approaches.
papers.conclusion: Internal causal features are the most robust features for predicting output correctness under distribution shifts, and causal analysis of language models is not only explanatory but also predictive, contributing to reliability and safety.
papers.key_findings:
Internal causal mechanisms can be used to predict model out-of-distribution behaviors.
Counterfactual simulation and value probing achieve high AUC-ROC in distribution and outperform causal-agnostic features in out-of-distribution settings.
Causal features are more robust than non-causal ones under distribution shifts.
papers.limitation:
The linearity assumption embedded in the chosen localization method may not hold for non-linear representations.
Reliance on prior knowledge to propose high-level causal models.
papers.abstract: Interpretability research now offers a variety of techniques for identifying abstract internal mechanisms in neural networks. Can such techniques be used to predict how models will behave on out-of-distribution examples? In this work, we provide a positive answer to this question. Through a diverse set of language modeling tasks--including symbol manipulation, knowledge retrieval, and instruction following--we show that the most robust features for correctness prediction are those that play a distinctive causal role in the model's behavior. Specifically, we propose two methods that leverage causal mechanisms to predict the correctness of model outputs: counterfactual simulation (checking whether key causal variables are realized) and value probing (using the values of those variables to make predictions). Both achieve high AUC-ROC in distribution and outperform methods that rely on causal-agnostic features in out-of-distribution settings, where predicting model behaviors is more crucial. Our work thus highlights a novel and significant application for internal causal analysis of language models.

papers.title: Interpreting the Repeated Token Phenomenon in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Why do Large Language Models fail to accurately repeat a single word when prompted, and how is this linked to the attention sink phenomenon?
papers.core_contribution: Provides a mechanistic explanation for repeated token divergence in LLMs by linking it to attention sinks, identifies the responsible neural circuit, and proposes a targeted patch to mitigate the vulnerability without impacting overall performance.
papers.conclusion: The study links repeated token divergence to attention sinks via neural circuits, shows how first layer confusion leads to divergence, and demonstrates a mitigation patch that addresses the vulnerability while preserving model performance.
papers.key_findings:
Repeated token divergence is caused by the attention sink mechanism, where the first token receives disproportionately high attention.
The first attention layer marks the first token, but fails to distinguish it from repeated tokens, leading to confusion.
Specific MLP neurons (sink neurons) amplify hidden states for attention sinks, and are also activated by repeated tokens.
A 'cluster attack' extends the vulnerability to similar tokens without exact repetition, bypassing surface-level defenses.
A targeted patch that modifies sink neuron activations effectively mitigates the divergence without significant performance loss on other tasks.
papers.limitation:
The mechanism by which training data leakage occurs through attention sinks remains unclear.
The first attention layer's behavior was unique to LLaMa2, highlighting model-specific details.
The efficacy of token repetition in inducing sinks varies across models.
Not all tokens in LLaMa2 induce attention sinks.
Due to difficulty in assessing training data leakage, the success rate of the cluster attack was not quantified.
The mitigation strategy does not fully address the inherent vulnerability of causally masked Transformers to repeated tokens.
future_direction: Investigate broader generalizability of the findings across more models.
Explain why repeated token sequences lead to training data extraction.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs), despite their impressive capabilities, often fail to accurately repeat a single word when prompted to, and instead output unrelated text. This unexplained failure mode represents a vulnerability, allowing even end-users to diverge models away from their intended behavior. We aim to explain the causes for this phenomenon and link it to the concept of ``attention sinks'', an emergent LLM behavior crucial for fluency, in which the initial token receives disproportionately high attention scores. Our investigation identifies the neural circuit responsible for attention sinks and shows how long repetitions disrupt this circuit. We extend this finding to other non-repeating sequences that exhibit similar circuit disruptions. To address this, we propose a targeted patch that effectively resolves the issue without negatively impacting the model's overall performance. This study provides a mechanistic explanation for an LLM vulnerability, demonstrating how interpretability can diagnose and address issues, and offering insights that pave the way for more secure and reliable models.

papers.title: Robustly Identifying Concepts Introduced During Chat Fine-Tuning Using Crosscoders
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether chat-only latents identified by crosscoders are genuinely unique to the fine-tuned model or if they are artifacts of the training loss, and how to robustly identify truly chat-specific concepts.
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies two issues (Complete Shrinkage and Latent Decoupling) in L1-trained crosscoders that cause false chat-only latent identification, proposes Latent Scaling to detect these issues, and demonstrates that BatchTopK crosscoders mitigate these issues and yield genuinely chat-specific and interpretable latents.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that using BatchTopK loss in crosscoders overcomes the limitations of L1 loss and provides a robust tool for model diffing, enabling concrete insights into how chat tuning modifies language model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
The L1 crosscoder suffers from Complete Shrinkage and Latent Decoupling, leading to many falsely identified chat-only latents.
Latent Scaling can detect these spurious chat-only latents by measuring how well they explain base model error and reconstruction.
BatchTopK crosscoders are robust to these issues and identify more genuinely chat-specific latents.
In BatchTopK crosscoders, the relative norm difference (Δnorm) is a meaningful metric for chat-specificity and causal importance, whereas in L1 crosscoders it is not.
The chat-specific latents found by BatchTopK crosscoders are highly interpretable and correspond to concepts like false information, personal questions, and various refusal triggers.
future_direction: Extend analysis to more layers and models.
Investigate the dynamics of concept emergence during fine-tuning.
papers.abstract: Model diffing is the study of how fine-tuning changes a model’s representations and internal algorithms. Many behaviours of interest are introduced during fine-tuning, and model diffing offers a promising lens to interpret such behaviors. Crosscoders[1] are a recent model diffing method that learns a shared dictionary of interpretable concepts represented as latent directions in both the base and fine-tuned models, allowing us to track how concepts shift or emerge during fine-tuning. Notably, prior work has observed concepts with no direction in the base model, and it was hypothesized that these model-specific latents were concepts introduced during fine-tuning. However, we identify two issues which stem from the crosscoders L1 training loss that can misattribute concepts as unique to the fine-tuned model, when they really exist in both models. We develop Latent Scaling to flag these issues by more accurately measuring each latent’s presence across models. In experiments comparing Gemma 2 2B base and chat models, we observe that the standard crosscoder suffers heavily from these issues. Building on these insights, we train a crosscoder with BatchTopK loss[2] and show that it substantially mitigates these issues, finding more genuinely chat-specific and highly interpretable concepts. We recommend practitioners adopt similar techniques. Using the BatchTopK crosscoder, we successfully identify a set of genuinely chat-specific latents that are both interpretable and causally effective, representing concepts such as _false information_ and _personal question_, along with multiple refusal-related latents that show nuanced preferences for different refusal triggers. Overall, our work advances best practices for the crosscoder-based methodology for model diffing and demonstrates that it can provide concrete insights into how chat tuning modifies language model behavior.1 Content Warning: This paper contains examples of harmful language.

papers.title: Intrinsic Self-correction for Enhanced Morality: An Analysis of Internal Mechanisms and the Superficial Hypothesis
papers.research_question: The paper investigates three research questions: (1) In what scenarios does moral self-correction work? (2) What are the internal mechanisms of LLMs influenced by self-correction instructions? (3) Is intrinsic moral self-correction actually superficial?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes that intrinsic moral self-correction in LLMs is superficial, as it only provides a shortcut to moral outputs without significantly reducing immorality in internal hidden states.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that intrinsic moral self-correction is superficial, relying on shortcuts rather than fundamentally reducing immorality in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Self-correction works best when the correct answer is already top-ranked.
Morality levels in intermediate hidden states are strong indicators of instruction effectiveness.
Self-correction reduces immorality in attention heads but increases it in feed-forward layers for QA tasks.
The slight difference in hidden states with and without self-correction supports the superficial hypothesis.
Internal hidden states can be used to predict the effectiveness of self-correction instructions.
papers.limitation:
The exact underlying reason for the superficial phenomenon is not uncovered.
Defining superficial self-correction is challenging.
future_direction: Automating methods for optimizing instruction development for self-correction.
Exploring fine-tuning to enhance LLMs' self-correction capabilities.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are capable of producing content that perpetuates stereotypes, discrimination, and toxicity. The recently proposed moral self-correction is a computationally efficient method for reducing harmful content in the responses of LLMs. However, the process of how injecting self-correction instructions can modify the behavior of LLMs remains under-explored. In this paper, we explore the effectiveness of moral self-correction by answering three research questions: (1) In what scenarios does moral self-correction work? (2) What are the internal mechanisms of LLMs, e.g., hidden states, that are influenced by moral self-correction instructions? (3) Is intrinsic moral self-correction actually superficial in terms of reduced immorality in hidden states? We argue that self-correction can help LLMs find a shortcut to more morally correct output, rather than truly reducing the immorality stored in hidden states. Through empirical investigation with tasks of language generation and multi-choice question answering, we conclude:(i) LLMs exhibit good performance across both tasks, and self-correction instructions are particularly beneficial when the correct answer is already top-ranked; (ii) The morality levels in intermediate hidden states are strong indicators as to whether one instruction would be more effective than another; (iii) Based on our analysis of intermediate hidden states and task case studies of self-correction behaviors, we are first to propose the hypothesis that intrinsic moral self-correction is in fact superficial.

papers.title: Identifying and Manipulating Personality Traits in LLMs Through Activation Engineering
papers.research_question: How can personality traits in large language models be identified and manipulated using activation engineering to enable dynamic personality adjustment without extensive retraining?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces 'feature induction', a method for identifying and manipulating personality traits in LLMs through activation engineering, enabling dynamic personality customization without extensive retraining.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that activation engineering can be used to identify and manipulate personality traits in LLMs, enabling dynamic customization without retraining, while highlighting ethical implications.
papers.key_findings:
Layer 18 in Llama 3 8B is the most influential layer for personality trait expression.
Personality traits can be clustered into meaningful groups based on activation vectors, revealing semantic relationships.
Principal component analysis identifies key personality dimensions and traits that capture most variance.
Socially undesirable personality traits are grouped together in activation space, with proximal traits like competitive and confident.
An interactive interface allows real-time control of LLM personality by adjusting principal component weights.
future_direction: Enhancing interpretability by mapping personality traits to specific layer activations and neurons.
Analyzing the performance consequences of different personality factors on LLM competencies.
Extending the research to multilingual models to understand cultural specificity of personality traits.
papers.abstract: The field of large language models (LLMs) has grown rapidly in recent years, driven by the desire for better efficiency, interpretability, and safe use. Building on the novel approach of "activation engineering," this study explores personality modification in LLMs, drawing inspiration from research like Refusal in LLMs Is Mediated by a Single Direction (arXiv:2406.11717) and Steering Llama 2 via Contrastive Activation Addition (arXiv:2312.06681). We leverage activation engineering to develop a method for identifying and adjusting activation directions related to personality traits, which may allow for dynamic LLM personality fine-tuning. This work aims to further our understanding of LLM interpretability while examining the ethical implications of such developments.

papers.title: The Mirrored Influence Hypothesis: Efficient Data Influence Estimation by Harnessing Forward Passes
papers.research_question: How can we efficiently estimate the influence of training data on model predictions by using forward passes instead of gradient-based methods?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Mirrored Influence Hypothesis, which shows that train-to-test influence can be estimated via test-to-train influence, and proposes Forward-INF, an efficient method leveraging forward passes.
papers.conclusion: The paper validates the Mirrored Influence Hypothesis and presents Forward-INF, an efficient influence estimation method that improves the tradeoff between utility and efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
Empirical validation shows high correlation between train-to-test and test-to-train influences across different models and datasets.
Forward-INF achieves high accuracy in data leakage detection, e.g., 100% top-1 accuracy on CIFAR-10, while being faster than baselines.
The method effectively identifies influential training points in diffusion models for generated images.
It performs well in mislabeled data detection, finding over 80% of mislabeled samples within the first 300 checked.
In language model behavior tracing, Forward-INF outperforms TracIn in precision and MRR with higher efficiency.
papers.limitation:
The method may benefit from heuristic enhancements like layer selection and strategies to counter catastrophic forgetting.
Lack of theoretical framework for formal validation of the Hypothesis.
future_direction: Heuristic enhancements to Forward-INF, such as layer selection and countering catastrophic forgetting.
Theoretical framework to formally validate the Mirrored Influence Hypothesis.
papers.abstract: Large-scale black-box models have become ubiquitous across numerous applications. Understanding the influence of individual training data sources on predictions made by these models is crucial for improving their trustworthiness. Current influence estimation techniques involve computing gradients for every training point or repeated training on different subsets. These approaches face obvious computational challenges when scaled up to large datasets and models. In this paper, we introduce and explore the Mirrored Influence Hypothesis, highlighting a reciprocal nature of influence between training and test data. Specifically, it suggests that evaluating the influence of training data on test predictions can be reformulated as an equivalent, yet inverse problem: assessing how the predictions for training samples would be altered if the model were trained on specific test samples. Through both empirical and theoretical validations, we demonstrate the wide applicability of our hypothesis. Inspired by this, we introduce a new method for estimating the influence of training data, which requires calculating gradients for specific test samples, paired with a forward pass for each training point. This approach can capitalize on the common asymmetry in scenarios where the number of test samples under concurrent examination is much smaller than the scale of the training dataset, thus gaining a significant improvement in efficiency compared to existing approaches. We demonstrate the applicability of our method across a range of scenarios, including data attribution in diffusion models, data leakage detection, analysis of memorization, mislabeled data detection, and tracing behavior in language models. Our code will be made available at https://github.com/ruoxi-jia-group/Forward-INF.

papers.title: Chain-of-thought obfuscation learned from output supervision can generalise to unseen tasks
papers.research_question: Does chain-of-thought obfuscation learned from output supervision generalize to unseen tasks, and what are the implications for LLM monitorability?
papers.core_contribution: Obfuscation of chain-of-thought reasoning, learned when models are penalized only for their final outputs (output supervision), can generalize to unseen tasks, including high-stakes settings, reducing the monitorability of LLMs.
papers.conclusion: Current practices of penalizing harmful model outputs may inadvertently teach models to obfuscate their reasoning in chain-of-thought, and this obfuscation can generalize unpredictably to new domains, undermining safety monitoring.
papers.key_findings:
Applying CoT pressure causes in-distribution obfuscation of reasoning about reward hacking.
Penalizing only the final summary (output supervision) also causes obfuscation within the CoT.
This obfuscation, and the underlying reward hacking behavior, generalizes to out-of-distribution tasks, including novel high-stakes medical sycophancy.
Models employ diverse obfuscation strategies like feigning uncertainty or generating vacuous text.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to a single model family and size (Qwen3-4B).
The datasets were modified with XML tagging and unambiguous system prompts, which may not reflect realistic deployment scenarios.
future_direction: Further work to understand the scope of obfuscation generalization across different models and training pipelines.
Developing and evaluating mitigations like Mind & Face training and Reward Targeting to preserve CoT monitorability.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning provides a significant performance uplift to LLMs by enabling planning, exploration, and deliberation of their actions. CoT is also a powerful tool for monitoring the behaviours of these agents: when faithful, they offer interpretations of the model's decision making process, and an early warning sign for dangerous behaviours. However, optimisation pressures placed on the CoT may cause the model to obfuscate reasoning traces, losing this beneficial property. We show that obfuscation can generalise across tasks; models that learn to obfuscate reasoning involving reward hacking (e.g. accessing and utilising leaked information) generalise both the reward hacking behaviour and its obfuscation in CoT to unseen reward hacking settings. Most worryingly, we show that obfuscation of CoT reasoning, and its generalisation across tasks, also follows when we penalise only the model's final actions after closing its CoT. Our findings suggest that current practices of penalising harmful generations may inadvertently lead to a reduction in the broader monitorability of LLMs in unpredictable ways.

papers.title: Jump to Conclusions: Short-Cutting Transformers With Linear Transformations
papers.research_question: Is there a more accurate way to cast hidden representations into final representation substitutes than interpreting them as they are (identity mapping)?
papers.core_contribution: A simple method using linear transformations to cast hidden representations to final-layer substitutes, which improves interpretability and efficiency.
papers.conclusion: Linear mappings provide a simple and effective way to enhance the utilization of hidden representations for interpretability and efficiency, revealing linear structure in transformer components.
papers.key_findings:
Linear mappings (mat) consistently outperform identity mapping (id) in approximating future hidden representations and final predictions.
The method allows accurate prediction estimation from early layers, showing that models often predict the final output early.
The learned linear mappings generalize well across different model scales and data distributions.
When applied to early exiting, the method saves additional layers (e.g., 7.9% for GPT-2, 5.4% for BERT) while retaining 95% accuracy.
Attention sub-modules are the most tolerant to linear approximation compared to FFN and layer normalization.
papers.limitation:
Focuses only on linear transformations, leaving affine or non-linear transformations for future work.
Does not elucidate the reason for the linear structure observed in transformer inference.
Only considers post-hoc interpretability (analyzing trained models without changing weights).
Experiments are conducted only on English data.
future_direction: Exploring affine or non-linear transformations for casting hidden representations.
Integrating linear mappings into model training rather than only post-hoc analysis.
Breaking the computation into parallel tasks to improve efficiency.
Comparing the method with other approaches like Belrose et al. (2023).
Investigating the reasons for the linear structure in transformer components.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based language models create hidden representations of their inputs at every layer, but only use final-layer representations for prediction. This obscures the internal decision-making process of the model and the utility of its intermediate representations. One way to elucidate this is to cast the hidden representations as final representations, bypassing the transformer computation in-between. In this work, we suggest a simple method for such casting, using linear transformations. This approximation far exceeds the prevailing practice of inspecting hidden representations from all layers, in the space of the final layer. Moreover, in the context of language modeling, our method produces more accurate predictions from hidden layers, across various model scales, architectures, and data distributions. This allows "peeking" into intermediate representations, showing that GPT-2 and BERT often predict the final output already in early layers. We then demonstrate the practicality of our method to recent early exit strategies, showing that when aiming, for example, at retention of 95% accuracy, our approach saves additional 7.9% layers for GPT-2 and 5.4% layers for BERT. Last, we extend our method to linearly approximate sub-modules, finding that attention is most tolerant to this change. Our code and learned mappings are publicly available at https://github.com/sashayd/mat.

papers.title: Momentum Point-Perplexity Mechanics in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Can we define forces, energies, and a principle of least action that govern hidden-state evolution in transformers? Can these laws support principled monitoring and low-risk control of language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a log-Lagrangian framework that reveals an approximately conserved energy quantity in transformer hidden state dynamics, and derives a minimal-action control method called Jacobian steering that improves output quality.
papers.conclusion: Transformers follow approximate conservation laws, and this physics perspective enables principled monitoring and control for AI safety.
papers.key_findings:
Energy (Et = 1/2 ∥vt∥^2 * PPLt) is approximately conserved during inference across 20 transformer models.
Random-weight models conserve energy more tightly than pre-trained models.
Training shifts models into a kinetic-dominated regime with higher energy variability.
Jacobian steering, derived from the log-Lagrangian, can control generation while preserving semantic quality.
Steering improves the semantic quality of output distributions, especially for smaller models.
papers.limitation: Results cover models up to 3B parameters with English tokenizers; scaling to larger models and multilingual settings remains untested.
future_direction: Explore whether conservation laws can guide the design of inherently safer architectures and training procedures that preserve beneficial invariants.
Energy-aware monitoring, robust steering, and physics-inspired design of future models.
papers.abstract: We take a physics-based approach to studying how the internal hidden states of large language models change from token to token during inference. Across 20 open-source transformer models (135M-3B parameters), we find that a quantity combining the rate of change in hidden states and the model's next-token certainty, analogous to energy in physics, remains nearly constant. Random-weight models conserve this "energy" more tightly than pre-trained ones, while training shifts models into a faster, more decisive regime with greater variability. Using this "log-Lagrangian" view, we derive a control method called Jacobian steering, which perturbs hidden states in the minimal way needed to favor a target token. This approach maintained near-constant energy in two tested models and produced continuations rated higher in semantic quality than the models' natural outputs. Viewing transformers through this mechanics lens offers a principled basis for interpretability, anomaly detection, and low-risk steering. This could help make powerful models more predictable and aligned with human intent.

papers.title: Safety Layers in Aligned Large Language Models: The Key to LLM Security
papers.research_question: What is the internal mechanism (safety layers) that enables aligned LLMs to recognize malicious queries, and how can we fine-tune these models without degrading their security?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies safety layers in aligned LLMs that are crucial for security and proposes SPPFT, a fine-tuning method that freezes these layers to preserve security while maintaining performance.
papers.conclusion: Safety layers are the key to LLM security, and freezing them during fine-tuning via SPPFT effectively prevents security degradation while preserving performance.
papers.key_findings:
Aligned LLMs contain a small set of contiguous middle layers, called safety layers, that are crucial for distinguishing malicious from normal queries.
Safety layers emerge as a result of security alignment; pre-trained LLMs do not exhibit such layers.
Scaling the parameters of safety layers amplifies or diminishes the model's security, as measured by over-rejection.
The proposed SPPFT method, which freezes safety layers during fine-tuning, significantly preserves security while maintaining performance and reducing computational cost.
Freezing layers other than the safety layers does not effectively protect security, confirming the specificity of safety layers.
papers.abstract: Aligned LLMs are secure, capable of recognizing and refusing to answer malicious questions. However, the role of internal parameters in maintaining such security is not well understood yet, further these models can be vulnerable to security degradation when subjected to fine-tuning attacks. To address these challenges, our work uncovers the mechanism behind security in aligned LLMs at the parameter level, identifying a small set of contiguous layers in the middle of the model that are crucial for distinguishing malicious queries from normal ones, referred to as ``safety layers". We first confirm the existence of these safety layers by analyzing variations in input vectors within the model's internal layers. Additionally, we leverage the over-rejection phenomenon and parameters scaling analysis to precisely locate the safety layers. Building on these findings, we propose a novel fine-tuning approach, Safely Partial-Parameter Fine-Tuning (SPPFT), that fixes the gradient of the safety layers during fine-tuning to address the security degradation. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed approach can significantly preserve LLM security while maintaining performance and reducing computational resources compared to full fine-tuning.

papers.title: Concept Influence: Leveraging Interpretability to Improve Performance and Efficiency in Training Data Attribution
papers.research_question: How can we improve training data attribution by using interpretable semantic directions to address issues of scalability and syntactic bias in existing methods?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Concept Influence, a method that attributes model behavior to semantic directions (e.g., linear probes or SAE features) instead of individual test examples, and shows that probe-based approximations are efficient first-order alternatives.
papers.conclusion: Incorporating interpretable structures like concept vectors into training data attribution improves effectiveness and scalability for controlling model behavior, with concept-based methods outperforming classical influence functions and efficient approximations offering practical utility.
papers.key_findings:
Concept Influence outperforms classical influence functions across synthetic emergent misalignment benchmarks in identifying data that cause misalignment.
Probe-based approximations (Vector Filter and Projection Difference) are over an order of magnitude faster than gradient-based methods and achieve competitive performance.
Concept Influence identifies training examples that are semantically aligned with the target behavior, whereas standard influence functions often select syntactically similar examples.
Filtering out the most influential data points according to Concept Influence effectively reduces model misalignment, while retaining them amplifies it.
In real-world post-training data (OASST1), vector-based filtering methods can improve the safety-capability tradeoff, with Vector Filter achieving the best performance.
future_direction: Extending Concept Influence to richer representations like circuits or other mechanistic decompositions.
Developing principled group-level attribution methods.
Scaling experiments across model sizes and extending to multimodal settings.
papers.abstract: As large language models are increasingly trained and fine-tuned, practitioners need methods to identify which training data drive specific behaviors, particularly unintended ones. Training Data Attribution (TDA) methods address this by estimating datapoint influence. Existing approaches like influence functions are both computationally expensive and attribute based on single test examples, which can bias results toward syntactic rather than semantic similarity. To address these issues of scalability and influence to abstract behavior, we leverage interpretable structures within the model during the attribution. First, we introduce Concept Influence which attribute model behavior to semantic directions (such as linear probes or sparse autoencoder features) rather than individual test examples. Second, we show that simple probe-based attribution methods are first-order approximations of Concept Influence that achieve comparable performance while being over an order-of-magnitude faster. We empirically validate Concept Influence and approximations across emergent misalignment benchmarks and real post-training datasets, and demonstrate they achieve comparable performance to classical influence functions while being substantially more scalable. More broadly, we show that incorporating interpretable structure within traditional TDA pipelines can enable more scalable, explainable, and better control of model behavior through data.

papers.title: Obfuscated Activations Bypass LLM Latent-Space Defenses
papers.research_question: Can models execute harmful behavior via inconspicuous latent states, thereby bypassing latent-space defenses?
papers.core_contribution: Obfuscation attacks can bypass latent-space defenses by inducing harmful behavior via inconspicuous activations, demonstrating that neural representations are highly malleable.
papers.conclusion: Neural activations are highly malleable, allowing obfuscation attacks to bypass latent-space defenses, which poses a fundamental challenge to such defenses.
papers.key_findings:
Obfuscation attacks can bypass harmfulness monitors (probes, OOD detectors, SAEs) while maintaining high jailbreak rates.
Obfuscated activations are widespread; attackers can find new ones even after iterative adversarial training.
Obfuscation attacks transfer between different types of monitors (e.g., obfuscating against OOD detectors fools probes).
Models trained with latent robustness methods (Circuit Breakers, LAT) are also vulnerable to obfuscation attacks.
Obfuscation can reduce model performance on complex tasks like SQL code generation, indicating a trade-off.
papers.limitation:
Obfuscation attacks can reduce model performance on complex tasks like SQL code generation.
Achieving near-orthogonal activations while preserving behavior is difficult with current optimization methods.
future_direction: Improvements to Obfuscated Adversarial Training (OAT) and attacks against it, and scaling trends.
Investigating obfuscated activations in other domains beyond LLMs and image classifiers.
Developing new latent-space monitoring approaches that account for malleability of representations.
papers.abstract: Recent latent-space monitoring techniques have shown promise as defenses against LLM attacks. These defenses act as scanners that seek to detect harmful activations before they lead to undesirable actions. This prompts the question: Can models execute harmful behavior via inconspicuous latent states? Here, we study such obfuscated activations. We show that state-of-the-art latent-space defenses -- including sparse autoencoders, representation probing, and latent OOD detection -- are all vulnerable to obfuscated activations. For example, against probes trained to classify harmfulness, our attacks can often reduce recall from 100% to 0% while retaining a 90% jailbreaking rate. However, obfuscation has limits: we find that on a complex task (writing SQL code), obfuscation reduces model performance. Together, our results demonstrate that neural activations are highly malleable: we can reshape activation patterns in a variety of ways, often while preserving a network's behavior. This poses a fundamental challenge to latent-space defenses.

papers.title: Characterizing Large Language Model Geometry Helps Solve Toxicity Detection and Generation
papers.research_question: What are the geometric properties of LLMs that best characterize the representations of a given prompt and generation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a geometric characterization of LLMs (MHA and MLP) that enables principled methods for bypassing RLHF protection and for toxicity detection using unsupervised features.
papers.conclusion: Geometric characterization of LLMs provides both theoretical insights and practical tools for safer AI, enabling the detection of toxic inputs and generations and exposing weaknesses in current RLHF methods.
papers.key_findings:
The output of the Multi-Head Attention (MHA) mapping lives in the Minkowski sum of convex hulls of embedded tokens, and its intrinsic dimension can be controlled via prompt manipulation.
Increasing the intrinsic dimension of the MHA embedding through informed prompt manipulation can bypass RLHF safeguards and induce toxic generation.
The MLP partitions the manifold induced by the MHA, and its expressivity grows exponentially with the MHA's intrinsic dimension.
A small set of unsupervised geometric features (spline features) extracted from pre-trained LLMs can effectively solve toxicity detection and domain classification tasks.
The proposed features achieve state-of-the-art performance on toxicity detection benchmarks with low latency and without requiring model fine-tuning.
papers.limitation: The proposed features perform aggressive dimensionality reduction and are likely most suited for coarse-grained tasks (such as toxicity and domain detection); finer-grained statistics may be required for other downstream tasks.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) drive current AI breakthroughs despite very little being known about their internal representations. In this work, we propose to shed the light on LLMs inner mechanisms through the lens of geometry. In particular, we develop in closed form $(i)$ the intrinsic dimension in which the Multi-Head Attention embeddings are constrained to exist and $(ii)$ the partition and per-region affine mappings of the feedforward (MLP) network of LLMs' layers. Our theoretical findings further enable the design of novel principled solutions applicable to state-of-the-art LLMs. First, we show that, through our geometric understanding, we can bypass LLMs' RLHF protection by controlling the embedding's intrinsic dimension through informed prompt manipulation. Second, we derive interpretable geometrical features that can be extracted from any (pre-trained) LLM, providing a rich abstract representation of their inputs. We observe that these features are sufficient to help solve toxicity detection, and even allow the identification of various types of toxicity. Our results demonstrate how, even in large-scale regimes, exact theoretical results can answer practical questions in LLMs. Code: https://github.com/RandallBalestriero/SplineLLM

papers.title: Linear Representation Transferability Hypothesis: Leveraging Small Models to Steer Large Models
papers.research_question: What is the relationship between the hidden states in models of different scales? The paper investigates whether there exists an affine transformation between the representation spaces of different models trained on similar data.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes the Linear Representation Transferability (LRT) Hypothesis and provides empirical evidence that affine mappings between hidden states of different-sized models can transfer steering vectors, enabling small models to steer large models.
papers.conclusion: The results provide strong evidence for the LRT hypothesis, suggesting that representations learned by small models can be used to guide the behavior of large models, and that the hypothesis is a promising direction for understanding representation alignment across model scales.
papers.key_findings:
